title.rendered: A Deliciously Devilish Romp: “Point Loma” Serves Up Retro Horror

content.rendered:
This Off-Broadway horror comedy delivers campy 1950s thrills in NYC’s Black Box theater scene.

Manhattan Repertory Theatre has struck theatrical gold with Tim Mulligan‘s wickedly entertaining “Point Loma,” a gleefully campy horror spoof that channels the best of 1950s B-movie schlock while delivering genuine scares and belly laughs in equal measure. Under Ken Wolf’s spirited direction, this off-Broadway gem transforms the intimate black box space of the Chain Theatre into a haunted playground where paranormal podcasters meet their match in a sinister San Diego hospice house.

Plot and Premise: Podcasters Meet Paranormal Terror

Mulligan’s script is a love letter to classic horror tropes, filtering them through a contemporary lens of true-crime podcasting culture. The story follows Chad (Parker Jenkins), an earnest night-shift nurse caring for a comatose patient named Hank in a historic Point Loma home, and the chaos that ensues when paranormal investigators from the podcast “Ghosting” arrive to document the supernatural activity that has been terrorizing the day and night nurses. What begins as a seemingly straightforward ghost hunt spirals into a deliriously entertaining revelation about the house’s murderous past.

L-R: Jevon Nicholson, Michelle Park, Mathew Hernandez (foreground), Ian Brady, and Parker Jenkins in Point Loma at the Chain Theatre. Photo by Chris Bentley

Outstanding Cast Performances Anchor the Supernatural Mayhem

Leading Performances Drive the Horror-Comedy Balance

Jenkins brings a perfect blend of vulnerability and determination to Chad, grounding the increasingly absurd proceedings with genuine human emotion. His chemistry with Ian Brady’s exuberant boyfriend Todd provides the production’s emotional anchor, while Brady’s infectious enthusiasm for all things supernatural delivers some of the evening’s biggest laughs. Their relationship feels authentic even amid the supernatural mayhem, giving weight to the stakes when things turn chiller theater deadly.

Paranormal Investigation Team Delivers Podcast-Perfect

Parker Jenkins as Chad and Jessica Luhmann as Anna in Point Loma at the Chain Theatre. Photo by Chris Bentley

The paranormal investigation team proves equally compelling. Jevon Nicholson’s Rick perfectly captures the self-important bravado of a podcast host, while Michelle Park’s Kim brings depth to what could have been a stereotypical goth medium character. Mathew Hernandez rounds out the trio as Carl, the perpetually terrified cameraman whose reactions to the escalating horror provide consistent comic relief.

Supporting Cast Elevates the Ensemble Work

Jessica Luhmann deserves particular praise as Anna, the day-shift nurse whose wine-fueled breakdown and ultimate heroism steal several scenes. Luhmann navigates the character’s journey from professional competence to frazzled desperation to wine-bottle-wielding savior with impressive range and impeccable comic timing.

Dave Silberger‘s Hank is a masterclass in misdirection. For most of the evening, he lies comatose in his hospital bed, a seemingly helpless figure who gradually reveals himself as the production’s most chilling antagonist. Silberger’s transformation from invalid to serial killer is genuinely unsettling, providing the horror backbone that keeps the comedy from becoming purely frivolous. And the surprise ending with Silberger? Well, you’ll have to see for yourself.

Chelsea Clark, Nathan Cusson, and Patricia Griffith’s ensemble work as various ghostly manifestations adds layers of atmospheric dread. Their haunting presence throughout the production creates a practical sense of otherworldly menace that flawlessly complements the script’s blend of scares, moans, and laughs.

Immersive Staging Transforms Theater Into Haunted Experience

Director Ken Wolf’s Innovative Use of Black Box Theater Space

Wolf’s direction proves particularly ingenious in using the Chain Theatre’s intimate space to create a truly immersive theatrical experience. Rather than confining the action to the traditional stage area, the production transforms the entire venue into a haunted environment. Ghostly figures materialize from behind unsuspecting audience members, creating genuine jolts of surprise that ripple through the theater.

Jevon Nicholson as Rick and Michelle Park as Kim in Point Loma at the Chain Theatre. Photo by Chris Bentley

Audience Becomes Part of the Paranormal Investigation

The paranormal investigators enter through the house aisles, their green-lit flashlights cutting through the darkness as they navigate between rows of spectators who suddenly find themselves part of the investigation. Most memorably, supernatural manifestations appear directly in front of the front row, placing audience members mere inches from the otherworldly action. This proximity creates an electric tension that no traditional staging could achieve – viewers become unwitting participants in the séances and supernatural encounters rather than passive observers.

Breaking the Fourth Wall With Supernatural Encounters

The effect is genuinely disorienting and thrilling when ghostly voices echo from various points throughout the theater space. This immersive approach expertly balances the production’s tonal shifts, never allowing the horror elements to overwhelm the comedy or vice versa. The pacing builds momentum steadily through the first act’s establishing scenes to the séance centerpiece and the explosive final confrontation.

Technical Excellence Enhances the Horror-Comedy Experience

Lighting Design Creates Atmospheric Mood Shifts

The technical elements deserve special recognition. The lighting design creates an appropriately moody atmosphere that can shift from cozy domesticity to spine-tingling terror at a moment’s notice while accommodating the challenges of illuminating action throughout the audience space. Particularly effective are the sequences involving supernatural manifestations, where shadows and strategic illumination create genuine unease without relying on cheap jump scares, whether occurring on stage or emerging from the theater’s periphery.

R-L: Ian Brady as Todd and Parker Jenkins as Chad in Point Loma at the Chain Theatre. Photo by Chris Bentley

Sound Design Delivers Immersive Audio Landscape

The sound design proves equally crucial to the production’s success. From the eerie creaks and unexplained thuds that plague Chad’s night shifts to the ghostly voices emanating from Bluetooth speakers and séance trumpets positioned throughout the space, the audio landscape creates an immersive haunted house experience. With its deliciously retro sensibility reminiscent of classic horror film composers, the musical underscoring perfectly captures the B-movie aesthetic Mulligan and Wolf are clearly celebrating while enhancing the feeling that supernatural forces have invaded the entire theater.

Why “Point Loma” Works: Affectionate Horror Homage Meets Contemporary Relevance

What makes “Point Loma” particularly successful is its affection for its source material and characters. Rather than simply mocking horror conventions, Mulligan’s script embraces them while finding fresh angles through the podcast framing device. The play’s exploration of how we consume true crime and paranormal content feels timely without being heavy-handed.

The immersive staging elevates this material beyond traditional theatrical boundaries. When audience members share space with living characters and supernatural entities, the fourth wall doesn’t just break – it dissolves. This creates a unique theatrical experience where the line between performer and audience, reality and supernatural fiction, becomes thrillingly blurred.

Parker Jenkins as Chad and Jessica Luhmann as Anna in Point Loma at the Chain Theatre. Photo by Chris Bentley

Final Verdict: Must-See Off-Broadway Entertainment

“Point Loma” succeeds as both a loving homage and an effective horror-comedy in its own right. Manhattan Repertory Theatre has delivered a thoroughly entertaining production that will satisfy horror aficionados and newcomers. In a theatrical landscape often dominated by heavy drama, this delightfully demented romp offers pure, unapologetic fun—exactly what off-Broadway theater should provide. It is enhanced by an immersive staging concept that makes every seat in the house feel like the front row of a supernatural encounter.

Wolf clearly understands that effective horror-comedy requires treating both elements seriously, and his cast follows suit with performances that never wink at the audience, even when they’re performing literally within touching distance of patrons. For theater lovers seeking an innovative, entertaining escape into the deliciously macabre, “Point Loma” delivers thrills, chills, and laughs equally.

A Deliciously Devilish Romp: “Point Loma” Serves Up Retro Horror

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Lunar Eclipse is a mild investigation into a decades old marriage that still has some mystery left in the saddlebags.  Reed Birney as George and Lisa Emery as Em imbue every ounce of their considerable talents into their characters.  It is not quite enough to make this production soar.

Donald Margulies has written a story that, at first glance, is chock-a-block full of metaphors and symbolism. Set in Western Kentucky, it is the night of a lunar eclipse.  The eclipse offers lessons in life, continuity, time – all the biggies.  They can look back on the passage of time reflected in their decades old relationship and look up at the moon and see time passing in the here and now.  There is mystery in the past and the present and certainly the future.  They live on the farm founded by George’s ancestors.  These two are the last generation. George and Em have two adopted children.  Tim is dead and was always a problem.  Marianne turned out okay but she lives far away.

Instead of digging deep into the various rabbit holes presented by the circumstances, Margulies chooses to skirt these and stick to what is in front of us.  These two are officially on each other’s nerves and yet still hopeful that a night in the company of a lunar eclipse might bring them some reassurance that they are not doomed to wither away while the other watches.

Most of what they do feels like chit-chat.  She is col.  He is not.  She feels guilty that she never gave him a child.  He admits he would have been okay with a dog or two or three.  There is no single issue that, when revealed, shows itself to be above all others.  And, funny thing –  the phases of the eclipse are very much part of the opening moments, but the progress fades out of the conversation about halfway through and is only indicated by the signage projected on an upstage scrim.

There is no, “ok it is almost over so I need to say this now,” moments.  There is no urgency.

And maybe there doesn’t have to be. Perhaps this is what Margulies was trying to say.  Maybe it is enough that these two old-ish folks are spending a night in the light of the silvery moon with no agenda other than to sit this one out.  It is, after all, reminiscent of how they first spent time together as teenagers.  Alone on a clear night with the stars to keep them company.

I wish there had been more “there” there, because these two actors are clearly up to the bit. I am sure of thief because as mild mannered as the text was, Birney and Emery made us believe that these two were the real deal.  As performers and characters their bond is mighty.  And that, my friends, is pretty much the whole deal.

LUNAR ECLIPSE by Donald Margulies, directed by Kate Whoriskey (Clyde’s, Sweat).

WITH Reed Birney and Lisa Emery

Scenic design by Walt Spangler, costume design by Jennifer Moeller, lighting design by Amith Chandrashaker, sound design by Sinan Refik Zafar, video design by S. Katy Tucker, and original music by Grace Mclean.

Therogh June 22 at The Irene Diamond Stage at The Pershing Square Signature Center (480 West 42ndStreet). Single tickets are currently on sale at 2ST.com.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Stop reading and make a reservatioin for this spectacular event. Atlantic Stage II.

We wil lwait.

Welcome back.

A FREEKY INTRODUCTION – Don’t let the title fool you.  The only thing freeky about “A Freeky Introduction” is the astonishing amount of love, smarts and hope that one person – NSangou Njikam (Freeky Dee) – can fit into one tight 85 minutes, never mind one theatre.  With the aid of his DJ and sidekick DJ Monday Blue Njikam leaps onto the stage and into our hearts.  You don’t have a chance to deny him, because he is that slick.  The deed is done before  you realize it. S-L-I-C-K!!!

In the script he describes himself thusly – FREEKY DEE- half Man, half Amazing. A mix of Esu, Signifying Monkey, comedian, minister, poet and Emcee. 

After being welcomed musically by DJ Monday Blue (she is the musical guide extraordinaire) Freeky Dee begins with a parable about an eagle who thought he was a vulture.  Next up he tells us his purpose:

“By Divine Decree, I am sent here to satirize, paro-dize, and mytho-size all up and down your thighs. “

And THAT is only the half of it.  Freeky Dee doles out wisdom non-stop.  Honestly I cannot tell you too much more than that because we, the audience, took an oath to keep our Freek learning to ourselves, and only share it by the deeds we do as part of our Freek Training.

Let me tell you it was something we leapt at.  Freeky Dee is part griot, part snake charmer, part Three Card Monte dealer and part Shell Game aficionado.  The difference is that when he is in charge, everybody wins.  Even he wins when he shares the story of a mythical love that changed his life (as his father predicted).  Because of his downfall he was sent out into the world to preach the good news.

Which is this: EVERYONE has a FREEK (not FREAK) inside them.  And handing the wheel over to that entity might be the best thing you can do.  It is the ultimate guide.  FREEK is a combination of all your best bits, your lightbulb moments, your hunches, your lessons turned to blessings, the seed of destiny in every choice.

ALL THAT.  And NSangou Njika is your Tour Guide Supreme.

And don’t bother looking FREEKY up in AI because I tried that.

Instead get yourself over to Atlantic Stage II.

A FREEKY INTRODUCTION, written by and starring NSangou Njika, directed by Dennis A. Allen II

WITH  DJ Monday Blue.

Sets by Jason Ardizzone-West, costumes by U-U Bakr, lighting by Sim Carpenter, sound design by G Clausen, movement by Jill Vallery, and mural art by Dister Rondon

Through June 22

title.rendered: Billy Stritch and Gabrielle Stravelli Set Birdland Ablaze

content.rendered:
By Ed Kliszus

Electric Chemistry and Musical Mastery happen when two jazz virtuosos become one Musical force. And sometimes, the joint is truly jumpin’, and tonight was unquestionably one of those magical evenings at Birdland Jazz Club in New York City. The legendary venue bore witness to the extraordinary musical and romantic artistry of vocalist Gabrielle Stravelli and singer-pianist Billy Stritch, two masters whose combined talents created what can only be described as musical alchemy.

Tonight wasn’t merely a performance—it was a testament to what happens when two consummate artists, each formidable in their own right, unite to create something greater than the sum of their parts. As The Front Row Center noted about their previous collaboration, “Stritch and Stravelli have been touched by the same divine creative inspiration as Mel and Ella.”

The Art of Musical Chemistry: A Dynamic Duo in Perfect Synchrony

The evening’s magic began when Stritch and Stravelli took the stage, and it was immediately evident that their partnership exemplifies what jazz collaboration should be. Their interaction and audience rapport drove the romantic narrative throughout the night’s sets with sparkling charm, creating an atmosphere where music became conversation and conversation became art.

Billy Stritch. Courtesy billystritch.com

When Stravelli introduced her cleverly curated set of “revenge songs” by Willie Nelson—appropriately dubbed “The Karma Medley” featuring tracks like “Blame it On the Times” and “Little Old Fashioned Karma”—the audience erupted in knowing chuckles and affirmations. This playful moment perfectly encapsulated the duo’s ability to balance sophistication with accessibility and humor with heart.

Billy Stritch: The Keyboard Virtuoso Who Defines Musical Excellence

Accompanied by the exceptional rhythm section of Pat O’Leary on bass and Mark McLean on drums, the evening showcased why Billy Stritch is one of the musical artists of this generation. The Grammy-winning artist, who spent 25 years as Liza Minnelli’s musical director and has toured with Tony Bennett, brought his characteristic blend of technical mastery and emotional intelligence to every number.

Stritch’s piano work throughout the evening demonstrated the sophisticated harmonic sensibilities that have made him a legend. From the opening up-tempo blues that rocked the house to his nuanced accompaniment during intimate ballads, his musical leadership was commanding and supportive—the mark of a true collaborator.

Gabrielle Stravelli: A Voice That Transcends Genres and Expectations

Vocal Chameleon with Unparalleled Versatility

If Billy Stritch is the evening’s architectural foundation, Gabrielle Stravelli is its soaring spire. Her performance tonight exemplified what Opening Night Online described as her ability to “reshape every tune to reflect her distinct artistic fingerprint.” Stravelli possesses that rare gift of being able to customize her sound not just to fit the music but to transform it entirely. Moreover, she’s authentic, personal, and relatable.

Stravelli’s vocal arsenal proved limitless throughout the evening. During the opening blues, she belted with a rich, textured fullness that could command any room, spinning dizzying scat lines demonstrating technical prowess and intuitive musicality. Yet when the moment called for subtlety—as in her elegant, tasteful rendition of “Close to You”—she shifted effortlessly to gentle, coaxing tones that The New York Times once described as having “a confidence and playfulness that recalled Ella Fitzgerald in her prime.”

Gabrielle Stravelli. Photo by Jenny Anderson

The Art of Musical Conversation: Trading Fire and Finesse

The duo’s scat trading throughout the evening revealed the depth of their musical relationship. Each exchange felt like a conversation between old friends—playful, supportive, and endlessly creative. Stritch responded to Stravelli’s blues fire with his piano pyrotechnics, and when she soared into harmonic territory, he was right there to catch her and lift her higher.

A Journey Through Musical Time: Song Selection and Storytelling

From Standards to Hidden Gems: Curating the American Songbook

The evening’s repertoire demonstrated both artists’ deep understanding of the American Songbook’s breadth and beauty. Their interpretation of Jule Styne’s “Just in Time” showcased their ability to reimagine familiar material, beginning as a rich ballad before seamlessly transitioning into an up-tempo showcase of their combined firepower.

Michel LeGrand’s “Watch What Happens,” presented in a medium Latin groove, allowed the band to trade solos and explore the song’s harmonic possibilities. This choice reflected both artists’ understanding that outstanding jazz performance is more about creating space for spontaneity than executing predetermined arrangements.

Intimate Moments and Emotional Landscapes

Stravelli’s interpretation of “Close to You”—the Burt Bacharach classic made famous by The Carpenters—became the evening’s emotional centerpiece. As The Front Row Center previously noted, her expressive qualities create “a calming ambiance” while showcasing her “lovely and strong” vocals. She gently coaxed and coddled the lyrics, supported by Stritch’s gentle piano poetry, creating an intimate moment in the packed club.

Musical Mentorship and Artistic Legacy

The Everly Brothers Inspiration: When Dreams Take Flight

One of the evening’s most enchanting sequences came when Stritch switched stylistic gears with his version of The Drifters’ “Up On the Roof,” which flowed seamlessly into an Everly Brothers-inspired medley exploring a theme of dreaming. Opening with the rock classic “All I Have to Do Is Dream” and concluding with Henry Mancini’s “Dreamsville,” the sequence had audience members practically swooning as the duo worked their collaborative magic.

This section particularly highlighted Stritch’s role as both performer and curator—his deep knowledge of American popular music allows him to create thematic connections that feel inevitable and surprising.

Gabrielle Stravelli. Courtesy SoapBox Gallery. Photo by Lynn Redmile

Cy Coleman: A Master’s Tribute to a Master

A particularly charming medley of Cy Coleman ballads, including “The Rules of the Road,” “I’m Going to Laugh You Right Out of My Life,” and an unpublished gem titled “Write Me a Letter To Read When It’s Over,” demonstrated both artists’ commitment to preserving and revitalizing the works of great songwriters. This segment showcased their role as musical archaeologists, bringing lesser-known treasures to contemporary audiences.

The Grand Finale: Imagination and Reality Intertwined

As the evening drew to a close, the duo presented a medley entitled “Get It Together” that epitomized their artistic vision. Beginning with “Pure Imagination” from Willy Wonka and flowing into John Lennon’s “Imagine” before circling back to “Pure Imagination,” the arrangement was both ambitious and profoundly moving. Amazing. Heartwarming. Transcendent.

The Mel and Ella Legacy: Swing That Electrifies

As part of their ongoing “Mel and Ella Swing Show,” Stritch and Stravelli performed a medley featuring “I Hear Music,” “Fascinating Rhythm,” and “Lady Be Good.” This selection proved electrifying, showcasing rich harmonies, cinematic scat work, and another demonstration of Stritch’s solid piano foundation supporting Stravelli’s remarkable gift for “coloring and tailoring her sound at will.”

As The Front Row Center observed about their Mel and Ella collaboration, “Stravelli is tiny in stature, but her vocal range is Mount Everest. She hits magical, unreachable notes that just blew us away with her immense talent.”

Standing Ovation Worthy: The Audience’s Verdict

The packed, standing-room-only crowd’s response told the complete story. The audience’s endless accolades culminated in an extended standing ovation that seemed to surprise even these seasoned performers. In an era where live music competes with countless digital distractions, Stritch and Stravelli proved that nothing can replace the magic of witnessing master artists at the peak of their powers.

Billy Stritch. Courtesy billystritch.com

The Bottom Line: Essential Viewing for Jazz Lovers

Audiences should experience Billy Stritch and Gabrielle Stravelli in duo or solo performances whenever possible. As tonight proved conclusively, you can’t get too much of a good thing—especially when that “thing” represents the highest levels of musical artistry, emotional intelligence, and pure, unadulterated joy.

Their partnership embodies everything that makes jazz America’s most significant cultural export: spontaneity, sophistication, soul, and the magical alchemy that occurs when exceptional artists trust each other completely. In a world that often feels divided, Stritch and Stravelli remind us that harmony, both musical and human, remains not just possible but transcendent.

For more Billy Stritch and Gabrielle Stravelli coverage, visit The Front Row Center and Opening Night Online.

Billy Stritch and Gabrielle Stravelli Set Birdland Ablaze

Birdland Jazz Club

315 West 44th Street
New York, NY 10036
(212) 581-3080

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

“I’m going to make each strand of your hair into an instrument. Your hair will stand on end as it plays my music and become a hair orchestra. It will fly you up into the sky.”

Sarah Ruhl’s Eurydice is a poetic net capturing the sorrow and magic felt when simultaneously falling in love with a partner while grieving a beloved. This play digs into grief: how it reemerges, tugs on us, prevents us from moving forward.

The opening scene grounds us in time and in young Eurydice (Maya Hawke) and Orpheus’s (Caleb Eberhardt) harmonious love. Ruhl gives us a fresh, modern take on this myth from Eurydice’s perspective.

Photo by HanJie Chow

On Eurydice’s wedding day, we meet her deceased father (Brian d’Arcy James), residing in the Underworld. He is one of the only residents of The Underworld that remember his past and how to write.

“But a wedding is for a father and a daughter. They stop being married to each other on that day.”

Rather than watching the moment Eurydice is united with Orpheus at the alter, we see Father with his elbow hinged, imagining walking down the aisle with his daughter.

Eurydice is drawn to the “interesting” aspects of life: interesting characters and arguments. A Nasty Interesting Man/The Lord of the Underworld (T. Ryder Smith) appears outside Eurydice’s wedding, whisking her away with the temptation of a letter from her father. The Man loses control and puts on a pleading, pathetic, and horrific performance for Eurydice to leave Orpheus, the man who only thinks of music, and choose him. The Man writhes on the ground, contorting his body, morphing into a more visibly conniving, evil version of himself. He resembles Voldemort, wriggling on the ground once he’s been reduced to a child-like form….which IS what The Man as he trades a tricycle for platforms to show his “growth.”

Photo by HanJie Chow

When Eurydice tries to escape, she falls into the Underworld.

The doors of an elevator part and there she is, umbrella in one hand, empty suitcase in another. The deep, resonant sound of rain drops colliding with her umbrella, the high-pitched echoes of the water splashing onto the floor, pouring into the grates. Moments when sound alone shifts one tone, one scene, into another highlights Ruhl’s ability to seamlessly allow poetry to guide the play. The projection of sound is one technical piece that carried Eurydice‘s production from remarkable to unforgettable. The incredible projection of the actors on stage, without microphones, especially considering Hawke’s debut Off-Broadway performance.

The chorus of Stones, composed of Maria Elena Ramirez (Loud Stone), Jon Norman Schneider (Little Stone), David Ryan Smith (Big Stone), observe and police those who enter the Underworld, ensuring that nobody cries, that nobody remembers their pasts.  The sing-songy unified trio keep us as on edge as they do Eurydice. They remind that death should be silent.

Photo by HanJie Chow

Characters are balanced in their presence on stage, which I think is quite the feat with the Chorus of Stones and The Lord of the Underworld filling just as much space as Eurydice and her beloveds. Grounded in Greek mytholgy, Euydice is set in the 1950’s, as highlighted by the music; the costuming is loosely antiquated. The set is simple and beautifully abstract. Letters written from Eurydice’s Father flower the walls; he has no idea how to reach Eurydice. His untimely death leaves his young daughter father-less for her wedding day.

Photo by HanJie Chow

Orpheus’s song of Eurydice take him into the Underworld to find his wife. Whether you’ve seen another adaptation, you should be curious to see how Eurydice will navigate her emotional pulls, and whether the couple’s love and commitment to each other will carry them away from the gates of Hell together–or if they’ll be eternally lost, destined to be dipped into the River of Forgetfulness.

This rich production gives us a classic myth through a cohesive, impassioned cast, making this story timeless and real. What would you sacrifice for an eternity with a parent lost too soon? How far would you go for someone you love? While this may be a very similar recreation of Ruhl’s 2004 Eurydice adaptation, Les Waters has returned to direct this production over 20 years later. It is memorable and it works.

After Ruhl’s 2023 production of Letters to Max and her 2024 production of Orlando, Eurydice is the concluding piece of her residency at Signature.

Written by Sarah Ruhl; Directed by Les Waters.

CAST: Caleb Eberhardt (Orpheus), Maya Hawke (Eurydice), Brian d’Arcy James (Father), Maria Elena Ramirez (Loud Stone), Jon Norman Schneider (Little Stone), David Ryan Smith (Big Stone), T. Ryder Smith (A Nasty Interesting Man/The Lord of the Underworld).

CREATIVE TEAM: Scott Bradley (Scenic Design), Oana Botez (Costume Design), Reza Bejat (Lighting Design), Bray Poor (Sound Design), Krystal Balleza, The Wig Associates (Co- Hair, Wig, and Makeup Design).

Eurydice  is playing at The Romulus Linney Courtyard Theatre, Signature Theatre, 480 W 42nd St, New York, NY until June 22, 2025. Tickets can be purchased here.

By Tulis McCall

Red Bull’s “Imaginary Invalid” is a perfection of a confection that will soothe the blues we are all experiencing.  I PROMISE it will make you laugh.  It made me laugh, and I am not a laugher.  I am an observer who, when something is funny, often makes a mental not to that effect.  But laugh out loud?  Not so much.  Wasn’t I suprised to be one of the people who nearly barked.

This is a condensed version of “Invalid” – first translated Mirabelle Ordinaire and then massaged into a new form by Jeffrey Hatcher.  The lights come up and the show breaks into a gallop from the start.  It never pauses, although the last third of the play sags a bit, and it never waits for us to catch up.  Dawdle at your own peril for this most excellent cast is on a mission: to get to the end of the story with the many, many loose ends (illness, deception, medical quackery, romance, betrayal, arranged marriage, class warfare, legal shenanigans and every element you can think of to blend into a satire) tied up in teeny weeny bows.

The story of “The Imaginary Invalid” is exactly what it says.  Argan, (Mark Linn-Baker at the top of his game) a wealthy man with too much time on his hands, spends his money on doctors who all have different opinions about the Nothing Burger that is his health.  So obsessed with himself is Argan that he arranges for his daughter Angélique (an exquisite Emilie Kouatchou) to marry a soon to be doctor, Thomas Diafoirus (Russell Daniels) the son of one of Argan’s doctors of the same name. By arranging his daughter’s marriage Argan plans on having free and immediate medical care for the rest of his days. (There are three manic doctors on 24 hours duty, Dr. Diafoirus, Dr. Purgon and Dr. Fleurant – all played with exquisite precision by Arnie Burton.) The combination of Daniels and Burton is filled with nuance that shoots them into the stratosphere.

Arnie Burton and Russell Daniels; Photo by Carol Rosegg

The fly in the ointment is that Angélique is in love with the empty headed but lovely Cléante (a still water John Yi) and is in cahoots with Argan’s wise-ass and the real boss of everyting maid Toinette (a snappy Sarah Stiles) to call a halt to the plan.  The pair are also committed to arranging the downfall of Argan’s second wife Béline (Emily Swallow) and her paramour DeBonnefoi (Maneol Feliciano) who are a brilliant duo.

 

Sarah Stiles and Mark Linn-Baker; Photo by Carol Rosegg

There are so many moving parts that this couldn’t be anything BUT a farce.  Once the players are presented all that is left is to watch it all unwind at a brisk pace.

The combination of talents has achieved a comic lift-off that is precise and surprising.  This is a very smart script.  Hatcher may have taken a page or two from the style of Coel Escola’s “Oh Mary” – which is a compliment to both authors.  Just when you think you have a handle on the proceedings, they spring a new plot twist on you.  Not only a new plot twist but several costume changes along with the requite exits and entrances that make your head spin.

Mark Linn-Baker and Russell Daniels; Photo by Carol Rosegg

“Imaginary Invalid”  is a DELIGHT – and can we not all use a little delight right now. Give your spirits a lift and go see this Invalid.

The Imaginary Invalid by Molière, adapted by Jeffrey Hatcher and directed by Jesse Berger.  Originally commissioned and developed by Red Bull Theater, this World Premiere adaptation is based on a new translation by Mirabelle Ordinaire.

Mark Linn-Baker, Arnie Burton, Russell Daniels, Manoel Felciano, Emilie Kouatchou, Sarah Stiles, Emily Swallow, John Yi

The creative team will include Beowulf Boritt (scenic), Tilly Grimes (costume), Mextly Couzin (lighting), Greg Pliska (sound & original music), Nina Field (sound), Lauren Page Russell (properties), Deborah Hecht (voice & speech), Rick Sordelet (action movement), and Tracy Bersley (choreography). Translator Mirabelle Ordinaire will serve as dramaturg.

At New World Stages (340 West 50th Street) for a limited Off-Broadway engagement through Sunday June 29th only.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: Laurie Roldan: A Song For You – The Music of Karen Carpenter at The Green Room 42

content.rendered:
Laurie Roldan’s outstanding cabaret performance honored The Carpenters’ timeless legacy in a sparkling return to classic cabaret at one of NYC’s Premier Intimate Venues.

In an era when the world feels increasingly fractured and complex, Laurie Roldan arrived at The Green Room 42 like a beacon of comfort and hope. Her tribute to Karen Carpenter, “A Song For You,” offered more than mere musical interpretation—it delivered a genuinely personal meditation on resilience, faith, and the healing power of song.

Laurie Roldan’s Stunning Stage Presence and Spiritual Journey

Resplendent in a white sequined ensemble that caught every stage light, Roldan commanded attention from her opening moments with Leon Russell’s “A Song For You”—a perfect choice that immediately established the evening’s intimate, confessional tone. But her warmth, not her sparkle, truly captivated the audience. Through thoughtful introductions and genuine anecdotes, she wove together the threads of her own life story with Carpenter’s timeless repertoire, creating a tapestry of shared human experience.

Laurie Roldan. Freeze frame courtesy Laurieroldan.com

A Fresh Perspective on Karen Carpenter’s Iconic Songs

Roldan’s approach to honoring Carpenter proved both reverent and revelatory. She understood that these songs—born during an era of hard rock rebellion and psychedelic experimentation—served as gentle counterprogramming, offering solace and clarity when the world grew too loud. Her rendition of “Yesterday Once More” became a meditation on memory and nostalgia, while “Close To You” transformed into something deeply personal rather than merely romantic. She suggested that tonight we need that same comfort that Carpenter once provided.

Her spiritual reflections on seeking truth through pain found perfect expression in “Rainy Days and Mondays,” where Roldan’s interpretation revealed new depths in Paul Williams and Roger Nichols’ lyrics about emotional resilience. When she spoke of hoping that potential love interests might become “the person I need you to be rather than the one you are,” she added poignancy to her later performance of “I Need To Be In Love.”

Memorable Musical Moments and Family Connections

The evening’s most touching moment came during “Those Good Old Dreams,” performed as a duet with her daughter, Bridgette Kinsella. This intergenerational collaboration embodied the show’s central theme: music creates bridges across time, connecting us to our past and future selves. The tender harmonies between mother and daughter gave the Bettis-Carpenter composition new emotional weight, suggesting how dreams and hopes pass between generations.

L-R: Bridgette Kinsella and Laurie Roldan on stage in “Laurie Roldan: A Song For You – The Music of Karen Carpenter” at The Green Room 42. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Roldan’s interpretation of “Top of the World” soared with unpretentious joy, while her take on “We’ve Only Just Begun” felt like both a wedding song and a philosophical statement about life’s endless possibilities. The Beatles’ “Ticket To Ride,” one of Carpenter’s more unusual covers, became a showcase for Roldan’s versatility and the band’s rock sensibilities.

Expert Musical Direction and Outstanding Band Performance

Under music director and pianist Nicolas Perez’s expert guidance, with Charlie Mac Call on bass and Mitch Bowers on drums, each arrangement honored Carpenter’s original interpretations while allowing space for Roldan’s artistic voice. Featured vocalists Bridgette Kinsella, Luis E. Mora, and Taylor Noll provided impeccable support throughout the ambitious evening, particularly shining during group numbers like Joe Raposo’s “Sing,” which became a joyful celebration of music’s communal power.

Roldan demonstrated remarkable vocal sensitivity during the more challenging material. Leon Russell’s “This Masquerade” showcased her jazz sensibilities, while “Superstar” (also by Russell, with Bonnie Sheridan) built to an emotional crescendo that left the audience breathless. Her interpretation of “Hurting Each Other” found fresh pain in the familiar lyrics, while “For All We Know” became a meditation on love’s uncertainty.

Personal Storytelling Elevates the Cabaret Experience

Roldan’s storytelling between songs proved equally compelling. Her journey from theater work to discovering her true calling as a vocalist felt authentic and earned. When she reflected on motherhood, spirituality, and the belief that “God can make it right” in our darkest moments during “Bless The Beasts and The Children,” the audience leaned in, recognizing their struggles in her words.

The Carole King composition “It’s Gonna Take Some Time” became a powerful statement about personal growth and patience, while “Only Yesterday” became a bittersweet reflection on time’s passage. Her performance of “I Won’t Last A Day Without You” felt vulnerable and strong, embodying the complex emotions that made Carpenter’s interpretations compelling.

Exploring Love, Loss, and Spiritual Awakening

Roldan understood these songs aren’t merely nostalgic artifacts—they’re vessels for exploring life’s most profound questions about love, loss, and meaning. Her interpretation of “Goodbye To Love,” one of Carpenter’s most emotionally complex recordings, became a master class in conveying heartbreak without self-pity. The evening’s spiritual themes found perfect expression in her approach to these deeply human songs.

Laurie Roldan: A Song For You – The Music of Karen Carpenter” at The Green Room 42. Photo by Edward Kliszus

A Powerful Conclusion to an Unforgettable Evening

The evening concluded with a reprise of “A Song For You,” bringing the performance full circle. By then, Roldan had accomplished something remarkable: she had channeled Carpenter’s voice and her spirit—that unique ability to find beauty in vulnerability and strength in gentleness.

Why This Karen Carpenter Tribute Matters in Today’s World

Just as Karen Carpenter once provided an alternative to the musical chaos of her time, Laurie Roldan offered something precious to ours: permission to feel deeply, hope openly, and believe that music truly can be “the art of our lives.” In a world that often demands we armor ourselves against emotion, this tribute reminded us that sometimes the bravest thing we can do is simply allow ourselves to be moved.

Laurie Roldan Sings A Song For You. Courtesy laurieroldan.com

A Must-See NYC Cabaret Experience

Music Director: Nicolas Perez | Bass: Charlie MacCall | Drums: Mitch Bowers | Featured Vocalists: Luis E. Mora, Taylor Noll, Bridgette Kinsella

About The Green Room 42

Located in New York City, The Green Room 42 continues to showcase exceptional cabaret performances in an intimate setting perfect for experiencing the artistry of performers like Laurie Roldan.

Laurie Roldan: A Song For You – The Music of Karen Carpenter at The Green Room 42

570 10th Avene
New York, NY 10036

content.rendered:
By Brittany Crowell

The scene is set; an abandoned pool descends the stage floor, sloping down in smooth arcs of grimy walls, as the audience take their seats in the round.  Designers Adam Rigg & Anton Volovsek have built out an environment of suburban emptiness that’s both familiar and dynamic at the Vineyard Theater for Nazareth Hassan’s BOWL EP.  The piece’s design serves as its fourth character, bringing the narrative to the next level with a soundtrack from Free Fool (with additional designs and composition from Ryan Gamblin), dynamic costumes from DeShon Elem, and narrative lighting support from Kate McGee.  

Enter Quinn (Oghenero Gbaje) and Kelly (Essence Lotus) two skaters and aspiring rap artists who fill the bowl with failed tricks and fledgling couplets.  For the first half of the piece, we jump through the EP’s tracks from moments of flirtation to moments of artistic inspiration; from seduction and light bdsm to smoking, snorting, drinking and skating.  Video and projection designs from Zavier Augustus Lee Taylor introduce each track as our two heroes jump between intimacy and artistry, all while skating or lounging beside the stained and abandoned pool.

The episodic structure of the first half of the piece leaves something to be desired and the energy doesn’t reach full force until the second half, when an acid trip leads to Kelly exorcising a demon (of intimacy) from Quinn, giving the show a bump of surrealistic energy.  The side of the pool bowl opens to reveal Lemon Pepper Wings, played by a raw and unrelenting Felicia Curry, who takes the audience on an emotional roller coaster through a surreal rap performance from Quinn and Kelly to an emotional soliloquy outlining what becomes of them once they leave the “bowl.”  Curry is ferocious, fearless, and unforgettable in her performance as the demon, oscillating moment to moment between manic fits of laughter to pulsating wails. The audience is rapt, the narrative string pulled taut when Curry is on the stage.

Performers Lotus and Gbaje are also called to attention, the beautiful subtleties of their first act performances get heightened under the influence of the drugs as they rise to the occasion of the concert and then find themselves bending to the whims of the demon.  It’s rewarding to see them break from the nuanced restraint of their characters early in the piece to come to their full selves in the performances of the rhymes they’ve been developing.

Bowl EP is unexpected.  It’s a play about two skaters smoking and drinking and writing their first rap album together, yes; but more than that it’s about the cost of intimacy and what happens when two people connect deeply but never fully before that connection is severed. It shows us what happens when they lose each other and how that lost intimacy may follow them throughout the rest of their lives.  Bowl EP is about the beauty and importance of small moments  – and the danger of shying away from revealing how you really feel.  All things said, it’s an album that we should all listen to.

 

BOWL EP – written and directed by Nazareth Hassan; music by Free Fool

FEATURING – Felicia Curry, Kalonjee Gallimore, Oghenero Bgaje, and Essence Lotus

Scenic design by Adam Rigg & Anton Volovsek; costumes by DeShon Elem; lighting by Kate McGee, sound design and additional composition by Ryan Gamblin; video and projection design by Zavier Augustus Lee Taylor; fight choreography and intimacy direction by Teniece Divya Johnson; props and special effects by Daniel Brothers; rap consultant, Judah “Free Fool” Girvan; skateboarding consultant, Faheem Allah.  Presented by Vineyard Theater (Sarah Stern, artistic director; Douglas Aibel, artistic director; Moogive Brooks, managing producer) & National Black Theater (Sade Lythcott, chief executive officer; Jonathan McCrory, executive artistic director); in association with The New Group (Scott Elliott, artistic director; Adam Bernstein, executive director).  At the Vineyard Theater (108 E 15th Street) through June 15. https://vineyardtheatre.org/shows/bowl/

title.rendered: Fire and Fate: Ballet Hispánico’s CARMEN.maquia Ignites New York City Center

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Tonight’s performance by Ballet Hispánico was a triumphant celebration of heritage and innovation!

Last evening at New York City Center, Ballet Hispánico delivered a breathtaking interpretation of Gustavo Ramírez Sansano‘s CARMEN.maquia, transforming Bizet’s timeless opera into a visceral contemporary dance experience. This performance marked both the 150th anniversary of Carmen and Ballet Hispánico’s 55th Emerald Anniversary season, creating a perfect storm of artistic celebration.

A Temple of Kinetic Poetry

The Ballet Hispánico dancers transformed New York City Center into a temple of kinetic poetry, where every gesture carried the weight of passion and the lightness of profound artistry. Their movements possessed an intoxicating blend of raw power and ethereal grace—bodies that could explode into fierce, angular expressions one moment and melt into fluid, serpentine lines the next.

The ensemble’s technical virtuosity was breathtaking. Dancers like Antonio Cangiano and Amanda del Valle demonstrated remarkable agility, seamlessly executing complex lifts and intricate partnering. Yet beyond the technical mastery lay something deeper—an expressiveness that transcended mere movement to become pure emotional communication.

Ballet Hispánico performs CARMEN.maquia at New York City Center. Courtesy Ballet Hispánico

Each dancer embodied Carmen’s untamed spirit differently, creating a kaleidoscope of interpretation within Sansano’s cohesive vision. Their faces told stories as vividly as their bodies, conveying the tragedy and triumph of love with devastating honesty. The way they inhabited Bizet’s musical phrases was magnetic, breathing life into every crescendo and diminuendo.

Audiences will fall in love with this ensemble because they don’t simply dance; they live it. Their collective energy creates an irresistible gravitational pull, drawing viewers into Carmen’s world of passion and peril. This is dance that speaks directly to the soul, reminding us why live performance remains one of humanity’s most powerful art forms.

The Choreographic Vision

Under the masterful direction of Gustavo Ramírez Sansano, CARMEN.maquia reimagines the classic tale of Carmen through the lens of tauromaquia—the art of bullfighting—creating a powerful metaphor for desire, power, and destruction. Sansano’s choreography fuses contemporary dance with passionate nods to Spanish paso doble and flamenco, resulting in a movement that feels both authentic and revolutionary.

The narrative is transformed from a simple tale of love and jealousy into a sophisticated metaphor where the dynamics of bullfighting—the dance between matador and bull, predator and prey, dominance and submission—mirror the fatal attraction between Carmen and Don José.

A scene from Carmen.maquia at New York City Center. Courtesy Ballet Hispánico

Movement Language Fusion

 Rather than relying on the original libretto’s dialogue and vocal narrative, Sansano creates a purely physical storytelling approach that fuses Contemporary dance techniques, Spanish paso doble rhythms and movements, Flamenco influences, and Picasso-inspired angular aesthetics

Structural Reimagining in the Art of Dance

The choreographer maintains the essential dramatic arc but restructures it through dance-specific storytelling. In the Prelude, we see Don José in his prison cell, staging the entire work as a psychological flashback. The audience experiences a non-linear narrative as the story unfolds through memory and consciousness rather than chronological events. Visual metaphors are effectively utilized, and in the cards scene, for example, it becomes a moment of physical prophecy rather than sung dialogue.

Cultural Lens Transformation

 While Mérimée’s novella and the Meilhac/Halévy libretto presented Carmen through a 19th-century French perspective on Spanish culture, Sansano approaches the material through contemporary Latino artistic sensibilities, bringing authentic cultural understanding to movements and dramatic interpretation.

A scene from Carmen.maquia at New York City Center. Courtesy Ballet Hispánico

Contemporary Relevance

Sansano strips away the period-specific elements to focus on the timeless psychological dynamics—obsession, freedom, possession, and destruction—making them speak to contemporary audiences through the universal language of the body in motion.

In this approach, CARMEN.maquia honors the source material while creating something entirely new—a work that captures Carmen’s essence without the boundaries of the original’s specific cultural and temporal constraints.

The work’s Picasso-inspired aesthetic brought angular beauty to every gesture, while the dancers embodied Carmen’s untamed spirit with remarkable physicality and emotional depth.

Musical Brilliance and Sonic Landscapes

The evening’s sonic foundation rested upon Bizet’s immortal score, performed by the Slovak Philharmonic, Prague Philharmonic, and Ensemble Carmen Fantasy. These recorded performances provided a rich tapestry of sound that elevated every moment of dance. Pablo de Sarasate’s Carmen Fantasy, performed by the Apollo Symphony Orchestra, added layers of virtuosic brilliance that perfectly complemented the dancers’ technical prowess.

Outstanding Performances

The Ballet Hispánico company dancers delivered performances of extraordinary intensity and precision. Each artist brought unique artistry to their roles, creating a cohesive ensemble that pulsed with collective energy while allowing individual brilliance to shine through.

Dancers from the company performing Carmen.maquia at New York City Center. Courtesy Ballet Hispánico

Antonio Cangiano and Amanda del Valle, among others, demonstrated the technical mastery and emotional commitment that have made Ballet Hispánico America’s premier Latino dance company. Their interpretation of Carmen’s complex narrative—from seduction to tragedy—held the audience spellbound throughout both acts.

Visual Artistry and Design

Luis Crespo’s set designs created an atmospheric backdrop that enhanced rather than overwhelmed the choreography. Emilio Lavarias’s lighting design painted the stage with shadows and brilliance, while David Delfín’s costume design added visual poetry to every movement.

New York City Center: The Perfect Stage

 The Neo-Moorish splendor of New York City Center provided an ideal venue for this celebration of cultural fusion. Since 1943, this Manhattan landmark has served as a beacon for accessible performing arts, and last evening’s performance continued that proud tradition.

The theater’s intimate yet grand atmosphere allowed every nuance of Sansano’s choreography to resonate with the audience, creating the kind of transformative experience that makes live performance irreplaceable.

Artistic Legacy and Innovation

This production stands as a testament to Ballet Hispánico founder Tina Ramirez’s vision and the continued leadership of Artistic Director Eduardo Vilaro. Under Vilaro’s guidance, the company continues to push boundaries while honoring its cultural roots.

Sansano’s choreographic mastery, honed through his work with Nederlands Dans Theater, Compañía Nacional de Danza, and other prestigious companies, brought sophisticated artistry to this beloved story.

A Night to Remember

CARMEN.maquia succeeds brilliantly in its ambitious goals: honoring Bizet’s masterpiece while creating something entirely new, celebrating Latino culture while speaking to universal human experiences, and maintaining classical dance excellence while pushing contemporary boundaries. This is more than entertainment—it’s cultural dialogue made manifest through movement, a conversation between past and present that leaves audiences both satisfied and hungry for more.

Looking Forward

For those who missed this extraordinary evening, Ballet Hispánico continues to redefine American dance with innovative programming and world-class artistry. Their upcoming performances promise the same level of excellence and cultural celebration that made CARMEN.maquia such a triumph.

This performance reminded us why live dance remains one of our most powerful art forms—capable of transcending language, culture, and time to touch something essential in the human spirit.

title.rendered: Amy Engelhardt and Erin Hill in “Good Night and Good Pluck” at Pangea

content.rendered:
By Nicole Itkin

Pangea is a supper club in the East Village with adorable sequined animal pictures on the walls, great food and drinks, and even better entertainment. This night, Amy Engelhardt and Erin Hill took the stage–Amy first, then Erin–in a one-night show called “Good Night and Good Pluck.”

Engelhardt talk-sang (and played the piano) through her set. She sang about familiar issues: commuting from New Jersey, leg injuries, love, and the issue of being so entranced in an NPR segment that it’s impossible to stop listening until the segment is over,  sitting in the car long after the garage door has come down to listen until the very end. She bantered with family and friends in the audience as she sang a variety of songs, including songs off of her three EPs: “Finish,” “Finish What,” and “Finish What You.” The songs, and anecdotes that interspersed the songs, were lovely, sweet, and familiar. My favorite song was “Deep Blue Sea,” the song inspired by the NPR segment she couldn’t stop listening to. Lyrics include: “My job is to photograph wildlife / And I am here studying you / You are a large wild predator / I’m your small possible meal / Though I have watched you for hours and hours / I can’t assume that you know, what you feel because / You’re a You. I’m a Me. You are beautiful. / I’m beautiful, sure, but you need dinner and I need a photograph.” Stunning!

Then, Hill took the stage with her harp. To call the harp angelic is nothing new, but the command that Erin Hill had over the harp, her vocals, and the room was extraordinary. As soon as Hill started singing, the entire room went SILENT. Hill called her genre of music “sci-fi harp”– she does indeed have “the market cornered” in that area! It’s surprising but absolutely brilliant. In both topic and sound, the songs were celestial and lovely. Hill tells us that she is used to playing with a band and projections and that this is her first time doing a solo show. This experience was so beautiful–I truly hope (and know!) that this is the first of many solo shows. She deserves every stage! Over the course of the evening, Hill plays and sings songs from a number of her previous shows— her show “Harp Oddity,” her 80’s show “Total Eclipse of the Harp,” her Kate Bush show, and others. All of her covers were beautiful—including her haunting cover of Kate Bush’s “Wuthering Heights” and her cover of “Video Killed the Radio Star.” But her originals were out of this world. Her single “The Buttoned Sky” was just splendid. Its visuals drew me in and kept me absolutely suspended in another world. I could see the girl, the gown, the sky, the love. I can’t emphasize enough how stunning this, and all of the other songs, were. Take any chance you can to go see Erin Hill perform!

Pangea is a great option for dinner and a show! Take a look at Pangea’s cabaret shows here.

content.rendered:
By David Walers

It’s dance: graceful leaping, pulling, carrying, lifting, bodies beautifully twisted and arched in space.

It’s circus: gravity-defying balancing, juggling, magic, suspense.

It’s theater: three friends live together in a small space (30″x30″x7′); one finds another place to live and decides to move. Considering the tiny space, you would think this would be a welcome thing, but the change instead disrupts the emotional balance established between the three of them, which made their tight living work. They all must make an effort to find their peace with the disruption to their lives and strive to maintain the friendship.

Three art-forms, put into a box, shaken and stirred; interject into that three gifted physical artists with the restrictions of a confined space as their palette, and what happens is a world that reaches beyond those physical limitations and into your heart.

The show was presented by Parallel Exit, an innovative physical theater company that has spanned the globe with their presentations and charmed audiences along the way. And, in collaboration with 3AM Theatre, a performance space in an old factory in the far reaches of Queens.

Parallel Exit’s Artistic Director, Mark Lonergan, a circus director for many years, creates an intimacy between performers and audience with this piece as he plays with the three artists’ gifts and the three artistic disciplines. For most of the performance, I was truly transported with the artists as they played with their box home, forgetting my personal concerns and being fully present with what was happening in front of me. Those are marvelous moments when we can become so captivated.

—–

Created and conceived by: Joel Jeske; Direction: Mark Lonergan
Collaborators & Performers: Kyle Driggs, Ryan Shinji, Saffi Watson
Lighting Design: Kyle Driggs

Unfortunately, the show only ran May 22-24. Count yourself blessed if you were one of the lucky ones. I imagine this is a show that Parallel Exit is contemplating taking on the road, so do keep an eye out for what’s to come.

3AM Theatre, 920 35th Avenue, Queens, New York 11106

title.rendered: Nina Conti: Whose Face is it Anyway?

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Nina Conti, British Comedy Award Winner, is returning to NYC with her comedy show Nina Conti: Whose Face Is It Anyway? 

A rack of masks (inclusive in facial features and color) accompanies Nina on stage. Members of the audience are brought on stage to put on these masks while Conti “speaks” through them, using a remote control to move their mouths–and whatever accent or voice she mismatchedly chooses. Who doesn’t enjoy an hour with a veteran ventriloquist? And to make the show special and unique in itself—audience members brought to the stage, to laugh themselves, behind their masks, at what Conti creates, while being laughed at? Bring a date, bring your family, bring yourself. However you arrive for the late-night show will be a new experience each night Conti takes the stage. It was my first time seeing one of Conti’s productions, but I’m almost tempted to return to see how a new audience engages.

Conti’s show really does rely on audience participation; their responses to her questions direct the evening. On the night I attended this sold-out ventriloquist show, Conti began the evening with her darkly humorous and straightforward sidekick, Monkey. A ragged, years-old stuffed monkey emerges from a bag and made several appearances, breaking up segments. While funny at first, bits with Monkey hosting mini therapy session for participants who volunteer themselves to step onto the stage is slow, repetitive, and feels like reaching really desperately to fill time. But, perhaps that’s partly determined by the audience of the evening.

Conti asked numerous people what they did for work: a tax guy, a tech guy, and a woman that sells breast pumps. Clearly, the most interesting was the latter, and she and her sister were brought to the stage, after their father overexcitedly drew attention to their row when the audience was asked who had attended with family. Conveniently, her sister was a divorce attorney. They were given their “faces,” did a song and dance, with an accompaniment on guitar. Conti moved their “mouths” to lyrics of breast pumping, babies, and marriage. The pair worked, but unfortunately the rest of the evening did not offer as much excitement—maybe the audience engagement and selection just weren’t there. It almost pains me to recall the topic of breast milk pumps because of how heavily it was incorporated into the rest of the night; Conti already wore it out during the sisters’ time on the stage. It quickly transitioned into “drying out;” need I say more? I felt dried out by the time I left the theater. That’s the thing, though, with comedy that relies on audience participation. Sometimes it works all too well; sometimes it starts out strong and fizzles out.

The very first woman brought on stage (working in building aircraft, if I recall correctly) did what Conti asked: she confidently and actively “spoke” with her hands and allowed Conti to do the talking. Essentially, confidence and humor from those brought on stage made the show memorable–

I imagine the show is difficult to prepare, unknowing of the audience participation, but despite the 50/50 chance of a flop or hit, it’s an exhibition of ventriloquism I’d never seen before.

Nina Conti: Whose Face Is It Anyway? is running until June 1, 2025 at Soho Playhouse, 15 Vandam St., New York, NY. Run time is 1 hour. Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Brittany Crowell

The Public Theater is taking audiences to Kenya this spring with Goddess, a new musical with a book by Saheem Ali and music and lyrics by Michael Thurber.  Also directed by Ali, the piece transforms the Public’s Newman theater into Moto Moto, the jiving, afrobeat jazz cave of your dreams, and indeed – the draw of its beats bring folks from all across Mombasa to dance together.  The colorful cave, designed by scenic designer Arnulfo Maldonado and expertly enhanced by Bradley King’s vibrant lighting design and Dede Ayite’s colorful and lively costumes even draws in the campaigning governor, Omari (Austin Scott).

The story of Goddess centers on Omari, torn between two mortal callings: one politically conservative, the other musically free; and Marimba, a goddess who traveled down to earth, concealed as the night club singer, Nadira, to escape her evil mother’s godly duties in search for a deeper understanding of mortal love. Together the two of them discover the power of music to bring people together, to bridge the gap between god and mortal, and to inspire you to reach your highest potential.  Both characters grow in their bravery throughout the piece as Omari sacrifices duty for love and Nadira learns that falling in love is more complicated and more painful that she could have ever imagined.

Amber Iman has a voice of the gods, easily filling the theater with beautiful tones as the goddess of music.  Iman leads the audience down a winding path of emotion with Thurber’s labyrinthine compositions. You feel it in your feet which begin to tap, and your heart, which swoops along with the melody; her heavenly timbre brings a musical vibration through the audience, materializing through the dancers pulsing to the heartbeat of Darrell Grand Moultrie’s choreography on the stage.

Arica Jackson and Nick Rashad Burroughs in GODDESS; photo by Joan Marcus

She is supported by a wonderful cast of characters who share a love of music and embody the way that music fosters community.  Nick Rashad Burroughs shines as Ahmed, who in trying to woo Moto Moto bartender Rashida (Arica Jackson) winds up winning over the whole audience.  Ayana George Jackson gives a beautiful performance as the controlled Siti, choosing duty over passion, but showing great patience and love for her betrothed; and our fates in absolutely divine outfits caution us to “watch,” to “learn,” to “listen.”

Moto Moto is a temple to humanity.  It embodies love in all forms, and gives passion, music, and joy to those who groove through its cavernous rooms.  Anyone leaving will feel lighter and more free.  Get out to the Public to witness how love and music bring out the best in us with Goddess.

 

 

GODDESS – music and lyrics by Michael Thurber; book by SaheemAli; Additional book material by James Ijames

Choreographed by Darrell Grand Moultrie

Directed by Saheem Ali

FEATURING – Brandon Alvion, Jason Bowen, George Brown, Nick Rashad Burroughs, Melessie Clark, Zachary Downer, Amber Iman, Arica Jackson, Ayana George Jackson, Quiantae Mapenzi Johnson, Christina Jones, Parris Lewis, Kareem Marsh, Nayah Merisier, J Paul Nicholas, Isio-Maya Nuwere, Teshomech Olenja, Destinee Rea, Jasmin Richardson, Awa Sal Secka, Austin Scott, Teddy Trice, Ekele Ukegby, Wade Watson, Reggie D White, Christopher Henry Young

Scenic design by Arnulfo Maldonado; costumes by Dede Ayite; lighting by Bradley King; sound by Nevin Steinberg; hair and wig design by Nikiya Mathis; puppet design by Julian Crough; props by Clair M. Kavanah.  Presented by the Public Theater: Oskar Eustis, artistic director; Patrick Willingham, executive director.  Through June 8.  https://publictheater.org/productions/season/2425/goddess/

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Dulé Hill is a triple threat.  He can act (so pure you think he is not acting).  He can sing (oh boy can he sing).  He can dance (look  for the wings on his feet).  He can do all three at once, if encouraged.  That is because he is also a magician.

It is one thing to go to a show, whose subject is an icon – Nat “King” Cole – and be entertained.  It is another thing entirely to be transported as soon as the person playing Cole, Dulé Hill, begins to sing.  It is as though Hill dropped into another dimension and stayed there long enough to soak up the very molecules that made Cole an extraordinary talent.

Hill is more than a mimic.  He is the pilot taking us on a journey that we do not expect.  “Lights Out” is not a linear take on the life or music of Cole.  We are there to witness something bigger than that.

On December 17th, 1957, it was LIGHTS OUT on “The Nat ‘King’ Cole Show.”  Colman Domingo and Patricia McGregor have taken a deep dive into what might have been going on in the heart and head of the first black entertainer to host his own variety show. He was also the center of the success of Capitol Records.  In spite of the fact that the show followed all the racial rules (no touching and covid-like distance between Cole and the guests) the advertisers pulled out due to pressure from the South.  As the news reported “Madison Avenue was afraid of the dark.”  Sammy Davis, Jr. (Daniel J. Watts) appears as the fool to this King.  And like most fools, he is the wisest apple in the bushel.  He enters Cole’s psyche and refuses to leave.  “Use the platform,” he tells Cole.  “Go out with a bang!”  Davis is not about sugar coating.  He is about throwing a match into the center of Cole’s world.

This “King” Cole is not a merry old soul in any way.  What Davis is suggesting, however, that Cole tells his truth, frightens him.  He clings to what he knows, and what he knows is his music.  There are nearly 20 songs that are represented.  Partial snippets or complete numbers.  Each is given enough time to register.  Yes, yes we know them all.  Because of Hill’s magicianship, each number hits us on a level deeper than we were prepared for.  There are moments when Hill’s performance is so pure we would swear it was 1957 and the game was truly on.  The game of survival, race, rage and madness.  We are hurled back and forth by the velocity of this story.  It is a train threatening to jump the track.  The forces in play are monumental, and Domingo, McGregor, Hill and Watts have their hands on the throttle.

Nowhere is this clearer than in the tap dance challenge between Davis and Cole (Tap Choreography by Jared Grimes).  This is a piece of fiction that is off the charts and executed with brilliance that takes your breath away.

The supporting cast – Krystal Joy Brown, Kathy Fitzgerald, Christopher Ryan Grant, Ruby Lewis, Elliott Mattox, Kenita Miller, Mekhi Richardson, Walter Russell III is superb.  Under McGregor’s direction they play dozens of characters that surround Cole and imbue the story with a cockeyed authenticity, moving on and off stage so quickly you think there must be more of them than is the case.

The band is every bit as sensational as the rest of this assembly: Vadim Feichtner , John Lowry, Andrew Gutauskas, Meredith Moore, Ayodele Maakheru, Caylen Bryant, Jakubu Griffin.  They were strategically placed with black performers on stage right and white performers on stage left.  Coincidence?

The only omission from the credits was the lack of a named vocal coach.  Hill and Watts performances were so nuanced they must have had guidance. Ditto for the rest of the cast and their many character changes.  Odd omission that.

This is such an extraordinary piece of work that, honestly, the next time I hear Nat “King” Cole sing, I may think it is Mr. Hill.  Tickets will be scooped up in a flash so get yours NOW.

Lights Out: Nat “King” Cole, written by Tony and Academy Award nominee Colman Domingo and NYTW Artistic Director Patricia McGregor. Directed by McGregor,

WITH Krystal Joy Brown, Kathy Fitzgerald, Christopher Ryan Grant, Dulé Hill, Ruby Lewis, Elliott Mattox, Kenita Miller, Mekhi Richardson, Walter Russell III, Daniel J. Watts.

Scenic design by Clint Ramos, costume design by Katie O’Neill, lighting design by Stacey Derosier, sound design by Alex Hawthorn & Drew Levy, video design by David Bengali, and wig design by Nikiya Mathis, choreography by Edgar Godineaux, with Tap Choreography by Jared Grimes. Music supervision, orchestrations and arrangements by John McDaniel

 Lights Out features Nat’s hit songs, like “Nature Boy,” “It’s a Good Day,” “The Christmas Song,” “Straighten Up And Fly Right,” “Smile” and “Unforgettable”
