title.rendered: Transcendent Motion: Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company Celebrates Heritage Through Sublime Movement

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Tonight’s event was a miraculous fusion of sound, visual art, and movement honoring Asian American Pacific Islander heritage.

The Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company presented an extraordinary celebration at the CitiGroup Theater in New York City, marking their 37th anniversary season and commemorating Asian American Pacific Islander Heritage Month 2025. Under the Artistic Direction of Greta Campo and Executive Direction of Andy Chiang, the company continues the vision of founder Nai-Ni Chen, whose choreographic brilliance endures.

Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company – Dance and Visual Art. Courtesy nainichen.org

Philosophical Tenets

In approaching the Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company‘s celebration at CitiGroup Theater, I frame my observations through dance’s profound theoretical lenses: Susanne Langer‘s “virtual power” concept, Daniel Nagrin‘s “search for the invisible becomes visible,” and Martha Graham‘s assertion that “movement never lies.” These philosophical frameworks, as explored in The Bloomsbury Handbook of Dance and Philosophy and other literary works on philosophy, aesthetics, and art forms, allow us to appreciate the depth of artistic achievement displayed in this transcendent motion of cultural celebration. As Graham McFee argues in his essential work The Philosophical Aesthetics of Dance, dance illuminates philosophical questions about embodiment and expression that transcend conventional aesthetics.

Nai-Ni Chen and Aesthetics

“My purpose is to create a unique style combining the West and East—the aesthetics, the essence of both,” Chen explained in a PBS documentary. “Root is so important for artists. You must find your root and have it shown naturally in your work.” When discussing her transition to modern dance, Chen revealed: “The one thing that fascinated me was the freedom. You can feel free to do anything with your body.” This philosophy permeated the evening’s performance.

Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company – Colors and Motion. Courtesy nainichen.org

The Legacy of Nai-Ni Chen: Bridging Cultural Divides

Chen’s journey from Taiwan to the United States in 1982 yielded over 80 original works that toured globally. Her vision—marrying Chinese cultural traditions with the dynamic spirit of modern dance—epitomizes what Langer identified as dance’s primary illusion: “movement transformed into expressive gesture, transcending locomotion.” Chen’s works embody what Nagrin described as “the search for the invisible become visible,” earning her multiple Choreographer Fellowships from the National Endowment for the Arts and the New Jersey State Council on the Arts, cementing her legacy as a visionary cross-cultural choreographer.

A Sublime Sanctuary: The CitiGroup Theater Experience

With impeccable acoustics and intimate design, the CitiGroup Theater at the Alvin Ailey American Dance Center wrapped the audience in sensory immersion. Lighting designer Jane Chan masterfully shaped environments from cool blues washing over “Unfolding” to fiery reds illuminating “Way of Fire,” making it the ideal setting for Chen’s boundary-crossing works.

The Dance Program: Transcendent Works

The celebration began with “Unfolding,” an exploration of energy flow through Korean Chan-Go music. Dancers embodied Yin and Yang principles with exquisite control, clad in ethereal blue costumes that rippled like water. As Graham said, “Dance is the hidden language of the soul of the body.” These azure-clothed performers embodied the Taoist principle that “the universal way of life is ever-changing.” The performance exemplified what Aili Bresnahan, in Thoughts on the Philosophy of Dance, describes as dance’s unique ability to manifest philosophical concepts through embodied practice, making abstract principles tangible through disciplined movement.

Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company – A panoply of colors, movement, and music. Courtesy nainichen.org

Shadow Force

“Shadow Force,” created during the pandemic, highlighted the vital importance of human connection. Dancers in muted gray costumes amplified the sense of shadows and spiritual connection. As Graham observed, “The body is a sacred garment.” This piece transformed absence into presence through the “virtual power” of gesture.

Way of Fire

“Way of Fire,” Chen’s exploration of the Five Elements theory, erupted with volcanic intensity. Dancers in vibrant red costumes designed by Chen herself blazed against the darkened stage—each movement extending like flames seeking oxygen. As Graham declared, “Movement never lies. It is a barometer telling the state of the soul’s weather.” This piece perfectly illustrates what Bojana Cvejić explores in “From Odd Encounters to a Prospective Confluence: Dance-Philosophy,” where choreography serves as a means of “posing problems” that contribute to rethinking philosophical concepts through embodied expression.

“Way of Fire” juxtaposes contrasting ideas—motion versus stillness, animal versus plant, strength versus beauty. Male dancers in earthy tones suggest the tiger moves with dynamic intensity, while females in pristine white create images of serene beauty. This epitomizes Graham’s understanding that each dancer’s unique vitality creates an unrepeatable moment of artistic truth.

Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company – Carousel. Courtesy nainichen.org

Musical Splendor: The Ahn Trio’s Contribution

The renowned Ahn Trio— pianist Lucia Ahn, cellist Maria Ahn, and guest violinist Zach Brock—perfectly complemented the company’s cross-cultural ethos. Their rendering of Pat Metheny‘s “Yuryung” underscored “Shapes of Water.” At the same time, Maria Ahn’s solo cello performance accompanied the world premiere of “UNANILLUSION”, featuring dancers in diaphanous blue garments that captured and released light with every movement. As noted in an article from OpeningNight.Online, this synergy between music and movement exemplifies the type of “artistic passion” that can transform a performance into a complete “Gesamtkunstwerk”—the Wagnerian ideal of a total work of art controlled by the composer that simultaneously engages multiple senses.

A Legacy Continued: The Company’s Future Vision

Under Greta Campo’s artistic direction, the company honors Chen’s legacy while forging new paths. Campo understands what Graham meant: “Great dancers are not great because of their technique, they are great because of their passion.” The company remains dedicated to reflecting “the immigrant’s journey” through performances exploring identity, authenticity, and artistic excellence.

The evening concluded with “Tomorrow,” featuring dancers in a harmonious blend of the evening’s palette—blue, white, red, pink, and gray—creating a visual symphony that celebrates unity. As the final movements dissolved, the audience rose in an ovation, acknowledging the multidimensional artistic power of the sublime, transcendent embodiment of brilliance, energy, colors, sound, and movement that unfolded before them.

Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company featuring cellist Maria Ahn, a guest artist and member of The Ahn Trio. Courtesy nainichen.org

Why Supporting This Transcendent Motion Matters

As we navigate the cultures of a richly diverse world, the Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company becomes not merely art but a necessity. Their performances serve as cultural bridges, inviting audiences to experience different traditions through the universal languages of music, dance, sound, light, and visual art. Each ticket purchased supports these exceptional artists and educational programs for underserved communities.

When authentic connections feel increasingly precious, these performances provide transformative experiences that resonate long after the final bow. As The Front Row Center critic noted in a similar performance review, such productions can leave audiences “enthralled and stuck to your seat, incapable of moving, wishing the story and dancers would continue long after the final bow.” The company’s next season promises exciting new works alongside cherished repertoire pieces—an artistic journey worth taking. As philosopher Nietzsche might have appreciated, here is a performance where one can honestly “believe in a God who knew how to dance.” Support transcendent motion. Witness beauty. Be transformed.

Motion frozen in time by the Nai-Ni Chen Dance Company. Courtesy nainichen.org

content.rendered:
By Vicki Weisfeld

Some shows you enjoy, some inspire a “meh,” and some occupy a “don’t miss!” category. In our family, Oscar Wilde’s The Importance of Being Earnest is in that last group, and the new production at the Shakespeare Theatre of New Jersey, which opened Saturday and runs through June 1, knocks it out of the park! STNJ artistic director Brian B. Crowe and the cast reveal and revel in every bit of the penetrating wit that makes this show perennially popular.

The crux of the story is that two young women are determined to marry men with the given name Ernest, a name epitomizing sober seriousness. Unfortunately, they’ve fixed on a pair of society gentlemen of the complete opposite temperament. Neither is named Ernest, though both pretend to be. Even worse, because a man needs certain credentials to marry a society daughter, the origins of one of them are completely unknown. It’s left to dowager Aunt Augusta to get to the bottom of the case, or suitcase, as it were.

While the play is most definitely a comedy, and in this production the audience appreciated the humor immensely, the humor works because of Wilde’s spot-on observations about human behavior at the extremes.

Christian Frost plays Algernon Moncrieff, nephew of Aunt Augusta, and Tug Rice plays Jack Worthing, aspirant to the hand of her daughter, Gwendolen. Not only do these two actors deliver their lines with perfect comic timing, their body language and gestures make the always-slightly-ridiculous situation even more so.

Marion Adler is perfection as the unyielding Lady Augusta Bracknell, with Carolyne Leys her besotted daughter, Gwendolen. She believes all is well with her engagement to Worthing until she meets his hitherto unknown and suspiciously beautiful ward, Cecily Cardew, played by Joyce Meimei Zheng. The two young women immediately feign deep friendship, but you know the claws will come out once the unmasking of the pseudonymous Ernests begins.

In smaller roles, Richard Bourg plays both manservant to Algernon and later to Jack. Though he’s in the background, his reactions to the young people’s shenanigans add a great deal. Alvin Keith plays the country parson being tapped to christen or re-christen the men with new names, and Celia Schaefer plays Miss Prism, tutor to Cecily, who unexpectedly holds the key to the whole dilemma.

The young men may not be Ernests, yet, but they are definitely Earnest when it comes to love!

A word about the set. There are three scenes (Algernon’s flat, Worthing’s country garden, and, finally, his drawing-room), and the design accommodates all three with just enough elegant detail. Lovely lighting effects in the garden scene too.

Production credits to Sarah Beth Hall (set design), Andrew Hungerford (lighting design), and Austin Blake Conlee (luscious costumes).

STNJ productions are hosted at Drew University in Madison, N.J. (easily reachable from NYC by train). For tickets, call the box office at 973-408-5600 or visit the Box Office online.

title.rendered: A Magnificent Journey: PACS Spellbinding “Symphonic Storytelling” Concert

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

In an age where the average concertgoer’s attention span has been whittled down to the duration of a TikTok video, there exists a profound oasis where time expands rather than contracts—where stories unfold not in bytes, but in glorious, symphonic narratives that transport us to realms both fantastical and profound. Such was the recent Park Avenue Chamber Symphony presentation of “Symphonic Storytelling” at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music, where the indefatigable Maestro David Bernard, with narrator DeCarlo Raspberry, once again demonstrated why this ensemble has become one of New York’s most cherished treasures.

As the audience settled into the acoustically sublime space, an electric anticipation was already hovering in the air. And why not? In our fractured modern existence, what could be more revolutionary than sitting together to experience the communal magic of storytelling through music, that most universal of languages?

David Bernard with Narrator DeCarlo Raspberry and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in a concert of Symphonic Storytelling. Photo courtesy PACS

David Bernard’s Innovative Approach to Classical Music Engagement

Bernard, ever the charismatic musical ambassador, began the afternoon with welcoming remarks that instantly dissolved the artificial barrier between performer and audience. “You know all you need to know to enjoy today’s concert,” he assured us with characteristic warmth, inviting listeners to engage with the musicians and immerse themselves in the experience. This statement was not merely reassuring but a profound philosophical stance on how we should approach art: with openness rather than trepidation, heart rather than intellect alone.

The maestro’s introduction echoed what Leonard Bernstein once described as “the infinite variety of music that can transform the listener.” Bernard’s approach reminds us that music isn’t merely to be analyzed but felt—a sentiment that resonates with what philosopher Susanne Langer called “the embodiment of feeling in logical form.” Bernard’s gentle encouragement to look around during the concert was not just permission but an invitation to witness the living, breathing organism that is an orchestra in full flight.

Exploring Ravel’s Mother Goose Suite: Childhood Wonder Through Masterful Performance

The program began with Ravel’s exquisite “Mother Goose Suite” (Ma Mère l’Oye), a most perfect marriage of childlike wonder and sophisticated musical architecture. What struck one immediately was how Bernard approached this score not as a cute curiosity or mere programmatic diversion, but as a profound statement worthy of the most serious consideration.

Sleeping Beauty’s Delicate Pavane: Wong’s Violin Mastery

The opening “Pavane of Sleeping Beauty” emerged like a delicate watercolor painted in sound. Concertmaster Francis Wong led the violins with a gossamer touch that seemed to suspend time. His phrasing contained just enough rubato to suggest breath without distorting the architectural integrity of Ravel’s meticulous construction. One was reminded of what critic Harold Schonberg might have called “the aristocracy of restraint”—that paradoxical ability to communicate deep emotion through disciplined precision.

Théâtre des arts: Répétition générale: Jeannine: Pupazzi: Ma mère L’oye, Paris Musées 20231023171213. Public Domain via Wikipedia Commons

Tom Thumb’s Forest Adventure: Woodwind Excellence

The “Tom Thumb” movement showcased the orchestra’s exceptional woodwind section, with the lyricism of oboist David Greenwald and percussionists creating evocative bird calls, one could almost see the forest materializing. The string section’s portrayal of scattered breadcrumbs through meandering passages demonstrated Bernard’s attention to the storytelling aspect of the music, with each note serving the narrative rather than merely displaying technical skill.

East Asian Inspirations: Laideronnette’s Exotic Soundscape

“Laideronnette, Empress of the Pagodas” transported us to an exotic soundscape where one could feel the influence of the 1889 Paris Exposition on Ravel’s imagination. The pentatonic scales and crystalline textures evoked not merely a superficial orientalism but a genuine exploration of sonic possibilities. Principal flutist Jenn Forese delivered passages that sparkled with the clarity of fine porcelain—an apt metaphor for the miniature ceramic characters dancing in the story.

Beauty and the Beast: Contrasting Characters Through Instrumental Dialogue

In “Beauty and the Beast,” the orchestra achieved a remarkable contrast between the contrabassoon’s growling portrayal of the Beast and the clarinet’s graceful depiction of Beauty. Principal clarinetist Yoyo Chan brought exceptional warmth to her solos, creating a dialogue with the contrabassoon (Phil Murphy) that perfectly captured the emotional essence of this timeless transformation tale. As OpeningNight.online noted in a prior examination of programmatic music, “When listening, one is philosophically transported through time, space, and existence while envisaging the chimera of eternal questions facing humankind.”—a principle perfectly demonstrated here.

The Fairy Garden: Orchestral Magic Unleashed

The suite concluded with “The Fairy Garden,” where Bernard’s interpretation revealed the full measure of Ravel’s genius for orchestration. The gradual build-up to the luminous climax was handled with exceptional pacing, allowing the audience to experience the entire emotional arc of awakening. Wong’s violin solo here was particularly moving, rich with pathos yet never indulgent, revealing the profound seriousness that can exist within music ostensibly written for children.

Throughout this performance, what impressed most was Bernard’s ability to balance the fairytale elements with genuine emotional depth—a reminder that these stories endure not for their surface simplicity but for the profound truths they contain. As TheFrontRowCenter.com observed in their coverage of Bernard’s innovative approach to audience engagement, his “InsideOut” philosophy transforms listeners from passive recipients to active participants in the musical experience.

World Premiere: James Bernard’s “Where the Wild Things Are” Brings Sendak’s Classic to Symphonic Life

Following intermission came the world premiere of James Bernard’s “A Musical Realization of Maurice Sendak’s ‘Where the Wild Things Are.’ This ambitious undertaking seamlessly integrated pictorials, captions, and narration with original music. The younger Bernard (the maestro’s son) demonstrated remarkable compositional acumen in balancing accessibility with artistic integrity—no small feat in contemporary classical composition.

David Bernard with Composer James Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony in a concert of Symphonic Storytelling. Photo courtesy PACS.

Composer James Bernard’s diverse output includes song cycles, chamber music, concertos, symphonic tone poems, film scores, pop songs, and hip-hop beats. James aspires to create music that is both accessible and authentic, achieved through his skilled use of rhythm and groove. He is a student of Dr. Melinda Wagner at the Juilliard School and has had the privilege of working with renowned composers David Dzubay, Martin Amlin, Manuel Sosa, and Mary Kouyoumdjian during his studies at Tanglewood, Interlochen, and Mannes. When not composing, he enjoys taking walks through Central Park and listening to music from all periods and styles.

James Bernard, Composer. Courtesy James Bernard

Composer James Bernard notes that “It is important to see that ‘Where the Wild Things Are’ reaches everyone, not just children. No matter how old you are, sometimes you just have to let a rumpus out and join the wild things, but at the end of the day, the best parts of being a kid, or even more a human being, are the people who care about you. Being able to capture this arc of discovery for Max through music was an absolute joy!”

Wild Rumpus: Musical Chaos and Control

The score proved dramatically effective, particularly during the “Wild Rumpus” section, where controlled chaos in the orchestra brilliantly mirrored Sendak’s famous illustrations. One couldn’t help but think of what philosopher Gaston Bachelard called “the poetics of space”—how imagination transforms our experience of the world around us. Just as Max creates his world in Sendak’s tale, James Bernard created a sonic landscape that invites listeners to inhabit their imaginative realms.

Sendak’s Artistic Legacy Honored Through Music

The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony navigated the demanding score with remarkable precision, demonstrating why this ensemble has earned multiple First Prize distinctions in The American Prize Competition. Their ability to pivot between tonal accessibility and edgy contemporary elements spoke to their technical prowess and interpretive intelligence.

Wildflowers and where they grow (1882) from Maurice Sendak’s ‘Where the Wild Things Are.’. Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons

The familial connection between composer and conductor made this premiere particularly touching—a multigenerational artistic dialogue that added resonance to the performance. As Maurice Sendak once remarked in an NPR interview, “I refuse to lie to children…the fantasy is what’s true.” This philosophical approach found its perfect musical expression in Bernard’s composition, which treated the emotional complexities of childhood with the seriousness they deserve.

Rimsky-Korsakov’s Scheherazade: The Ultimate in Symphonic Storytelling

The concert culminated in Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov’s magnificent “Scheherazade,” a dazzling orchestral showpiece based on “One Thousand and One Nights.” From the stern, unison brass proclamations representing the tyrannical Sultan to Wong’s seductive violin solos portraying Scheherazade herself, the orchestra created a vivid contrast between despotic power and creative imagination.

Sinbad’s Maritime Adventures: Orchestral Seascapes

Maestro Bernard’s approach to this warhorse was anything but routine. His interpretation revealed fresh insights into a familiar masterpiece, emphasizing the architectural grandeur while never losing sight of the intimate storytelling at its core. As Russian literary theorist Mikhail Bakhtin might have noted, the performance captured both the “dialogic imagination” of the narrative frame and the “polyphonic” nature of the tales within tales.

The first movement, “The Sea and Sinbad’s Ship,” featured undulating string passages that vividly captured the rolling waves. Bernard’s meticulous attention to dynamic contrast allowed the orchestra to paint pictures of tranquil waters and turbulent storms. Principal Flutist Lindsay Brillson’s lyrical contributions evoked gentle sea breezes with crystalline clarity, while the brass section handled the majestic ship theme with commanding authority.

David Bernard and Concertmaster Francis Wong with the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony in a concert of Symphonic Storytelling. Photo by Edward Kliszus

The Kalendar Prince: Mysterious Tales Through Musical Dialogue

In “The Kalendar Prince,” Principal Bassoonist James Marshall’s haunting solo set the mysterious tone with exceptional control and expressivity. The interplay between woodwinds and strings throughout this movement created a compelling dialogue that enhanced the narrative quality. Principal Clarinetist Anna Bush delivered her solo passages with remarkable agility and character, her instrument weaving gracefully through Rimsky-Korsakov’s exotic harmonies.

Royal Romance: The Young Prince and Princess Movement

“The Young Prince and The Young Princess” showcased Rimsky-Korsakov’s gift for melodic invention through one of classical music’s most beautiful love songs. Wong’s violin soared above the orchestra with heartfelt lyricism, his warm tone perfectly capturing the passionate yearning between the young lovers. Bernard shaped these lyrical passages with remarkable sensitivity, allowing the music to breathe naturally while maintaining forward momentum.

Dramatic Finale: From Festival to Shipwreck

The finale, “Festival at Baghdad – The Sea – The Ship Goes to Pieces Against a Rock,” combined all the musical elements into a tour de force of orchestral brilliance. Bernard unleashed the full power of the ensemble to depict the bustling Baghdad festival, with its whirling dances and exotic instrumentation. His precise conducting maintained clarity even in the most densely orchestrated passages, while his dynamic gestures inspired the musicians to deliver performances of thrilling intensity.

During the tumultuous shipwreck sequence, Bernard’s physical gestures seemed to summon the storm itself from the orchestra. Wong’s recurring Scheherazade violin solos provided essential contrast, reminding listeners that we were experiencing these adventures through the storyteller’s voice. His final solo, accompanied by gentle harp arpeggios, was delivered with ethereal beauty, gradually fading to a whisper as Scheherazade concluded her tales and secured her life from the Sultan.

Scheherazade and Sultan Schariar by Ferdinand Keller (1880). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Ensemble Excellence: The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s Virtuosic Unity

What distinguished this concert was not merely the excellence of individual performances but the remarkable cohesion of the entire ensemble. As Bernard later commented, “Scheherazade demands virtuosity from every orchestra section. It’s not enough to have brilliant soloists—the entire ensemble must breathe and move as one entity to truly capture Rimsky-Korsakov’s vision.”

Technical Mastery Across All Sections

The string section’s unified bowing and precise articulation in the fastest passages demonstrated exceptional technical preparation. The brass section, often challenged by Rimsky-Korsakov’s demanding writing, maintained power and refinement. The woodwind section displayed a remarkable blend and character in solo and ensemble passages.

InsideOut Concerts: Redefining the Classical Music Experience

In an era when classical music is often treated as a museum piece—revered but distant—Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony offered a powerful reminder of its immediate emotional impact and narrative power. Through their InsideOut Concerts approach, they have pioneered a model that builds new audiences without compromising artistic integrity—a model that deserves to be emulated across the classical music world.

As the final, shimmering string chord representing Scheherazade’s triumph faded into silence, the audience remained in rapt stillness before erupting into thunderous applause. In that moment of collective appreciation, one felt the unique power of music to transcend boundaries of time, culture, and language—to tell stories that speak to our shared humanity.

David Bernard with Composer James Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music in a concert of Symphonic Storytelling. Photo courtesy PACS.

Experience the Magic: Upcoming Park Avenue Chamber Symphony Performances

The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s 2025-26 Season promises more superb immersive experiences, ranging from Saint-Saëns’ Organ Symphony to Tchaikovsky’s The Nutcracker. Based on this performance, they will undoubtedly continue to showcase why storytelling through music remains one of civilization’s most profound achievements—and why this ensemble has become such an indispensable part of New York’s cultural landscape.

Click HERE for information and tickets for the 2025-26 season.

A Magnificent Journey: PACS Spellbinding “Symphonic Storytelling” Concert

At the DiMenna Center for Classical Music
450 W 37th St, New York, NY 10018

The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

Conducted by Maestro David Bernard with featured narrator DeCarlo Raspberry

Francis Wong: Concertmaster (solos in all works)

Principal chairs in Scheherazade

Lindsay Brillson: Flute
Heather Donnelly: Oboe

Principal chairs in Mother Goose Suite

Jenn Forese: Flute
David Greenwald: Oboe

Phil Murphy: Contrabassoon (the Beast)

David Bernard, Music Director and Conductor

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

Grace’s Diner, the setting for William Inge’s classic, slice of life drama, Bus Stop, serves homemade pies and cakes. But the customers and wait staff who find themselves stranded overnight at this Kansas eatery are hungry for much more than dessert. These unhappy folks come in eight flavors of loneliness and are served up with generous scoops of desperation and naivete. Under the direction of Jack Cummings III, Inge’s play still rings with poignancy 70 years after its Broadway premiere, while the cast members range in style from perfectly understated to misguidedly rambunctious. 

Grace’s is located 30 miles west of Kansas City and is the preferred rest stop for the bus heading to Topeka. But when a March snow storm blows in, the highway closes down, so Grace (Cindy Cheung) and her teenage waitress, Elma (Delphi Borich), are stuck in place along with the watchful town sheriff, Will (David Lee Huynh), sly bus driver Carl (David Shih) and Carl’s motley array of passengers.

First off the bus is Cherie (Midori Francis), a singer from Kansas City who works at a nightclub “down by the stockyards.” Turns out that she had been forced onto the bus by Bo (Michael Hsu Rosen) a rowdy young cowboy, “wild as a bronco,” who plans to marry Cherie, whether she wants to or not, and move her up to his isolated ranch in Montana. Virgil (Moses Villarama), an older cowboy, is Bo’s stoic sidekick and erstwhile voice of reason. And finally, there is Dr Lyman (Rajesh Bose), a thrice-married scholar with expertise in Shakespeare, getting drunk and seducing underage girls.

Inge’s work often focuses on the post-war despair of common Midwesterners and so it is here as the characters come to reveal their various heartaches. Grace is separated from her husband but doesn’t mind all that much, she was just as lonely with him as without. Cheung’s quiet and steely performance strikes just the right tone. The studious Elma has had no luck with boys so far and her insecurity makes her an easy mark for the lecherous Dr. Lyman, who is so full of self-hatred, he drinks till he blacks out. Borich’s Elma is pleasingly plaintive while Bose’s Lyman is full-on creepy. That she ultimately finds some confidence as a result of his attentiveness is a bittersweet reward. 

Cherie, uneducated, down on her luck and with a long history of brief affairs behind her is of two minds about making Bo her beau. He is physically abusive and inexperienced when it comes to relationships, but she suspects that underneath Bo’s gruff facade lies a tender soul, so she just might be willing to roll the dice with him if he stops throwing punches. Francis unearths Cherie’s heart of gold, making her a likeable waif whose bad choices come with good reasons. But Rosen’s performance is more problematic. Bo is meant to be mean and threatening on the outside, soft and naive underneath. And while the softness eventually comes through, he seems frantic rather than mean, nervous instead of threatening; more neurotic New Yorker than beefy cowpoke.

Three different companies share the credit for this production: The National Asian American Theatre Company (This is the first Bus Stop to feature an all-Asian American cast.), the Transport Group (the only New York company now to have produced all of Inge’s major plays) and the Classic Stage Company, who serves as host at its Lynn F. Angelson Theater. The space’s thrust stage means that some actors will have their back to some of the audience for some of the time, but for those in the leftmost section, scenic designer Peiyi Wong’s set holds a surprise. With its counter, stools and coffee urn seemingly encased in a black frame, it may well remind you of Edward Hopper’s famous meditation on loneliness, the painting, Nighthawks.

 

Bus Stop – By William Inge; directed by Jack Cummings III

WITH: Delphi Borich (Elma), Rajesh Bose (Dr. Lyman), Cindy Cheung (Grace), Midori Francis (Cherie), David Lee Huynh (Will), Michael Hsu Rosen (Bo), David Shih (Carl) and Moses Villarama (Virgil).

Scenic Design by Peiyi Wong, Costume Design by Mariko Ohigashi, and Lighting Design by R. Lee Kennedy. Classic Stage Company, the National Asian American Theatre Company (NAATCO), and Transport Group at Classic Stage, 136 E 13th St., 212.677.4210,  https://www.classicstage.org. Through June 8. Running time: 2 hours

content.rendered:
By David Walters

It’s not easy living in New York City. It’s not easy being an artist in New York City. It’s not easy being a woman artist living in New York City.

She Takes Flight is composed of the personal stories, told through monologues and skits, of five actresses, aged 40s to 60s, and their journeys living, creating, and becoming themselves in a city that both rewards and punishes being a partner, mother, daughter, and a woman. There are no great reveals, only lives lived exposing a common thread woven into the universality of us all, tears shed that splash onto an already salted pavement, and a quest to understand what it’s all about that we ultimately all seek.

There are touching moments in the piece: the facing of what aging means, anger at what abortion has become (I was strongly moved by the memorializing of those who have suffered in the hands of our current abortion laws), confusion about what menopause inflicts, angst about birth trauma and its parental connection, rape, and the double sided mirror of personal revelation that both reflects and projects humanity in action.

I’ve had the privilege of attending several similar artist-inspired productions this year that bring to the stage the performers’ personal lives as the material that is the basis of the play. It takes courage to put yourself out there as an artist, and extra courage if it’s your personal story that you’re exposing. Unfortunately, it also means that everything is precious, leading to several false endings, and more time spent with material that does not add to the overarching through-line of the play being presented. But, with that said, it in no way takes away from the effort put forth in constructing She Takes Flight. Kelly O’Donnell’s directing keeps things lively and moving through much of the performance, but seems to run out of steam near the end as the production begins to fold in upon itself and an air of victimhood lingers over the piece. You won’t walk out feeling uplifted, but you will carry a sense of endurance as you tell your physical heart, as per Finding Nemo, “Just keep pumping. Just keep pumping.”

—–

She Takes Flight is written and performed by Sora Baek, Cindy Keiter, Adina Taubman, Gabriela Kohen, and Susan Ward.
Directed by Kelly O’Donnell

Scenic design by Ant Ma, costume consultation by Izzy Fields, lighting design by Kia Rogers, and sound design by Jeffrey Salerno.

In conjunction with Chrysalis Theatre Company, She Takes Flight is now playing at the Chain Theatre (312 W 36th St., New York, NY 10018)

May 17-June 8. Thursdays-Saturdays at 7P and Sundays at 3P.

Chain Theatre 312 West 36th Street, Floor 4, New York, NY, 10018

Tickets are available HERE. $28.22

Running time: 90 minutes

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

“Nora was like: how can I escape constraint and just experience the sublime?”

It’s the 70’s. Nora (Cricket Brown) wishes it were the 70’s. We’re at Hotel Chelsea; or rather, Nora places us at Hotel Chelsea: “the breeding ground for the Great American Artists.” She empties a suitcase of her belongings all over the floor, throws down a thin mattress covered by a sheet.

Lobster , written by Kallan Dana, and on stage at The Tank, introduces us to Nora; she’s 16 and is directing her high school’s production of Cowboy Mouth, written by Sam Shepard and Patti Smith. Shepard and Smith’s setting was loosely set in the hotel, and it was inspired by their own relationship. An actor in a literal lobster suit plays Lobster Man: a savior, symbolizing a source of inspiration for rock and roll.

Nora almost fetishizes Patti and Sam and their relationship brought to the stage. The fascination of the Hotel Chelsea, and the artists living and creating and struggling in the space. The drugs; the masterpieces; the beauty of the mess.

Conveniently, Beauty and the Beast is in rehearsals next door to Nora’s production. And Nora’s ex-girlfriend (or something like this), Imogen (Annie Fang), has been cast as Belle. This, alone, turns Nora to disbelief that her punk rock partner has chosen Disney musical theater instead of the play they were supposed to do together.

“Our play will mean something.” Nora wants to make something raw and punk rock.

Nora casts Medea (Coco McNeil) as Lobster Man. Medea idolizes, is not-so-subtly crushing on Nora.

Jeremy (Felix Teich) was told he’d get to drum if he played Slim in Cowboy Mouth.

Gwen (Sarina Freda) plays Cavale; she’s doing theater for the first time, and she doesn’t pronounce “Cavale” correctly.

Photo by Maria Baranova

Lobster captures the funny, cringey, budding desperation for love and identity we search for in high school. The acting and direction pinpoints this coming-of-age. It encapsulates what it means to be a theater kid, how theater can serve as a space for rawness and unleashing, and it highlights the pain of young love. Lobster shows how betrayal at any age depletes us, how it creates a need for control.

As though Nora had wanted Cowboy Mouth to be real and lived by its cast, Gwen and Jeremy begin to fall for each other—an unlikely match who abandons what’s familiar to create this piece together. Medea will part ways with Nora and her notion of Lobster Man–of which didn’t live up to Nora’s vision. Instead, Nora herself will become Lobster Man, in a last effort to build this production into something transforming, life-altering, memorable.

As the cast of three fall into character and emerge as artists, their vulnerabilities surface, their small, dirty room become a breeding ground for emotion. It will take on a 2015 version of Cowboy Mouth—anger, and violence, shattering and feeling. Nora and Imogen will reunite in passion and rage, delicacy, and innocence. Clips of their relationship over an evening in the abandoned classroom are mirrored with Jeremy and Gwen portraying Slim and Cavale; she’s holding him at gunpoint; they’re falling in love.

Photo by Maria Baranova

Lobster’s ending is a blurred frenzy; I don’t know what’s supposed to be Nora, what’s supposed to be Patti Smith—but maybe the finale is supposed to be as confusing as the overwhelming emotions of artistry are echoed with that of teenage love: something new and chaotic.

 

Written by Kallan Dana.

Directed by Hanna Yurfest; Produced by Emma Richmond and Needy Lover.

CAST: Annie Fang (Imogen), Coco McNeil (Medea), Cricket Brown (Nora), Felix Teich (Jeremy), Sarina Freda (Gwen).

CREATIVE TEAM: Pete Betcher (Scenic Design), Hayley Stahl (Costume Design), Jacqueline Scaletta (Lighting Design), Amelia (Mellie) Way (and Sound Design). Jonah Harrison (Assistant Producer), Cori Diaz (Production Stage Manager), Olivia Mermagen (Assistant Stage Manager), Sterling Gates (Costume Assistant), and Max Mooney (Intimacy Director), Amar Ahmad (Graphic design and photography).

Lobster is a New Georges supported production, and is produced with additional support from Clubbed Thumb, made possible by Venturous Theater Fund of the Tides Foundation.

Lobster is playing at The Tank, 312 West 36th Street, New York, NY, until May 17, 2025. Performances are Thursdays-Saturdays at 7pm; limited-run until May 17. Tickets can be purchased here.

Running time is 75 minutes with no intermission.

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

Maddie: A New Musical, at the Players Theatre, based on Jack Finney’s novel “Marion’s Wall” about the all-too-brief life of silent film actress Marion Marsh, promises a tale of second chances and spirituality.  Jan (Kelly Maur) and Nick (Joe Lewis) find a hidden message from 20’s starlet Maddie Marsh scrawled on in their vintage East Village apartment, conjuring the oft-shared dream of buried treasure or talking to ghosts.  Jan gets a little too close to that message, and Maddie leaps at the chance to experience the earthly world once more, but at what cost to Jan?  The metaphor of Maddie as spiritual guide and lens through which to explore untapped aspects of the self has promise.  Alas, that promise is not kept.  We reach no substantive epiphany and learn next to nothing about Maddie herself.  In.  Two.  Hours.

Despite its interesting set-up, the material somehow side steps the meat of the story.  I mean, they discover a message from a woman from the  1920s in an apt. in the 1970s.  20’s / 70’s.  Ding-ding ! 1920’s, the vote, women entering the workplace earning their own money for the first time, often as secretaries … just as Sally and Jan are secretaries …1970’s, Roe v. Wade, rebellion, feminism.  The exploration of self, independence, freedom, identity.  That would be interesting.  Yet the authors make one passing reference to the woman’s movement and include one creepy frisson of sexual harassment in Jan’s workplace and then just cast the idea aside.

So instead of excitement and political awakening, we are treated to a succession of namby pamby, earnest ballads that do nothing to push the muddled story forward.  The show is mostly lifeless, despite admirable effort by the cast.  Where is the directing?  Too much of the action takes place in little snippets of scenes, which do not hang together.  The action is also confusing; the stage is crowded; and the smaller characters given no space to breathe.  It’s as if everyone is in a different play, meeting only occasionally.  The best moments are in some of the group numbers, like the flapper dance in Act I, and the quartet of women in Act II.  Finally some zest and connection.

Maur is leggy and lovely, and she knows how to bevel (as any self-respecting film starlet would).  Her voice is nice but she is rather one dimensional.  Her elegance contrasts with Lewis as her husband.  Lewis sings with heartfelt voice, but he is stiff, and does not seem to know what to do with hands.  This is where a director could really help.  Instead Maur and Lewis are left hanging – awkward and hesitant in their scenes together and, I’m sorry to say, very mismatched.  The only actress who comes close to sticking the landing, as it were, is Lexis Trechak as the sidekick comedy friend, Sally.  She is dynamic, reaching out to the audience and taking stage.  Shannon Payette Seip as socialite Cordelia van Arc also has some understanding as to why she is onstage, elevating the clunky scenes in which she appears.  Several other actors whisk on and off stage, but are given little to nothing to do.  The playwright really needs to address this imbalance.

One consistently cannot hear a lot of the singing and dialogue, which I think is partly a function of the space.  There must some way to counter the theatre’s muffled acousticsHowever, I could hear Trechak easily, so clearly some of the actors need to work on their projection.  The unmistakable, Mondrian-esque ladder of wall struts, exposed during the apartment renovation, make an effective set design.  A few well chosen dramatic lighting cues also enhance the storytelling.  I believe the upstage projections were not working the night I saw the show, because in photographs I am discovering heretofore unseen backdrops.  They offer much-needed context and depth.

It is not, however, a good sign when the set and lighting are stronger than the direction.  And I challenge the idea that any of the writing team has spent an appreciable amount of time in New York, let alone the East Village.

I am sorry to be so unkind, but I honestly don’t understand how this piece has been so lauded.  Maybe I would feel differently if I could have heard more of the dialogue and music.  I am not sanguine, however.  In the end, Maddie: a New Musical is too long; the narrative muddy and the music unremarkable.  And there is too much of it.  I would cut several of the songs, particularly from Act I, and make this show 90 minutes, no intermission.  Not enough takes place over the course of the play to merit two hours.  Act II is stronger than Act I, with some character development and pace to the action, but it is too little, too late.  To top it off, the ending is utterly disappointing.  A pure capitulation that defeats the whole point of the preceding two hours.

Maddie the Musical, book by Shaun McKenna and Steven Dexter; lyrics by Shaun McKenna; music by Stephen Keeling.  Directed by Andrew Winans.

With: Kelly Maur, Logan Durrah Broadnax, Justin Burr, Truman Griffin, Joe Lewis, Zoe-Maria Rivera, Hanna Scotch, Shannon Payette Seip, Alexander Todd Torrenga, Lexis Trechak, Jorge Valero and Alysia Vastardis.

At the Players Theatre (115 MacDougall St.) through June 8th.  For tickets go to ovationtix.com.  Run time: 2 hours with one intermission.

excerpt.rendered: Maddie: A New Musical, at the Players Theatre, based on Jack Finney’s novel “Marion’s Wall” about the life of silent film actress Marion Marsh, promises a tale of second chances and mystery.   Alas, that promise is not kept. Maddie remains a mystery – not a sexy, ghostly, tantalizing mystery, just a carapace who has nominally served her purpose. Instead of excitement we are treated to a succession of namby pamby, earnest ballads that do nothing to push the story forward, with the occasional group number to relieve the sameness.  The musical is mostly lifeless, despite admirable effort by the cast.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

title.rendered: AN UPDATE ON NEA SUPPORT from MCC Theater

content.rendered:
In the late hours of last Friday evening, along with many of our colleagues from across the arts sector, MCC Theater was informed that our FY25 grant from the National Endowment for the Arts was abruptly terminated at the direction of the federal government. Our grant of $20,000 had been approved last fall in support of MCC Theater’s flagship education program, the MCC Youth Company, and our annual culminating productions of UNCENSORED and FRESHPLAY FESTIVAL, celebrating the 25th Anniversary of the program.

Cast of UNCENSORED: HOW DO YOU SLEEP AT NIGHT, 2025. Photo by Joseph O’Malley
Receiving this notice, less than a week following our closing performance of UNCENSORED, is especially disappointing. Of course, this happened not because of any issue with our work or impact but, according to our termination notice, because youth arts education is no longer a priority of the federal government.
We’re proud of the work we do. We’re proud of our students. And we’re not giving up on them.

This week, amid chaotic communications around this grant, MCC received the payment of funds for this year’s program. There’s been talk of a possible future attempt to rescind these funds we were awarded. We have formally appealed the NEA’s decision to terminate support of MCC, but the road ahead remains uncertain. From what we have learned, it appears unlikely MCC will receive any future funding from the NEA under their newly articulated funding priorities.
The loss of these funds and future awards would be detrimental to MCC, and more specifically, the young people we serve—and that’s why we are now asking for your support to secure our programming. By making a gift today, you’ll directly support:

  • MCC Youth Company’s 25 year-long commitment to supporting the next generation of artists, audiences, and changemakers
  • Spaces where young people can express themselves, grow, and be heard
  • The incredible teaching artists and mentors who guide our students
DONATE NOW
We know that our audiences believe in the transformative power of arts education. Time and time again, our community has stepped up in times of uncertainty. Together, we can ensure that whether we are a “funding priority” or not, the MCC Youth Company will continue to thrive for another 25 incredible years.
Sincerely,
Bernie Telsey, Artistic Director

Will Cantler, Co-Artistic Director

Blake West, Executive Director
P.S. If you believe that the federal government should honor its financial commitments to cultural organizations that have already fulfilled their grant obligations to the NEA, or if you simply want to express your concern about the future of NEA and its support of the arts, we encourage you to please contact your local representatives to make your voice heard. You can your congressional representatives, at 202-224-3121 – they HAVE to make a record of phone calls.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

We hear on the loudspeaker, “Kevin. Please, come inside when you finish that smoke. The team are waiting for you in meeting room 3.”

Looking out at the audience, standing in what looks like a dilapidated walled-in outdoor space of what could be a prison, a man dressed in pj’s and robe (actor/playwright Kwaku Fortune), smoking a cigarette, says, “You exist because I brought you into being?” (Every playwright dreams that they could make that happen.)

In 2022, New York’s Irish Repertory Theatre and Dublin’s Fishamble: The New Play Company began working together to address historical racial inequalities in theatrical representation of Irish plays. One of the outcomes of that initiative (entitled Transatlantic Commisions) is the play The Black Wolfe Tone, written by Kwaku Fortune, now playing at Irish Repertory Theatre’s downstairs performance space prior to its all Ireland tour.

The play is semi-autobiographical of the mental health journey that a soul “split in seven pieces” goes through in order to find peace and healing from the trauma of life. The setting is the mental institute (a kind of prison I guess) in Newcastle, Ireland, where Kevin has been placed. He is today, faced with the chance to leave if he can persuade the doctors in meeting room 3 that he is cured, or at least cured enough. The journey that he takes the audience on is what brought him to this place of deep mental confusion: his upbringing as an Irishman who is also black, his feelings of his father’s unavailability, and the societal stigma that isolated him and led to a diagnosis of bipolar disorder that he carries. We are not defined by our diagnoses, disabilities, or challenges, except by what we allow ourselves and society to define for us. Kevin’s journey leads him to find out that he is a person first, a person diagnosed with bipolar disorder, instead of a manic depressive.

Kwaku embodies Kevin (he wrote him after all) truthfully portraying the many non-linear thought processes that carry him through this reminiscence. It’s a powerful piece of playwriting as it withholds nothing of the inner turmoil that runs rampant in his psyche and acutely addresses depression, its roots and causes, questioning both self and society, and landing squarely on the question, “Am I well?” or will I ever be?

A little background on the title:

Theobald Wolfe Tone was an Irish revolutionary who, in the late 1700s, strove to unite all of Ireland, both Catholic and Protestant, against the British by eliciting French military support. Caught during his second attempt to land French soldiers on Ireland’s shores, he died in prison under mysterious circumstances.

Author/actor Kwaku Fortune channels Wolfe’s fight for independence through fighting for his own inner independence in understanding who and what he is and how he got here. Although The Black Wolfe Tone is not about Irish revolutionaries like Wolfe Tone, the play grabs the spirit of revolution in its search for inner liberation.

—–

The Black Wolfe Tone is written by Kwaku Fortune and directed by Nicola Murphy Dubey

Actors: Kwaku Fortune as Kevin, Clare Barrett as the Voice of the Nurse

Scenic & Costume Designer: Maree Kearns, Lighting Designer: Adam Honoré, Sound Designer: Denis Clohessy.

Standard Seating: $60, Member Price: $0-$48. Tickets can be purchased HERE.

This production contains a discussion of suicide, drug use, mental illness, as well as strong language. Recommended for ages 14 and up.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

There was a time in NYC when the city was filled with off-off-broadway spaces that were cleared out, damp basement spaces that had been given a deep scrub, a couple of cycles of a dehumidifier, chairs were set up, and a performance space was declared.

Donald Margulies’ play Collected Stories (’97 Pulitzer Prize finalist) takes place in the ’90s, a time when those places existed. It is being performed at a theater space called East Village Basement that is much nicer than most of those old venues, but reminiscent of and giving the same feeling as you descend the stairs to enter the space. What those performance spaces were able to give their audiences that other, more established theatres couldn’t was a true sense of intimacy, an intimacy with the performers and the material they were presenting. That feeling is a strength that is compounded in this production by the acting talents of Grace Kiley and Christina Toth, and makes this presentation of Collected Stories that much more close and personal for the whole audience. These two actresses have discovered a connection within their characters that gives them ease in their interacting together that is a pleasure to be a part of. Besides the tight, thought-provoking script, watching this acting pair psychologically dance together, exposing both their strengths and weaknesses, is the main reason to make a point of going to see this production.

Established writer Ruth Steiner (Grace Kiley) has hired a student of hers to be her new assistant. With the opportunity to spend time in the presence of one of her idols, Lisa Morrison (Christina Toth) entwines herself in Ruth’s life, so much so that she becomes her to a degree and takes on her personal history. When Lisa’s writing begins to get noticed by the literary world, the jealousy that ensues crosses the border between what is my story, my life, and what is yours.

Donald Margulies’ script is captivating as it delves into the bones of these two characters, exposing more than just professional rivalry that has grown from the rich soil of love and a deep connection to each other. It’s always a blessing when you’ve got a great script and great actors coming together in the same playing space.

—–

Collected Stories, written by Donald Margulies, directed by  Lori Kee.
Performers, Grace Kiley and Christina Toth.

The creative team: Giovanni Valleri (light & sound design), Josie Underwood (prop coordinator), Carol Brodsky (costume coordinator), Akash Inti Katakam (set coordinator).

Collected Stories runs May 8 – 18 with performances on Mondays at 7pm, Wednesday – Friday at 7pm, Saturdays at 3pm and 7pm, and Sundays at 5pm. Performances take place at the newly opened East Village Basement, located at 321 E 9th Street (between 1 & 2 avenue) New York, NY 10003. Tickets are $40 – $78 and are on sale HERE.

content.rendered:
Review by Brittany Crowell

Ana (Tatianna Córdoba) is keeping her family together.  But Ana has a secret, and a dream; a dream that she can fly away from Boyle Heights, Los Angeles to attend Columbia University and become a journalist. Except, for Ana, it’s not so simple.  Her family are immigrants who are struggling to make their way in America and rely heavily on her for support on everything from signing the rent checks to helping build dresses at their factory.  ‘

None of this brings Ana down, however, as she learns to appreciate and own the struggle of her parents, learns how the system is broken, learns how to work with the system, and inspires all around her (herself, her community, the audience) to fight for your dreams and support your community.  Real Women Have Curves, Ana’s story, is an inspirational coming-of-age that shines a light on first loves, self-love, and learning not just what to fight for, but how to fight.  Audiences will leave the show feeling 1000x lighter and inspired by Ana’s journey to spread our wings, take action, and give joy.

Set in the 1980s, the show resonates tonally with the landscape of today’s America and current politics: it celebrates women of all sizes and uplifts immigrants from all backgrounds, highlighting an unforgotten American dream and lauding those who struggle to make better for themselves in a land that often works to bring them down.

Directed and choreographed by Tony and Olivier Award winner, Sergio Trujillo, Real Women Have Curves features a strong ensemble cast chocked full of talent (and Broadway debuts!).  Justina Machado brings tears to your eyes and a smile to your face as the tough immigrant mother, Ana; and Florencia Cuenca brightens the stage as Estela, Ana’s older sister who runs the dress factory.  

Mason Reeves and Tatianna Córdoba; photo by Julieta Cervantes

Factory workers played by Shelby Acosta, Carla Jimenez, Jennifer Sanchez, and Sandra Valls bring personality and color to the stage picture.  During my performance, Elisa Galindez (understudy) was brought into the cast and shined as the Guatemalan immigrant, Itzel. The ensemble team is rounded out by Mauricio Mendoza as Ana’s father and Mason Reeves as Henry, Ana’s quirky young boyfriend who charms Ana and audiences alike with his naive eagerness and innocence and provides many moments of comic relief throughout the show.

Complimenting the energetic ensemble is the colorful and dynamic scenic design by Arnulfo Maldonado, with video by Hana S. Kim and lighting by Natasha Katz.  The show’s designs work together to transport us into Ana’s surreal and colorful perspective, crafting a beautiful tapestry of color, light, flowers, embroidery, and fabric and painting a picture of a world of beauty and possibility that can only be seen through the eyes of youth and ambition.

“Give me your tired, your poor” Lady Liberty reads. Real Women Have Curves lifts up those tired and poor, it celebrates them (and the audience) and encourages us to show up as we are.  It teaches us to fight for our dreams and stand up for what we believe in; to hope.  It lifts the lamp beside the golden door and shines a light on the immigrant story – and what an inspirational story that is. 

 

REAL WOMEN HAVE CURVES – music and lyrics by Joy Huerta and Benjamin Velez; book by Lisa Looner with Nell Benjamin

Directed and choreographed by Sergio Trujillo

FEATURING: Tatianna Córdoba; Justina Machado; Florencia Cuenca; Mauricio Mendoza; Mason Reeves; Shelby Acosta; Carla Jimenez; Aline Mayagoitia; Jennifer Sánchez; Sandra Valls; Ariana Burks; Shadia Fairuz; Elisa Galindez; Quincy Hampton; Omar Madden; Zeus Mendoza; Claudia Mulet; Christopher M. Ramirez; and Monica Tulia Ramirez

Set design by Arnulío Maldonado; lighting design by Natasha Katz; costume design by Wilberth Gonzalez & Paloma Young; sound design by John Shivers; video design by Hana S. Kim; hair, wig, and makeup design by Krystal Baleza & Will Vicari; creative consultant, Mark Kaufman; music director, Roberto Sinha; music coordinator, Michael Aarons; resident director, Emilia Lirman.  James Earl Jones Theater (138 W 48th Street).  https://www.realwomenhavecurvesbroadway.com/

title.rendered: A Musical Time Machine: American Classical Orchestra Illuminates Mozart and Beethoven at Lincoln Center

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

There are certain rare evenings when the walls between centuries dissolve, when the spirits of long-departed composers seem to hover in the air, nodding with approval as their intentions are realized with breathtaking authenticity. Last night at Alice Tully Hall, the American Classical Orchestra, under the inspired direction of Thomas Crawford, delivered precisely such a transporting experience with its “Magnificently Mozart” program.

When one opened the elegantly designed program booklet, it was clear this would be no ordinary concert. With their 19th-century accoutrements and historically accurate constructs, the ACO’s commitment to period instruments transformed familiar works into vivid new sonic experiences.

Illuminating Introductions: Crawford’s Engaging Pedagogy

Before the first notes sounded, Maestro Crawford established an extraordinary rapport with the audience through his illuminating remarks. With the affable charm and pedagogical brilliance reminiscent of Leonard Bernstein’s famed talks, Crawford deftly guided listeners through the architectural scaffolding of the evening’s program.

Using the orchestra as his demonstration tool, Crawford illuminated the principal themes of Mozart’s “Haffner” Symphony and Beethoven’s Piano Concerto No. 4, having various sections play motifs in isolation before showing how these musical building blocks would later interact. His explanations were never pedantic but infused with the joyful enthusiasm of someone sharing treasured secrets, seasoned with wit that made the education feel like entertainment.

Maestro Thomas Crawford and the American Classical Orchestra on stage in Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall in New York City. Photo by Edward Kliszus

Mozart’s “Haffner” Symphony: A Sonic Time Capsule

The concert proper began with Mozart’s Symphony No. 35 in D Major, K.385, known as the “Haffner.” Commissioned in 1782 by the Haffner family for Sigmund Haffner Jr.’s ennoblement ceremony, this work has a fascinating genesis. Conceived as a serenade with more movements, Mozart later adapted it for concert performance.

The ACO’s rendition revealed dimensions of this familiar work rarely heard in modern performances. The period instruments’ distinctive timbres allowed Mozart’s intricate orchestration to emerge with crystalline, authentic clarity. With their discrete 19th-century characteristics, the strings produced a warm, rounded sound that blended perfectly with the winds without being overwhelmed. Concertmaster Edson Scheid led the violin section with precise articulation that illuminated the sprightly dotted rhythms of the opening Allegro con spirito.

Young Mozart holding a music book, 1768. By Johann Eusebius Alphen, (Vienna 1742-1772). Elektromagikum, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Crawford’s interpretation emphasized the dynamic contrasts essential to the Classical period’s expression. The dramatic unison opening statement, with its majestic octave leaps, established both the work’s ceremonial character and the ensemble’s virtuosic capabilities. The second movement, Andante, unfolded with graceful lyricism, while the Menuetto balanced aristocratic poise with pastoral charm. The Presto finale—which Mozart directed to be played “as fast as possible”—sparkled with infectious energy and wit.

Schwartz Brings Mozart’s Bassoon Concerto to Vibrant Life

The first half concluded with Mozart’s Bassoon Concerto in B-flat Major, K.191, featuring the remarkable Andrew Schwartz as soloist. This work, completed when Mozart was 18 years old in 1774, is the only surviving bassoon concerto of the five he is believed to have written.

Schwartz, playing a period bassoon, brought both technical brilliance and expressive depth to this challenging work. The instrument itself, more delicate and nuanced than its modern counterpart, allowed for a surprising agility, highlighting Mozart’s ingenious writing for what is often considered an unwieldy instrument.

Andrew Schwartz, Bassoon. Courtesy handelandhaydn.org

The opening Allegro showcased the bassoon’s remarkable range, from its characteristic low notes to surprisingly agile passages in its upper register. Schwartz navigated Mozart’s demanding technical challenges—including rapid-fire note repetitions, dramatic leaps spanning nearly two octaves, and ornate trills—with apparent effortlessness while maintaining a singing tone.

The Andante ma Adagio movement revealed the lyrical soul of both performer and instrument. Schwartz shaped his phrases with a vocalist’s natural breathing and expression, the muted strings providing a cushion of sound that allowed the bassoon’s plaintive voice to soar above. The concluding Rondo danced with aristocratic elegance and playful humor, and Schwartz and the orchestra engaged in spirited dialogue that delighted the audience.

Somlai Transforms Beethoven’s Fourth Piano Concerto

Following intermission came Beethoven’s Piano Concerto No. 4 in G Major, Op. 58, with Petra Somlai performing on a fortepiano. This groundbreaking work, premiered by Beethoven in 1808, was dedicated to Archduke Rudolf, Beethoven’s patron and student.

Somlai’s choice of instrument—a fortepiano modeled after period instruments of Beethoven’s time—proved revelatory. The fortepiano’s more transparent texture and quicker decay allowed for a delicate balance between soloist and orchestra that modern pianos often struggle to achieve. This was immediately apparent in the work’s famous opening, where Beethoven broke tradition by having the soloist begin alone rather than waiting for an orchestral introduction.

Petra Somlai, Fortepiano. Courtesy aconyc.org

Somlai’s approach to this iconic opening—five gentle chords that establish both key and character—set the tone for her entire performance: thoughtful, nuanced, and deeply connected to the score’s architectural logic. Her fortepiano produced a warm and articulate tone, with a clarity that allowed each note of Beethoven’s complex passagework to register without becoming muddied.

The central Andante con moto, often described as a dialogue between the gentle piano and aggressive strings, unfolded dramatically. Crawford shaped the orchestral responses with rhetorical precision, and the strings’ articulation became gentler as the movement progressed.

The Rondo finale burst forth with irrepressible energy, Somlai navigating its technical challenges with precision and exuberance. With their escalating momentum and joyful spirit, the movement’s concluding passages brought the audience to its feet.

Period Instruments: The Time Machine of Sound

The visual and sonic landscape created by the ACO offered a remarkable window into the orchestral world of Mozart and Beethoven’s times. Following early 19th-century practice, the violins were divided left and right of the conductor, with first violins on the left and second violins on the right. This antiphonal seating allows the often dialogic writing for first and second violins to emerge more clearly than a Stokowski-inspired arrangement with cellos to the conductor’s right.

The string players used period bows—shorter, lighter, and more convex than their modern counterparts—naturally creating the articulated, speech-like phrasing essential to classical, early 19th-century style. Their gut strings produced a warmer, more transparent sound with a quicker response. Even how the musicians held their instruments reflected historical practice, with violinists and violists playing without chin rests.

Portret van Ludwig van Beethoven. Public Domain.

The woodwind section featured wooden flutes with a rounder, gentler tone than their metal descendants. The oboes have fewer keys than modern instruments, producing a more pastoral timbre. The clarinets, generally crafted of boxwood, gave a mellower, more organic sound. And Schwartz’s bassoon, with its narrower bore and fewer keys, allowed for remarkable agility while maintaining the instrument’s characteristic vocal quality.

The brass section exemplified some of the most dramatic differences from modern practice. The natural horns without valves change pitch through embouchure control and hand-stopping within the bell, producing a distinctive timbre for each note. Similarly, the valveless trumpets create a more varied color palette. Even the timpani featured calfskin heads rather than synthetic materials, providing a resonant thud that decays quickly.

Natural Trumpet in D. Metropolitan Museum of Art, DP-12679-012 CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Alice Tully Hall: Acoustic Perfection

The concert’s setting in Alice Tully Hall provided the perfect acoustic environment for these period instruments to flourish. Since its renovation in 2009, the hall has been transformed into one of the world’s premier chamber music destinations, with acoustics that pianist Wu Han has described as making it “the quietest place in New York City.”

The hall’s African moabi wood paneling creates visual warmth and acoustic intimacy, allowing the natural sound of period instruments to project with clarity without forcing performers to oversaturate their tone. The 1,086-seat Starr Theater strikes that difficult balance between being large enough for orchestral works yet intimate enough for chamber music, making it an ideal venue for the ACO’s historical approach.

Maestro Thomas Crawford and Petra Somlai, fortepiano, taking bows during extended applause with the American Classical Orchestra in Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall in New York City. Photo by Edward Kliszus

A Transformative Musical Experience

For those in attendance, the concert offered more than just beautiful music; it provided a form of time travel, transporting listeners to the sound world that Mozart and Beethoven knew. The crisp attacks, the transparent textures, the natural balances between sections, and the distinctive timbres of period instruments combine to create an authentic and fresh experience.

Crawford’s direction throughout was a model of elegant restraint, allowing the music’s inherent architecture to emerge without imposing interpretive idiosyncrasies. His conducting combined precise technique with expressive freedom, giving the musicians clear guidance while allowing them room for their artistic contributions.

In an age when classical music is sometimes treated as a museum piece, the American Classical Orchestra under Thomas Crawford proves that historical authenticity can yield performances of startling freshness and immediate impact. Last night’s concert demonstrated that period instruments are not academic curiosities but vital tools for revealing the full expressive range of masterworks we thought we knew.

A Musical Time Machine: American Classical Orchestra Illuminates Mozart and Beethoven at Lincoln Center

American Classical Orchestra

PO Box 366
New York
NY 10025-0007
Office: (212) 362-2727
For tickets and information, go to https://aconyc.org/.

excerpt.rendered: There are certain rare evenings when the walls between centuries dissolve, when the spirits of long-departed composers seem to hover in the air, nodding with approval as their intentions are realized with breathtaking authenticity. From the moment one opened the elegantly designed program booklet, it was clear this would be no ordinary concert. With their 19th-century accoutrements and historically accurate construction, the ACO’s commitment to period instruments transformed familiar works into vivid new sonic experiences.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

If you do not adore Sondheim – this could be the show that changes your mind.  On the other hand, if you don’t LIKE Sondheim, you may be suffering from some heretofore unnamed or unknown condition.  If, however, you do like/love/adore Sondheim, you might need smelling salts to get you through this two hour extravaganza.

I must tell you that I was somewhere in between.  I have my favorite songs and my favorite musicals, but the two were not necessarily connected or dependent on one another.  I didn’t even know that some of my favorites were penned by him.

This production may have been created to set the record straight for a whole bunch of us by collecting a cornucopia of songs by Sondheim and delivering them to us en masse.  blended withBy my count there are 40 songs here.  And I know for a fact that this ain’t all of them.  No idea how Cameron Macintosh, who lists himself as Devisor and Producer, and Director Matthew Bourne chose what they chose.  There are the familiar: Send In The Clowns, Tonight, The Ladies Who Lunch, Side By Side and of course Old Friends.  This, however,  is a mix and match night with the well-known blended with the lesser or even obscure..  If you are looking for the whisper of a plot – save yourself the trouble.  This is a shower of Sondheim.  Period.  It is a grand buffet that floats on the air and offers you delectable snippets one after the other.  And who are you to refuse?

The set up is reminiscent of the staging we have come to expect from Encores!  The orchestra, conducted by Annbritt duChateau, is platformed upstage and the “Performers” as each one is identified in the Playbill are all downstage.  The sets by Matt Kinley are minimal but imaginative.  They underscaore thatfor it is the music that is taking center stage.  Costumes, especially for for the women, are fleeting and fabulous.  All the elements conspire to deliver the best they can so that we receive the full grandeur and force of Sondheim.

Bernadette Peters; Photo by Matthew Murphy

Among the “Performers,” Bernadette Peters – her “Send In The Clowns” will shatter you – and Lea Salonga – who is a fantastic Mrs. Lovett from “Sweeny Todd” (along side the brilliant Jeremy Seacomb) are the clear leaders. The rest of the cast, however, is talented in the extreme.  They are each triple threats.  They can act, sing and dance.  The voices are thrilling.  The dance moves are dizzying.  I have no idea how they remember the many complicated transitions.  Fortunately the  folks in charge have managed to stagger the numbers so that there are plenty of solos sprinkled throughout that give those offstage a chance to slip into the costumes for their next incarnation.  It all appears to be done without a care.  Which means it is a boatload of coordination and work.

Jeremy Seacomb and Lea Salonga; Photo by Matthew Murphy

This is a dip into an experience of excellence from start to finish.  Every element shines.  When it is over, you walk out saying, “How did one person produce such a treasure trove of music?  How did one person create ALL THIS?”

When it’s over, you want it to start again.

Manhattan Theatre Club, in association with CMI and Daryl Roth, presents Cameron Mackintosh’s Production of Stephen Sondheim’s Old Friends. Directed by Matthew Bourne, side by side with Julia McKenzie

WITH Bernadette Peters, Lea Salonga, Jacob Dickey, Kevin Earley, Jasmine Forsberg, Kate Jennings Grant, Bonnie Langford, Beth Leavel, Gavin Lee, Jason Pennycooke, Joanna Riding, Jeremy Secomb, Kyle Selig, Maria Wirries, and Daniel Yearwood.

Choreography by Stephen Mear, Musical supervision is by Alfonso Casado Trigo and Stephen Brooker, musical arrangements by Stephen Metcalfe, and conducted by Annbritt duChateau. Set design by Matt Kinley, projection design by George Reeve, costume design by Jill Parker, lighting design by Warren Letton and sound design by Mick Potter.

At the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre (261 West 47th Street).  Through June 15.  TICKETS

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.
