content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

It’s love!  It’s love!  Wonderful Town has brought joy to the City Center stage – and boy do we need it.  Spread the news!  (Someone, please take this show to Broadway.)

In 1935, the wonderful town of New York was (and remains) a town of opportunity, and Greenwich Village a colorful mixed bag of eccentrics, artists and go-getters.  In walk Eileen (an effervescent Aisha Jackson) and Ruth (a luminous Anika Noni Rose) Sherwood, two sisters from Columbus OH, drawn to the big city by a dream.  And New York City does not disappoint.  The opening number sets the scene – the full panoply of life in the City, with its dizzying crowds and incredible diversity.  Bernstein excels at painting with music, the spirit of which choreographer Lorin Latarro captures beautifully.

On the modest City Center stage, further restricted by the presence of the onstage orchestra, ensemble numbers could easily become a bit of a circus, but Latarro and director Zhailon Levingston make the dance purr like a kitten.  They deftly keep the traffic flowing, with clear lines and intention.  This gives the impression of a larger playing space, on which the dancers can fully extend and leap with impunity (which they do).  Whether tapping, slinking across stage, or jumping and jiving, this ensemble delivers on every level.

The characters we meet — a boatload of conga-crazy Brazilian sailors, a besotted Irish policeman with a terrific tenor voice, a gingham clad tap dancer improvising a slightly tipsy interpretive dance, three earnest disciples of Martha Graham, and more.  It’s all such fun.  Yes, some of the writing hasn’t aged that well, and Act I is a bit long.  Yes, the energy drops in some of the non singing scenes, as the staging feels a little awkward and even at times aimless, but honestly, I kinda don’t care.

Among the notable performances Fergie Philippe as Wreck, the sweetheart, bull-in-a-china-shop, ex-football player, delights.  His ‘Pass the Football’ brought down the house.  Robert Baker (Javier Muñoz), an unexpected choice for romantic lead — solely because the character is a not some lovelorn male ingenu – is a study in contrasts: the City-savvy guy vs. the man with quiet depth.  Muñoz’s performance sneaks up on you, as the outer shell cracks and in a beautiful baritone voice he expresses Baker’s true desire for ‘A Quiet Girl.’  Dewitt Fleming Jr., as the slippery Speedy Valenti, the owner of the rather steamy Village Vortex nightclub brings Cab Calloway pizzazz to his wily character.

At the center, however, stand the sisters from Ohio.  As Eileen, Aisha Jackson sparkles with that special something that will not be denied.  Her smile, her capacity to beguile, her silvery voice.  It’s effortless.  Eileen is a role that could so easily be precious, but Jackson balances impishness with control, charming her way into every heart.  Anika Noni Rose grounds Ruth in big sister practicality, which she layers with warmth, humor and wit.  Her innocence vies with her ambition, to create a fizzy and creamy soda fountain confection.  Rose has a warm, rich voice.  She gives a particularly tour-de-force performance in not one but two devilishly difficult patter songs (a Comden and Green specialty).  Jackson and Rose’s voices blend perfectly, in duets like the wistful ‘Ohio’ and its polar opposite ‘Wrong Note Rag.’

Levingston milks the laughs just enough, reining in any character tempted to push the comedy too far, without squelching the actors’ exuberance.  He gives each individual a chance to shine, even in the smallest moments.  The depth of talent onstage is impressive, including old school hoofers, clean, legit voices, the luxury of a couple of real Irish tenors and several incredible baritones.  What a joy to hear full vocal harmony, and sung so well.  All backed by that kicking Encores! Orchestra.  It’s old school and I am here for it!

Don’t miss this opportunity to leave a theatre starry-eyed and happy-hearted, reliving the hopeful anticipation you felt as a newcomer to NYC.  You will fall more than little bit in love (again).

Wonderful Town book by Joseph Fields and Jerome Chodorov, music by Leonard Bernstein, lyrics by Betty Comden and Adolph Green.  Directed by Zhailon Levingston and choreographed by Lorin Latarro, with tap choreography by Ayodele Casel.  Mary-Mitchell Campbell, music director.

With Jimmy Ray Bennett, Etai Benson, Allison Blackwell, Dewitt Fleming Jr., Jessie Hooker-Bailey, Aisha Jackson, Javier Muñoz, Fergie Philippe, John Rapson, Anika Noni Rose and Daniel Torres.

Presented by New York City Center, Encores! (131 West 55th St.).  Runs through May 11th.  For tickets go here, or visit www.nycitycenter.org.

Runtime 2 hours and 30 minutes with one intermission (during which I suggest you check out the merch – heck, I bought the tote bag!)

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

Your mama’s dead

Your daddy’s dead

Whole family’s dead

And so are you.

After receiving seven Tony Award Nominations Thursday morning, the cast of Dead Outlaw was ready for an explosive performance on the night I was there.  They did not disappoint.  Let us hope that Dead Outlaw,  the captivating telling of the life of a real-dead outlaw will run as long as Elmer McCurdy’s legacy.

Previously being the home of Swept Away, a musical tale set in the 1880’s, Longacre fittingly holds yet another historical production featuring death. I left Longacre captivated, telling local theater goers and friends out of state alike. I can’t stop wishing my family, who are involved in the funeral and cemetery businesses had experienced this; they would absolutely eat this up.

Dead Outlaw, conceived by David Yazbek with a book by Itamar Moses, tells the story of Elmer McCurdy (Andrew Durand), who was not only a man with a traumatic childhood and drinking problem, but an infamously failed train robber, husband, and dead outlaw. But his life didn’t quite stop when he was shot dead during a shootout with police. I was wildly charmed by this chronicle of this corpse’s adventures, as directed by David Cromer.  McCurdy had no family or friends to claim his body, so he was preserved with arsenic. This preservation turns into a marvel, a phenomenon, a real-life mummy.

Photo Credit by Matthew Murphy

While it took decades for his body to make it to a grave, he remained completely intact for most of his post-death life.  He became a popular carnival attraction, actually making it in Hollywood, and touring the country alongside a cross-country foot-race.

Behind this outrageous plot is a full band, led by Jeb Brown, holding the narrative together with a foot-stomping score that produced guffaws and cackles from the audience the entire night.

Photo Credit by Matthew Murphy

Andrew Durand‘s performance both as an alive and dead outlaw, was poignant.  The straight-forward young years led into adulthood.  He didn’t ask for sympathy but garnered it still. When opportunity for a real family and community was given to McCurdy, his alcoholism and yearning for riches prevented him from staying. Durand, deathly still and silent, captivated me even more than he did as a live man—rightfully so.  McCurdy himself lived as a corpse more than double the number of years he was actually alive.

Unfortunately this story line may not have as much footing and plot strength as other shows opening this season, but it’s strength comes from its unique use of music to lighten and humorize what is a dark and appalling story.

Jeb Brown leads us through the loose theme of life using you up til you’re just a mangled corpse.

Let the mummy offer you some good advice 

You pick a road and you pay a price

They’ll use you up, they won’t think twice, so kid you better run.

Scenic Designer, Arnulfo Maldonado, presents us with a realistic graphic dummy of McCurdy after his corpse has been mutilated. It’s a prop that first cleverly helps to open the production, gearing us up for what’s to come.

Photo Credit by Matthew Murphy

While McCurdy and the band filled the stage, other characters seemed to linger in the shadows; his wife (Julia Knitel) and Dashiel Eaves, played several small roles but I wouldn’t remember them beyond their trivial roles as a pretty, gentle wife and a timid, awkward townsman. They filled scenes as McCurdy attempted robberies and managed to spend years penniless, train hopping, but their presence drifted beyond this.  Though, again, there just simply may not be purpose having in expanded those roles. The musical is what it set out to be: a fun, loud retelling of a dead outlaw’s life.

 

Directed by David Cromer.

Book by Itamar Moses; David Yazbek (Music & Lyrics, Conception); Erik Della Penna (Music & Lyrics, Co-Orchestrator).

CAST: Andrew Durand (Elmer McCurdy), Jeb Brown (Bandleader/Jarrett), Eddie Cooper (Press 3/Grampa/Conductor/Judge/Soldier/Posse/Coroner Johnson/Huckster/Dwain Esper/Delegate), Dashiell Eaves (Robber/Teamster/Charles/Bartender/Louis/Conductor/Soldier/Posse/Gawker/Charles Patterson/CC Pyle/Buyer/Delegate), Julia Knitel (Press 1/Helen, Maggie, Gawker, Huckster, Millicent, Delegate), Ken Marks (George/Root/MacArthur/Sheriff/Gawker/Sonney/Delegate), Trent Saunders (Robber/Press 2/Sadie/Victim/Bartender/Army Bud/Soldier/Possee/Luke/Huckster/Andy Payne/Dan/Delegate), Thom Sesma (Coroner Noguchi/Soldier/Possee/Gawker/James Patterson/Huckster/Delegate).

BAND: Jeb Brown, Rebekah Bruce, JR Atkins, Hank Heaven, Brian Killeen, Spencer Cohen.

CREATIVE TEAM: Arnulfo Maldonado (Scenic Design); Sarah Laux (Costume Design); Heather Gilbert (Lighting Design); Kai Harada (Sound Design); Emily Fink (Dance Captain); Ani Taj (Choreographer, Associate Director), Dean Sharenow (Music Supervisor).

Dead Outlaw is playing at Longacre Theatre, 220 W 48th Street, New York, NY. Run time is 1 hour and 40 minutes, no intermission. Tickets can be purchased here.

content.rendered:
By Yuval Jonas

If you’d like to hear fancy brands name-dropped ad infinitum—Givenchy, Ralph Lauren, Yves Saint Laurent—then head over to LCT3 for Caitlin Saylor Stephens’ new play Five Models in Ruins, 1981.

The premise has some potential: a high-fashion photo shoot set on a remote English estate in the early ‘80s, with five models posing for Vogue’s October Issue wearing Princess Diana’s rejected wedding gowns. There’s no telephone for miles, so the models and photographer are there all by themselves. The setup could have led to something satirical, haunting, perhaps moving. Instead, the play and the production drown in caricature, weak directing, and shallow chatter.

The models are portrayed as frantic, shrieking dolls. They only yell, speak in a strange chipped rhythm, and speed through the dialogue. I’m not sure if it’s supposed to be Brechtian alienation, but if it is, it was successful indeed: I was by all means Verfremdungseffekted.

Morgan Green’s directing doesn’t help. In between scenes, the actors launch into awkward, meaningless dances. Perhaps these serve to start the next scene with the actors staged differently—I, personally, prefer walking to achieve such ends. It’s all quite reminiscent of high school theater: the actors move in front of each other to grab attention; turn to the audience when speaking; and later on, the stage is split with one side talking while the other fakes conversation in silence—then they switch.

At the play’s center is Roberta (Elizabeth Marvel), a supposed “genius” photographer. When a character has a profession on stage, and we’re told they’re good at it, we want to believe it. We’re attracted to characters who are excellent at what they do. But Roberta does not persuade us. She’s hesitant, self-pitying, and hopelessly amateurish. At one point, she even tells the model to look through the camera and tell her how it looks; the scene continues with the model photographing her. I recommend Annie Leibovitz’s MasterClass as a start; maybe she teaches the respective roles (photographer takes photos; model models).

Vasilija Zivanic’s costumes are also distracting, particularly for the models. But even Roberta, whose dark blue suit is actually sharp, has her look undermined by a tie that runs longer than her vest.

Roberta tells the models to just “be yourselves.” The models are shocked: We? We’re “mannequins, hangers, girls.” So if the play is attempting some form of feminine empowerment, why has their creator made their personalities so shallow? They spend almost all of the play fussing with makeup, naming brands, and mentioning celebrities they’ve slept with.

Madeline Wise as Sandy gives a truthful performance. She’s subtle, and finds a dynamic rhythm with the text.

Five Models in Ruins, 1981 purports to examine femininity and the pressures of modeling, but ends up rehashing the old stereotypes. Instead of witnessing a great photographer battling with her models—for better or worse—we watch a poor imitation of a photographer battling with herself, a few models around by chance. Instead of watching these women defy our expectations, we see old caricatures bandied about to the detriment of all. 

FIVE MODELS IN RUINS, 1981 by Caitlin Saylor Stephens; Directed by Morgan Green.

With: Stella Everett, Elizabeth Marvel, Maia Novi, Britne Oldford, Sarah Marie Rodriguez, Madeline Wise.

Sets by Afsoon Pajoufar. Costumes by Vasilija Zivanic. Sound by Kathy Ruvuna.

Now playing through June 1 at LCT3, Claire Tow Theater, 150 W 65th St. Tickets available here.

Running time: 95 minutes, no intermission.

title.rendered: Triumph of Sound and Spirit: Oratorio Society of New York Delivers Monumental Carnegie Hall Concert

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

Maestro Kent Tritle led the OSNY through a magnificent musical journey at Carnegie Hall in a masterful marriage of classical heritage and contemporary urgency.

In the hallowed acoustic splendor of Carnegie Hall’s Stern Auditorium, the Oratorio Society of New York, under the masterful direction of Kent Tritle, presented a splendid concert of profound musical and spiritual significance that left one feeling intellectually enriched and emotionally transformed. The OSNY Carnegie Hall program opened with the world premiere of Paul Moravec and Mark Campbell’s “All Shall Rise” and, following intermission, continued with Mendelssohn’s monumental Symphony No. 2, “Lobgesang”—a brilliant juxtaposition illuminating the extraordinary capacity of these works to speak across centuries to our deepest human concerns. From beginning to end, this was an inspirational concert of rare distinction, accompanied by a superbly informative program booklet containing scholarly notes, complete texts, and lucid translations.

Kent Tritle leading the Oratorio Society of New York. Photo by Eduardo Patino, NYC

A World Premiere of Extraordinary Power and Relevance

The OSNY Carnegie Hall concert began boldly with the premiere of “All Shall Rise” by Paul Moravec (music) and Mark Campbell (libretto). This third OSNY-commissioned collaboration between the Pulitzer Prize-winning composer and Grammy-winning librettist tackles America’s complicated history with voting rights through a brilliant collage of historical texts and imagined personal narratives. Campbell’s libretto moves from the Founding Fathers’ debates through the struggles for enfranchisement by African Americans and women to contemporary matters, creating a work of stunning contemporaneous relevance.

L-R Paul Moravec, Composer. Courtesy paulmoravec.com and Mark Campbell, librettist/lyricist. Courtesy markcampbellwords.com

Moravec’s musical language proves ideally suited to this ambitious text. His writing seamlessly integrates a dazzling array of stylistic approaches while maintaining a unique, coherent, imaginative artistic vision. His work is an alchemy of a surpassingly inventive and sympathetic mind. With its sardonic epigrams of the Founding Fathers’ arguments against universal suffrage, the opening prologue displays Moravec’s gift for subtle text-setting that simultaneously honors and interrogates the words. Knowing chuckles rippled through the audience as the chorus intoned, “Leave it up to the states”—a phrase with inimitable contemporary resonance. Furthermore, the work’s structure masterfully balances larger chorus sections with intimate solo narratives that personalize the abstract political struggles.

Contemporary Music That Speaks with Emotional and Intellectual Force

Moravec’s score revealed a remarkable stylistic range while maintaining artistically original, vibrant, and cohesive musical arguments. (Please note that I mention other composers only to provide contextual references for readers who have not heard the score.) The delicate a capella quartet “I Will Be Heard” achieved clarity and pathos as exemplified in Fauré’s  In Paradisum  from his “Requiem.” The harrowing narrative “I Continue On,” depicting the dialectics of a Black woman’s terror-filled journey to vote in 1964 Alabama, built tension through minimalist repetitions that recall the economy of means along with hints of the delicate, sonically effulgent beauty of the serenata of Stravinsky’s “Pulcinella Suite.” Meanwhile, the rich string timbres in the Frederick Douglass sections evoked the luminous string and woodwind textures of Schoenberg’s “Verklärte Nacht.” At the same time, with the artistic restraint as demonstrated by Brahms in the Adagio of his Violin Concerto in D Major, Op. 77, Moravec’s harmonic language displayed seamless chromatic shifts reminiscent of the most expressive style noted in Delius’s “The Song of the High Hills.”

The OSNY Carnegie Hall chorus, orchestra, and soloists tackled Moravec’s demanding score with exceptional technical assurance and emotional commitment. Their ability to pivot between different musical textures and characters was awe-inspiring, from the biting irony of the opening debate to the overwhelming emotional power of the final “All Shall Rise” climax. Tritle’s direction maintained a perfect balance between instrumental and vocal forces, allowing every textual nuance to register with clarity while building to emotional climaxes.

Vocal Soloists Shine with Extraordinary Artistry

The OSNY Carnegie Hall performance showcased vocal soloists of exceptional caliber. Susanna Phillips’ soprano soared with crystalline purity and emotional depth in both works. Her seamless technique and expressive intelligence illuminated every phrase with meaning and beauty. In his Carnegie Hall debut, Charles Williamson deployed his stentorian tenor with remarkable flexibility and tonal beauty that was particularly moving in his delivery of Frederick Douglass’s words in “All Shall Rise.” The rich, velvety mezzo-soprano of Lucia Bradford imparted profound gravity to her solos, especially in the harrowing “I Continue On” narrative.

L-R Tenor Charles Williamson-Courtesy @charchats on Instagram, Soprano Susanna Phillips-Courtesy @susannaphillipssoprano on Instagram, and Mezzo Soprano Lucia Bradford-Courtesy @lucia_renate_b on Instagram .png

Steven Eddy’s baritone provided eloquent authority to his interpretations, bringing Benjamin Franklin’s wry observations to life with humor and philosophical weight.

Tenor Ongama Mhlontlo delivered with clear diction and emotional conviction, his resonant tenor voice emerging distinctively from the choir section. Like Gyasi Barber, who sang from among the chorus rather than as a stage-front soloist, Mhlontlo’s integration within the ensemble created a compelling democratic symbolism that perfectly complemented the work’s themes of inclusion and representation.

These remarkable singers formed a cohesive dramatic ensemble, each contributing individual artistry while blending seamlessly into the larger tapestry.

Resurrecting Mendelssohn’s Choral Masterpiece with Pristine Brilliance

Following intermission, the OSNY Carnegie Hall concert continued with Mendelssohn’s “Lobgesang” (Hymn of Praise), a work that occupies a curious position in the symphonic canon. This masterpiece bridges the worlds of symphony and cantata with unprecedented structural ingenuity. Commissioned for Leipzig’s 1840 celebration of the quadricentenary of Gutenberg’s movable type, Mendelssohn’s symphony-cantata brilliantly connects the concepts of enlightenment, divine revelation, and human progress through printed communication. Furthermore, it explicitly acknowledges its debt to Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony while simultaneously celebrating the German musical lineage from Bach to Handel.

An Instrument of Divine Proclamation

Tritle’s conception of this challenging hybrid form was revelatory. The three-movement sinfonia, unfolded by the virtuosic OSNY orchestra, displayed its classical proportions and crystalline textures. The opening trombone motif—a unifying element that would return at key moments throughout the work—emerged with majestic authority, establishing the work’s fundamental gravitas. Mendelssohn’s deliberate choice of the trombone for this crucial motif resonated with deep historical significance. In the Lutheran sacred music tradition that Mendelssohn so revered, the trombone held special status as an instrument of divine proclamation and eschatological significance. Bach frequently employed trombones to underscore texts related to the Last Judgment and divine revelation, while in Renaissance and early Baroque sacred music, the instrument was associated with supernatural or otherworldly events. By prominently featuring this sonority, Mendelssohn created a distinctive timbral signature for his symphony and situated the work within a centuries-old tradition of sacred music that would have been immediately recognizable to his 19th-century Leipzig audience.

Moreover, the orchestra exhibited remarkable precision in the intricate contrapuntal passages, honoring Mendelssohn’s profound understanding of Bach’s techniques while maintaining a distinctly Romantic sensibility. The trombone choir’s burnished tone, meticulously balanced by Tritle, evoked the instrument’s traditional role in Lutheran chorales, creating a sonic bridge between past and present that impeccably embodied the work’s celebration of cultural and spiritual continuity.

L-R Tenor Ongama Mhlontlo-Courtesy opusonemusic.org, Baritone Steven Eddy-Courtesy steveneddybaritone.com and Bass Gyasi Barber-Courtesy @gyasibarber on Instagram

The Spiritual Journey: From Darkness to Transcendent Light

When the chorus finally entered with the exultant “Alles was Odem hat” (All that has breath), the OSNY Carnegie Hall performance achieved a new level of sonic magnificence. The Oratorio Society’s 175 voices created a tapestry of sound, filling the hall with radiant power without sacrificing textural clarity. Particularly affecting was the central turning point of the cantata, where the anxious question “Watchman, is the night past?” receives its hopeful answer. Soprano Susanna Phillips delivered her response with a luminous tone and profound emotional conviction, perfectly calibrated to Carnegie’s acoustical properties.

Orchestral Grandeur

Throughout the “Lobgesang,” Tritle maintained an unerring sense of dramatic pacing and architectural coherence. The climactic setting of “Nun danket alle Gott” (Now thank we all our God) achieved a transcendent quality, with the a cappella chorus giving way to orchestral grandeur in a manner epitomizing the work’s fundamental message of gratitude and praise. Additionally, the final fugal chorus brought the journey full circle with breathtaking contrapuntal precision as the returning trombone motif provided structural unity across the work’s considerable span. It reinforced the instrument’s traditional association with religious solemnity and divine proclamation.

Felix Mendelssohn’s Leipzig study. Public Domain

Kent Tritle: A Visionary Conductor of Exceptional Insight

This extraordinary OSNY Carnegie Hall concert represents the culmination of Kent Tritle’s remarkable career trajectory in New York’s musical life. As music director of the Oratorio Society of New York, Cathedral of St. John the Divine, and Musica Sacra, Tritle has established himself as the city’s preeminent choral conductor. His background as an acclaimed organist informs his profound understanding of sacred musical traditions, while his innovative programming demonstrates a commitment to expanding the choral repertoire.

Tritle’s approach to both works displayed his signature blend of intellectual rigor and emotional expressivity. His meticulous attention to detail—from pristine choral diction to carefully calibrated dynamic markings—never came at the expense of the music’s larger rhetorical purpose. Furthermore, his courageous decision to present a challenging world premiere followed by a neglected 19th-century masterpiece demonstrated his commitment to advancing the art form and preserving tradition.

Carnegie Hall: The Perfect Acoustic Canvas for Choral Magnificence

There is no more fitting venue for this OSNY Carnegie Hall program than Stern Auditorium, with its legendary acoustics. Since its 1891 opening—when the Oratorio Society performed under Tchaikovsky’s direction—Carnegie Hall has provided the ideal acoustical environment for choral-orchestral masterworks. The hall’s warm resonance enhances the choral blend while maintaining textural clarity, allowing the full dynamic range from hushed pianissimos to overwhelming fortissimos to register with sublime definition.

As the final “All Shall Rise” chorus reached its climactic conclusion before intermission, and later as Mendelssohn’s “Lobgesang” drew to its majestic close, one could almost sense the ghosts of Carnegie’s illustrious past—Tchaikovsky, Damrosch, Toscanini, Bernstein—nodding in approval at this continuation of the hall’s grand choral tradition. Additionally, the historical significance of the Oratorio Society’s 150-year relationship with Carnegie created a palpable sense of living cultural continuity, where past and present engaged in profound dialogue through the universal language of music.

The final, extended standing ovations aptly affirmed well-earned approbations.

The Oratorio Society of New York. Courtesy osny.org

The Timeless Relevance of Musical Masterpieces

What ultimately elevates this OSNY Carnegie Hall concert beyond a mere excellent performance is its demonstration of music’s unique capacity to transcend historical periods while speaking to immediate human concerns. Mendelssohn’s “Lobgesang,” though rooted in 1840s Germany, explores themes of darkness transformed to light that resonate powerfully today. Similarly, Moravec and Campbell’s “All Shall Rise,” although it addresses specific American democratic deliberations, ultimately speaks to universal questions of human dignity and representation.

As America debates political doctrine in the face of obloquy, pairing these works offers historical perspective and contemporary urgency. The OSNY Carnegie Hall performance reminds us that great art can commemorate the past, illuminate the present, and inspire future action. In masterfully realizing both works, Tritle and the Oratorio Society have given New York audiences a magnificent concert and a profound meditation on democracy’s fragile promises.

This closing concert of OSNY’s 2024-25 season is destined to rank among the most significant choral events of the year. Through technical excellence, emotional depth, and programmatic boldness, Tritle and his forces have showcased the enduring vitality of the choral tradition and its essential role in our cultural conversation. One eagerly awaits next season’s offerings from this storied organization that continues to balance historical significance with contemporary relevance.

Triumph of Sound and Spirit: Oratorio Society of New York Delivers Monumental Carnegie Hall Concert

Oratorio Society of New York

Kent Tritle, Music Director and Conductor

New York, NY 10163

excerpt.rendered: In the hallowed acoustic splendor of Carnegie Hall’s Stern Auditorium, the Oratorio Society of New York, under the masterful direction of Kent Tritle, presented a splendid concert of profound musical and spiritual significance that left one feeling intellectually enriched and emotionally transformed. The OSNY Carnegie Hall program opened with the world premiere of Paul Moravec and Mark Campbell’s “All Shall Rise” and, following intermission, continued with Mendelssohn’s monumental Symphony No. 2, “Lobgesang”—a brilliant juxtaposition illuminating the extraordinary capacity of these works to speak across centuries to our deepest human concerns. From beginning to end, this was an inspirational concert of rare distinction, accompanied by a superbly informative program booklet containing scholarly notes, complete texts, and lucid translations.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

I have no idea what this enormous production is.  Well, I know I saw a bunch of actors having a great time onstage.  They sing.  They D-A-N-C-E.  They leap tall buildings at a single bound.  Ships.  They leap sips.  To and from Ships.  Ramin Karimloo (Pirate King) is the point person for that, and he does not disappoint.

I am not a Gilbert & Sullivan aficionado – and it might have helped if I were.  While there are no other writers listed, there are very few musical numbers that sounded like Gilbert & Sullivan.  I know that this production has been adapted by Rupert Holmes.  What he did remains a mystery to me.  Perhaps that is the point.  This is a stylized musical that reminds a person of Gilbert & Sullivan.  Relocated to the New Orleans French Quarter, it is the tale of a Pirate King (and orphan) who has blown into town with an 8-man crew who are released upon the city to hunt down eligible women.  They cross paths with Major-General Stanley (David Hyde Pierce) who happens to have fathered that same number of daughters in every continent.  They are all gathered under his protection in New Orleans.  The pirate of the day is Frederic (Nicholas Barasch) who is about to be released from his apprenticeship to the Pirates (a grammatical error had him sent to pirates instead of pilots).  Upon release he intends to join the police and hunt down his erstwhile friends.  Go figure.  On this day, however, he sees Mabel Stanley (Samantha Williams) who is, in Frederic’s eye, the standout of the 8 daughters.

Hot on Frederic’s trail is his nanny, Ruth (Jinkx Monsoon), who has more than a motherly instinct in his future.

There is great to-ing and fro-ing with some dazzling dancing that makes the people sitting in their chairs dizzy enough to stop the show with howls of appreciation.  There are the familiar music numbers – even for an uneducated person like me – “Poor Wand’ring One,” “I Am The Very Model Of A Modern Major General,” and several that are borrowed from other G&S productions.  These are duly noted in the program.

Barasch, Karimloo and Monsoon; Photo Joan Marcus

The rest of the music (and there is a boatload of it) I am presuming to be from “The Pirates Of Penzance” (produced here in 1981 New York by the Public Theatre, starring Kevin Kline and Linda Ronstadt).  As I knew none of these numbers, the performances were fascinating but not engaging.  I was busy trying to figure out the thread of the plot and how much of this was from “Penzance” the original.  I was wasting my own time.

The Artistic team of Scott Ellis, Rupert Holmes, Warren Carlyle, And Joseph Joubert who put this show together does not seem to have been reaching for anything other than having a good time.  Jolly good fun and all that.  While the choices of material may not be astonishing in any way – the only thing left out was the kitchen sink, but they did include washboards and one banjo – the cast they have assembled takes the show to the moon and back.  Karimloo brings the same stage electricity he brought to Nicky Arnstein in “Funny Girl”.  He is riveting.  Whoever is in his crosshairs gets a dose of his flare – whether it is David Hyde Pierce or the audience itself.  Pierce is perfection as the General with love in his heart and a lot of empty apace in his attic.  Jinkx Monsoon hurls herself into Ruth with a mighty force.  The romantic leads have little to do except sing their hearts out – and THAT they do indeed.  The ensemble cast is over-the-top with energy, enthusiasm, pipes of gold and a willingness not only to have a good time but to spread the wealth.

Whatever-the-heck “Pirates! The Penzance Musical” is trying to be, you can be assured that a good time is waiting for you in the French Quarter that never was.

Pirates! The Penzance Musical by W.S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, Adaptation by Rupert Holmes, Directed by Scott Ellis. Conceived By Scott Ellis, Rupert Holmes, Warren Carlyle, And Joseph Joubert

WITH  Ramin Karimloo (Pirate King), Jinkx Monsoon (Ruth), David Hyde Pierce (Gilbert/Major General Stanley), Nicholas Barasch(Frederic), Preston Truman Boyd (Sullivan/Police Sergeant) and Samantha Williams (Mabel Stanley). The cast also includes Kelly Belarmino, Maria Briggs, Cicily Daniels, Ninako Donville, Alex Dorf, Rick Faugno, Niani Feelings, Tommy Gedrich, Alex Gibson, Afra Hines, Dan Hoy, Ryo Kamibayashi, Tatiana Lofton, Nathan Lucrezio, Shina Ann Morris, Tyrone L. Robinson, Cooper Stanton, and Bronwyn Tarboton.

The design team includes scenic design by Tony Award-winner David Rockwell, costume design by Linda Cho, lighting design by Donald Holder, sound design by Mikaal Sulaiman, and dance arrangements by John O’Neill

 

Through July 27 at Roundabout Theatre Company’s Todd Haimes Theatre.  TICKETS

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: A New Take on Mahler’s Ninth: David Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony

content.rendered:
By Edward Kliszus

NEW YORK – David Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony capture the essence of Mahler’s final completed Symphony in a new release on Recursive Classics.

In the vast catalog of orchestral recordings, certain interpretations emerge as definitive statements that reshape our understanding of familiar masterworks. The new recording of Mahler’s Symphony No. 9 by the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony under David Bernard undoubtedly belongs in this rarefied category. Released by Recursive Classics to celebrate the orchestra’s 25th anniversary, this milestone recording achieves that most elusive of musical goals: making a well-known work sound freshly minted, as if the ink on Mahler’s manuscript had barely dried, delivering revelatory clarity.

Composed during the summer of 1909 in Toblach on the Austrian-Italian border, Mahler’s Symphony No. 9  languished in a peculiar interpretive limbo for decades following its premiere in 1912, a year after the composer’s death. Unlike his earlier symphonies or Das Lied von der Erde, this final completed work arrived without the composer’s explanatory guidance, program notes, or interpretive framework. This contextual vacuum proved particularly significant for a composer who had meticulously shaped public understanding of his earlier works through detailed commentaries and performance instructions.

Mahler’s sudden passing foreclosed any opportunity for him to defend the work against overly simplistic “farewell” interpretations, leaving the public to see it through the inescapable lens of posthumous melancholy, which was tempting as the work emerged from a period of profound personal upheaval. Just two years earlier, Mahler had endured the devastating loss of his four-year-old daughter Maria to diphtheria and scarlet fever. Furthermore, during the same traumatic period, doctors diagnosed the composer with a serious heart condition. These twin calamities cast long shadows over the symphony’s creation.

At the same time, this was also a period of extraordinary professional momentum in Mahler’s life. His appointment as Director of the New York Philharmonic in 1909 represented a prestigious new chapter, thrusting him into America’s vibrant cultural scene, where he conducted over 100 performances across four seasons. Concurrently, Mahler maintained a feverish creative pace, simultaneously sketching his Tenth Symphony while completing the Ninth and planning future conducting tours. 

Leonard Bernstein, the de facto leader of the Mahler revival, constructed the overarching narrative for the Ninth Symphony during the 1960s as Mahler’s conscious farewell to life. This interpretation filled the vacuum of interpretive context brewing over the decades. 

This takes us to the current Recursive Classics release.  Through the introspective liner notes by David Patrick Stearns and David Bernard’s thought-provoking essay, “Beyond the Farewell: Survivorship Bias and Musical Meaning,” we are given a refreshingly multidimensional alternative to the “Farewell” narrative. Whereas Bernstein highlighted the symphony’s supposed death-obsessed finality, Stearns emphasizes its role as a culmination of the composer’s creative journey rather than merely his surrender to mortality. At the same time, Bernard explores how narratives of works written close to composers’ deaths are co-opted by public sentiment and lie in conflict with the works themselves.  This suggests a recalibration of how we might understand Mahler’s final completed symphony: not as a morbid farewell but as a multifaceted reflection on artistic creation itself.  

The recording is consistent with the context in the liner notes and essay. Bernard’s reading of Mahler’s Symphony No. 9 stands apart in its remarkable textural transparency. Every line emerges with clarity, yet nothing feels clinical or detached. On the contrary, this approach intensifies the emotional impact of the music, as listeners can follow each thread in Mahler’s complex tapestry while experiencing an overwhelming cumulative effect.

The opening Andante comodo unfolds with extraordinary patience, its halting rhythm suggesting the composer’s irregular heartbeat. Bernard masterfully balances the movement’s disparate elements—tender nostalgia, passionate declarations, and serene acknowledgement—while maintaining the music’s underlying pulse. The Park Avenue Chamber Symphony responds with playing of remarkable sensitivity and precision, eliciting unprecedented lucidity from Mahler’s dense orchestration.

The second movement’s grotesque Ländlers display the orchestra’s impressive technical facility. Principal woodwinds navigate Mahler’s challenging solos with astonishing agility and characterful phrasing. The string section, meanwhile, alternates between rustic earthiness and refined elegance, perfectly capturing the movement’s sardonic humor and nostalgic yearning.

In the ferocious Rondo-Burleske, Bernard unleashes his ensemble’s full virtuosic capabilities. The contrapuntal complexities emerge with startling clarity; each voice is deftly articulated yet contributes to the movement’s overwhelming momentum. The brass section deserves particular praise for its incisive attacks and sustained power, while the percussion provides a foundation of rock-solid rhythmic constancy.

The heart of this recording lies in Bernard’s profound realization of the final Adagio. In music that ponders the impact of a creative life on the world, Bernard achieves a rare mystical transcendence. The string section produces heart-stopping beauty, from whispered pianissimos that seem to emerge from silence to rich, full-bodied fortissimos of prodigious emotional authority.

Principal winds offer solos of exquisite sensitivity, with particularly notable contributions from the principal horn and oboe. With its progressively dissipating string textures, the famous valedictory coda unfolds with such concentration that time seems to stand still. Bernard’s superb pacing control allows the music to evolve naturally, creating an otherworldly experience that lingers long after the final notes have faded into silence.

David Bernard leading the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony in a recording of Mahler’s Symphony No. 9 at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music, New York City

The engineering achieves a remarkable balance between presence and natural perspective, placing listeners in the sweet spot where the orchestral voices can be heard in perfect proportion.  Recorded at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music by Audiosmith Digital Solutions and engineered by Christian Amonson of Seeing Sound, the transparent sound quality reveals the full spectrum of Mahler’s orchestral palette, from the deepest bass notes to the most ethereal harmonics. Dynamic contrasts, essential in Mahler’s Symphony No. 9, register with extraordinary impact, from barely audible whispers to shattering climaxes that never sound harsh or strained.

What ultimately distinguishes this recording of Mahler’s Symphony No. 9 is its remarkable ability to transport listeners across time and space. Through Bernard’s visionary interpretation and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony’s committed playing, we experience not just the notes on the page but the full emotional and spiritual context of Mahler’s world.

As the final Adagio fades into silence, we feel we have undertaken a profound journey through life, death, and transcendence. This is not merely a fine recording of a masterpiece; it is a transformative experience that reminds us of music’s power to illuminate the deepest aspects of human existence.

Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony have created a document that will stand as a reference point for Mahler’s Symphony No. 9 recordings for years to come. In celebrating their 25th anniversary with this album, they have given music lovers a gift of immeasurable value—a fresh perspective on one of the towering achievements of Western music.

Mahler Symphony No. 9 with David Bernard and the Park Avenue Chamber Symphony is available on Amazon in all formats (CD, download, and streaming) here: https://www.amazon.com/Mahler-Symphony-No-David-Bernard/dp/B0F6KMRXT3 and on streaming services (Apple Music, Spotify, Deezer) through this link: https://orcd.co/mahler9

By Vicki Weisfeld

Hollywood loves the “high concept” vehicle—that is, a story whose premise you understand from the title alone. (Think Snakes on a Plane or Back to the Future.) The minute you realize The Shark is Broken, the George Street Playhouse’s current comedic production by Ian Shaw and Joseph Nixon, is a behind-the-scenes look at the making of Jaws, you get it. The possibilities for mayhem are boundless. And you can enjoy seeing them play out from now until May 18 in this lively production under the direction of Peter Flynn.

Playwright Ian Shaw is the son of Robert Shaw, who played boat captain and shark-hunter Quint in Stephen Spielberg’s 50-year-old movie. The script is witty with a few short voyages into deeper waters, the actors are top-notch and compelling, and the set is perfect. The half-section of the little boat appears to bob against a cyclorama on which film of ocean waves and sky are projected. When the curtain opened at the beginning of the play, boat and background received an enthusiastic round of applause.

In 1974, somewhere in the open ocean east of Martha’s Vineyard, between East Chop and Oak Bluffs, the aggressively-named, but tiny ship, the Orca, is about to encounter an impressive mechanical shark. One so impressive thousands of movie-goers won’t go in the water for years afterward, if ever. One so impressive . . . well, it would be impressive if it worked. But the three fake sharks produced for filming are mostly beached with mechanical difficulties, and the three-man crew of the Orca, who play the movie’s three principal actors, have enforced, seemingly endless waiting time. As you’ll recall, they are: Roy Scheider (played by Jason Babinsky); Robert Shaw (Jeffrey M. Bender), and Richard Dreyfuss (Max Wolkowitz).

A movie scheduled to involve just under eight weeks of filming required almost 23 weeks, and the play effectively conveys the enforced claustrophobia. How do these three temperamentally dissimilar men stuck on a small boat cope with day after day of downtime? Sometimes with comedy, sometimes with philosophical discussion, and sometimes with booze or cocaine, which rarely helped.

Increasingly bored, the actors mull over what they think the movie means, but Shaw brings the conversation to an abrupt close saying it’s about a shark. The ending incorporates the filming of Quint’s famous monologue about the USS Indianapolis tragedy, which Shaw has been rewriting throughout the play, an effective bit of backstory motivation. Although they are largely at odds, the characters do somehow come together, as evidenced by their body language on ship, as well as the massive success of the film they rallied around, which we know but they don’t.

Production credits to Anne Mundell (scenic design), Siena Zoë Allen(costumes), Alan C. Edwards (lighting), Joanna Lynne Straub (sound), Adam J. Thompson (projections), Jennifer-Reneé Mullins (hair, wigs, and makeup), and Jeffrey M. Bender (fight direction).

The Shark is Broken is on stage at the New Brunswick Performing Arts Center. Tickets available here or by calling 732-246-7717.

content.rendered:
By Stanford Friedman

Every mother thinks her child is special, but rare is the mom who believes her son is gifted to the point that he can communicate with the dead, seeing what others cannot. Playwright Julia Barry Bell introduces us to just such a woman in the New Light Theater Project’s Mystic Conversations. This meditation on mysticism also has something to say about marital troubles, child-rearing, Catholicism and misplaced grief. Add to that the fact that Bell proclaims the play to be based on real events involving her own son, and the stage is set for an intriguing drama. Unfortunately, given a problematic structure and a cast that has yet to discover its chemistry, the production struggles to find a pulse.

The play, stocked with nameless characters, is at its best when The Mom (Jenny Strassburg) confronts, head-on, her agony over a miscarriage she suffered in the early years of her marriage to The Dad (Brandon Jones). The path to that epiphany, though, begins at a salon where, to Mom’s surprise, her regular hairdresser is nowhere to be found, replaced by another stylist who just happens to be a Mystic (Brenda Braxton). Mom mentions to Mystic that she has two children, but Mystic remarks to Mom that she really has three. This does not come as a total surprise to the audience since lingering around the stage, from start to finish, is the Spirit Child (Nicky Torchia), a gangly, silent and invisible-to-Mom teen, dressed in black.

During dinner, the same evening, Mom tells her family about her strange interlude. Dad is skeptical, while their two children, 15-year-old Sister (Frenie Acoba) and 10-year-old Boy (Lincoln Cohen) are curious. They ponder the difference between seeing ghosts and what they’ve learned in church. “What I heard today isn’t any stranger than the ‘The Angel Gabriel spoke to the Virgin Mary,’” Mom tells her clan, but theology proves to be a conversation killer, with the kids scooting off and Dad scolding her for confusing them with “other stuff” beyond their Catholic upbringing.

That other stuff takes precedence though when the Boy summons the courage to tell Mom that the Spirit Child had visited him. It turns out he also has confrontations with glowing orbs, not all of which are friendly, and experiences visions of the past and the future which “randomly pop in his head like a movie.” Consultations with the Mystic ensue, including a Tarot card reading that foreshadows an unhappy marriage but acceptance of her boy’s talents. Mom performs an unlikely exorcism of the orbs and a dubious blessing of her house with homemade holy water, before finally processing her sorrow in the presence of her all-seeing Spirit Child. 

Under the direction of Joey Brenneman, the cast struggles to find a consistent tone, given their narrowly written characters. Strassburg’s Mom pivots from tentative to frantic. She would also be a great Jeopardy! contestant because so much of her dialogue is gratingly in the form of a question. Braxton’s Mystic has moments of empathy that dissipate in long pauses. Acoba does a fine job as the Sister but, as the less interesting sibling, has little to do. Cohen’s quiet portrayal of the boy is eerily and appropriately in a world of his own while Torchia ‘s mute Spirit Child is a study in the effectiveness of facial expressions.

Much of what occurs on stage feels repetitious with Mom having to explain to Mystic what we already know of the Boy, then rehashing to the family what she learns from the Mystic. But a bigger problem is the dozen or so back-and-forth scene changes, complete with soporific music that, across the play’s 90 minutes, slows the action and destroys the vibe. A practical life lesson of the night is that the upside of having a black-clad Spirit Child constantly around is that he is always there to assist the stagehands between scenes.

 

Mystic Conversations – By Julia Barry Bell, directed by Joey Brenneman

WITH: Jenny Strassburg (The Mom), Brenda Braxton (The Mystic), Lincoln Cohen (The Boy), Brandon Jones (The Dad), Frenie Acoba (The Sister) and Nicky Torchia (the Spirit Child).

Scenic and Prop Designer is Dana Weintraub. Costume Designer is Ghislaine Sabiti. Lighting Designer is Bobbi Reneé Fullerton. Sound Designer is The Roly Polys (Janet Bentley + Andy Evan Cohen). New Light Theater Project at Theatre Row, 410 W 42nd St., https://mysticconversations.com/. Through May 17. Running time: 90 minutes

content.rendered:
By Nicole Itkin

The Death of Rasputin is an immersive experience depicting the end of Rasputin’s life in 1916 Petrograd. The show allows audience members to walk through different rooms in a grand mansion and experience different scenes. Dancing. Singing. Love. Lies. All await behind different doors. There is a little room where revolutionaries are plotting and planning. There is a bar room where everyone is dancing and singing and drinking. There is a glamorously colored bedroom. All is wonderfully decorated. 

Here is an interesting element of the show—so much is constantly going on that it is impossible to see everything. This provides room for interesting commentary about what happens behind closed doors: that we miss as much as we see and that history is so fragmented and difficult to piece together. However, on the part of the audience, it also leads to a frustrating sense of lack—to a consistent sense that you are missing so much, that you simply do not understand the narrative, that you are missing so much that it does not even feel worthwhile to be there. 

Fundamentally, in the world of theater, one walks in with some expectation of a narrative. And I walked away with less of a sense of a narrative than I had when I walked in. 

All of the scenes were tucked away in their own little rooms, and the scenes were taking place all at the same time. There were a plethora of moments when I, and others, were milling about rooms, confused about where to proceed to and the staff simply looked at us and said nothing. There was no clear sense of how to proceed through the show or where to go at any given time. Further, even if I was in the right space at the right time—and that was just a series of lucky guesses—the setup of the show required audience members to be incredibly physical to actually see any of the actors or the action. The actors, who I think were meant to guide the audience to the next set of rooms, ended up being the only ones who knew where to go. Because of that, they were always getting there first and were always in the front row, which meant that the audience was often struggling to peer over and around them to see the show. 

Now, there were certainly beautiful moments in the show. A poisoning scene was well done. A ball at the end was beautifully conducted. If I had been able to see the show, I am certain that I would have enjoyed it. As it was though, I was left looking at closed doors and massive crowds.

This show had so much promise! I hope adjustments are made to crowd work so that future audience members can actually see the show.

 The Death of Rasputin began performances on April 17, 2025, at LMCC’s Arts Center at Governors Island (110 Andes Road New York, New York 10004) for a limited run through May 11, 2025. You can purchase tickets here.

The cast includes: Jake Ryan Lozano, Ginger Kearns, Zina Zinchenko, Adam Griffith, Audrey Tchoukoua, Manatsu Tanaka, Tim Creavin, John William Watkins, Lucy York Struever, Cashton Rehklau, and Louis Butelli.

The Death of Rasputin is directed by Ashley Brett Chipman & Hope Youngblood, with assistant direction by Julia Sharpe. is written by Julia Sharpe, David Campbell, Hope Youngblood & Ashley Brett Chipman. It features choreography by James Finnemore, production management by Allison Camali, and is produced by Kelly Bartnik. The Death of Rasputin will feature set design by Lili Teplan, costume design by Eulyn Colette Hufkie, lighting design by Devin Cameron and sound design by Stephen Dobbie.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

“Ceremonies In Dark Old Men” by Lonnie Elder III, is a long, beautifully constructed, old fashioned play.  The story is laid out with laser precision within the first few minutes.  The time is the early 1950’s.  The place is Harlem, specifically 126th Street between Lenox and Seventh.  We are in the barbershop of one Russell Parker (Norm Lewis) who, when we meet him, has not been doing much barbering for the past few years.  Since his dancing legs gave out he is a man without a purpose or a desire to fine one. He occupies  his time sitting in his throne of a barber chair reading the paper or playing checkers with his best friend William Jenkins (James Foster, Jr.) who has beaten Parker every single time they play.

Parker’s two sons Theopolis (Bryce Michael Wood) and Bobby (Jeremiah Packer) are similarly employed – or not.  The reason this trio can afford to spend time on nothing is that their sister Adele (Morgan Siobhan Green) has picked up the torch left by her mother, Doris, died a few years back.  Doris supported the household while her husband and sons did nothing.  It lead to her early and sad death – a fact that Parker carries with him.

Adele, however, has reached her breaking point.  She has given the gents a deadline.  Within the next six days they must find work or another place to live.  Full Stop.

Theopolis does indeed get a job, but it is with The Organization of a well dressed gentleman named Blue Haven (Calvin M. Thompson) who deals in anything that will give him control of the people who live in Harlem – this means the black folks who live there and the white folks who own businesses.  In this case he will support Theo who has perfected a killer Corn Liquor called Black Magic and in return Theo will run numbers and Bobby will continue to shoplift wherever and whenever he can.  This switch in circumstances makes Theo the breadwinner and releases Adele from financial responsibility.  None of this is good any way you look at it.

Occasionally we, the audience, are ahead of the game as observers, and it takes a restraining point of view to stop the actors from playing their hands too soon.  For the most part Clinton Turner Davis’s direction does that.  There is the occasional lapse but never for long.  The extraordinary set by Harry Feiner  deserves special mention.  The barbershop and its environs reek of life.  You can almost smell the hair tonic and cologne that Parker would use if he had any customers.  And while you know there is a life Inside – you can also feel the life Outside.  Well done indeed.

You will carry this family and their associates with you.  No matter your race or economic situation.  In this tiny little shop in this tiny little family rests the whole world.  Every hope and dream.  Every hurt and broken promise.  Mr. Elder packs the elements in and turns his characters loose on each other.  “Ceremonies” will stick to your ribs.   Norm Lewis bears the weight of the tale on his more than capable shoulders.  Story wise the tale could use a few nips and tucks toward the end of act two. Even Mr. Lewis seems to lose steam through no fault of his own.  Mr. Elder’s writing is strong enough to tolerate some brevity as the walls close in on the Parker family.  Perhaps in the next production – this is a play that should never really close.

CEREMONIES IN DARK OLD MEN

WITH Felicia Boswell, James Foster Jr., Morgan Siobhan Green, Norm Lewis, Jeremiah Packer, Calvin M. Thompson, and Bryce Michael Wood

The scenic design is by Harry Feiner; costume design by Isabel Rubio; and lighting design by Jimmy Lawlor.

Ceremonies in Dark Old Men will play a six-week engagement, April 11 – May 18, at Theatre at St. Clements, 423 W. 46th Street, NYC)

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

It is a situation devoutly to be wished – to be saturated with artistic excellence everywhere you look for over two hours.  “Just In Time” – recently opened at Circle In The Square will do that to you.  From the moment you enter the theatre you are surrounded with glowing blue lighting, drapes and cocktail table scattered across the orchestra section.  This is Bobby Darin’s world and welcome to it.  Your host for the show is the thrilling Jonathan Groff, who makes no bones about NOT being Bobby Darin.  He is there to tell the story.  Well, SING the story might be more accurate.

This is your standard come-from-nowhere and turn into a legend setup.  Like “A Beautiful Noise” (Neil Diamond) and “Beautiful” (Carol King).  It is written, however, in a way that pulls us in.  The audience is included in the telling of the tale.

Jonathan Groff; Photo by Matthew Murphy and Evan Zimmerman

Groff announces a few pit stops for the journey; New York, Las Vegas, Hollywood and even Portofino.  The journey is not easy.  Starting at 2nd Avenue and 125th Street where Walden Robert Perciville Cassotto was born.  He was a sick child, suffering from rheumatic fever  more than once which damaged his heart.  He overheard the doctor tell his mother that it would be a miracle if the kid lived past 16. A sense of urgency was planted.  He bummed around the music world in midtown New York, always looking for more.  Falling in love with Connie Francis (Concetta Rosa Maria Franconero) threw him into romance and music – and a new name.  Slowly the doors creaked open, but not with anything that makes him proud.  Even his first gold record, “Splish Splash” was not the acknowledgment he was looking for.

Darin does become the star he was looking for.  It is still not enough.  The outcome is dreary. His life is a short one.  Wisely, however, the creative team of Warren Leight and Isaac Oliver choose a path that focuses, not on Darin’s death but on on Darin’s style, the evolution of his music, and what he and Groff share.

Early on, Groff tells us “… all I ever wanted to do growing up was sing and dance on a stage, to entertain. To be trusted with a couple hours of your day. To find your eyes out there in the dark and make a connection… Bobby Darin was the same. I never would’ve guessed I’d have anything in common with him, the playboy crooner and me in Mom’s pumps, but turns out I do. He loved — (gestures back and forth between himself and the audience)— this. It was the only relationship he was any good at.” Groff admits, “me too.”

Groff plays both ends of the narration, sometimes as Darin and sometimes as  himself. .  He sings, dances, plays the piano, drums, and oh yeah he acts. Like I said – THRILLING.  The writers lets him weave in and out of the story.  He never strays too far ahead of the audience.  His spectacular supporting cast, singer/actors and band, zip in and out of the story as needed.  In particular his three henchmen Joe Barbara, Lance Roberts, Caesar Samayoa feel like they are everywhere at once.  They play everyone from Ed Sullivan to Murray The K and what seems like dozens more.  His Siren Singers (Christine Cornish, Julia Grondin, Valeria Yamin) harmonize, dance and change costumes faster than the time it takes to blink.  Gracie Lawrence and Erika Henninsgen open private elements of Darin’s life as Connie Francis and Sandra Dee respectively.  Michelle Pawk is deeply, deeply affecting as Darin’s mother.  And the band – OIY the band!  Led by Andrew Resnick they are perfection in every way.

Jonathan Groff: Photo by Matthew Murphy and Evan Zimmerman

Because of the focus on Darin’s music, when we all arrive at the spotlighted moment where he flips the switch on what to include in his first self-produced album, the moment has been earned.  How about a whacko combo?  Try “Up A Lazy River” (Hoagy Carmichael and Sidney Arodin,) and Mack The Knife (Music by Kurt Weill/ English lyrics by Marc Blitzstein).  Oh yes he did – and self produced it.  By that time we have tread on every lily pad, been through every face-plant and every on-again-off again moment.  We feel part of the journey because we are.  Groff makes sure of that, and the cast that surrounds him is the mortar that glues us all together.

When the show is over and we leave because they make us leave, we are not mourning the very short life of Bobby Darin.  Not even close.  We are celebrating.  We are high on the story of Bobby Darin.  He flew, and when the fates asked him to fly higher he went there.  He exited like a Roman Candle.  He did not go gentle into that good night.  “Just In Time” makes certain we remember that and gives us a piece of Bobby Darin to take with us. We don’t realize until later that we have left a piece of our hearts for safe keeping with Jonathan Groff.  Just the way Darin would have wanted.

JUST IN TIME book by Warren Leight and  Isaac Oliver.  Music supervision and arrangements by Andrew Resnick,  choreography by Shannon Lewis, and is based on an original concept by Ted Chapin.

WITH Jonathan Groff, Gracie Lawrence,, Erika Henningsen,  Michele Pawk, Joe Barbara, Emily Bergl, Lance Roberts, Caesar Samayoa, Christine Cornish, Julia Grondin, Valeria Yamin. John Treacy Egan, Tari Kelly, Matt Magnusson, Khori Michelle Petinaud, Larkin Reilly.

Scenic design by Derek McLane, costume design by Catherine Zuber, lighting design by Justin Townsend and sound design by Peter Hylenski

Tickets for the world premiere of the new Broadway musical JUST IN TIME are available at the Circle in the Square Theatre box office (235 West 50th Street) and at www.JustInTimeBroadway.com for performances through Sunday, July 27, 2025, with performances beginning Friday, March 28, 2025.  Tickets for JUST IN TIME start at $99, with exclusive Night Club floor seating available for an up-close and personal experience.  During previews the playing schedule for JUST IN TIME is as follows: Monday through Saturday at 8pm, with matinees Saturday at 2pm.  Please note: There will be no performance on Thursday, April 24.  Beginning April 25, the playing schedule for JUST IN TIME is as follows: Tuesday and Thursday at 7pm, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday at 8pm, with matinees on Wednesday, Saturday, and Sunday at 2pm.

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

Danish writer Olga Ravn‘s book The Employees is the launching point for director Łukasz Twarkowski‘s explosive theatrical production of the same name. I say explosive as it goes beyond theater, beyond film, and from beginning to end, it is a moving installation piece that takes over the whole of the Skirball Theatre where the audience has the complete freedom to move between the actors and the action, sitting right next to, peeking over their shoulders, and sticking their nose in whichever corner they choose.

It seems that Earth is no longer, and we are on a spaceship with six humans and their doppelganger humanoids headed to a distant planet. The whole operation is being overseen by the “Organization,” which is not only working to further the mission but also treating this expedition as a test tube experiment to discover how humans and their droids perform, work, and live together. There is a mingling between the two that makes it difficult at times (as is planned) to tell the difference between human and humanoid.

On stage is a thirty-six cubic meter cube with video screens mounted up above on all four sides. Below is a series of interchangeable doors and video monitors that are lit from within, without, and with neon lights mounted throughout. How they utilize the rooms and hallways that traverse the cube rivals the show Severance and their rooms and hallways. Two videographers walk backwards the whole show (a tip of the hat to them), capturing the intimate scenes and emotions that the characters go through. Intermixed with pre-filmed moments, the story plays out live, both in and outside the cube, and on video. As the space travelers’ journey progresses, they delve into what it means to be human and is it worth sustaining? Facing that end-of-everything question, the company expresses it in a beautiful artistic dance movement sequence that cements the production in the realm of art. All theater doesn’t have to be art, but when they both coalesce, theater and art, you know that you’re experiencing something valuable.

—–

The Employees, written by Olga Ravn, translated from Danish by Bogusława Sochańska, and directed by Łukasz Twarkowski.

Cast: Dominika Biernat, Daniel Dobosz, Maja Pankiewicz, Sonia Roszczuk, Paweł Smagała, Rob Wasiewicz, Miron Smagała, Małgorzata Hajewska- Krzysztofik (voice).

Producer STUDIO theatregallery, Warsaw; Set design Fabien Lédé; Video design Jakub Lech; Lighting Bartosz Nalazek; Costume design Svenja Gassen; Music Lubomir Grzelak.

The Employees runs only Thursday, April 24 – Saturday, April 26 at 7:30 pm. Running time is 150 minutes. Tickets are $65 and can be purchased online, by visiting the box office in person, or by calling 212.998.4941. NYU Skirball is located at 566 LaGuardia Place at Washington Square, New York, New York 10012.

This production is performed in Polish with English subtitles. Contains nudity, strobe lights, smoke, very loud music, and references to sexual violence. The performance is not recommended for people with epilepsy.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

If Ryan J. Haddad‘s script for “Hold Me In The Water” were any more spare it would disappear.  As a mater of fact, this enchanting piece already does that.  This is a master class in turning story into magic.

A sense of precision runs through this production from the tipity-top where Haddad emerges from out of nowhere to the final graceful denouement where he returns whence he came.  In between, Haddad holds us in the palm of his hand.  He is a gentle guide, beginning with his description of a a “Relaxed Performance.”

That means a few things. The house lights are dim but not fully out. Please feel free to come and go as you need, you will always be allowed re-entry.  

FYI all of the performances at Playwrights are Relaxed.  Haddad is a champion for people with special needs.  He is one himself.  This is obvious as he is standing with the aid of a walker (reverse posture-control walker to be precise).  Haddad describes everything we see on the stage, costume, set, lighting, and every word he says is projected on the screen above the stage.  Thus he accommodates audience members who may have visual or hearing needs.  (ASL interpreters are referenced in the script).  Once the technicalities are dispatched, we enter into his love story.

So it’s a love story.  Big deal.  However, because of Haddad’s focus and timing it IS a big deal.  It is an enormous, gigantic deal.  He moves slowly about the stage, not only because that is his natural rhythm, but because he wants to lay out the pieces of his story like breadcrumbs on a path.  We will be retracing these steps, but at the moment of the telling we do not realize it.   Haddad keeps us focused on the elements of the story.  On the boy, sometimes referred to as a man.  How the meeting happened almost by chance – except for the fact that Haddad’s sights were set early on.  And of course there is that water bit.

The story unfolds like a lotus blossom.  One petal at a time.  And the roots go deep.  Things are on again and off again and on and off, and so on and so forth.  The moments together are intense and at times very, very intimate.  Haddad’s delivery is steady with an undertone of thrilling.  What will happen?  And when will it happen?  The tale stretches out over a year, and each date is a meticulous note in the story.

Did it work out?  I cannot tell you, and shame on anyone who does.  What does work out is the joy of the journey.  I know that sounds like a load of horse hockey, but in this case it is true.

Haddad understands the unspoken promise that every actor makes.  “You can trust your heart to be safe with me,” actors tell their listeners, “Because I have already given my heart to you, whether or not you want it.”   This exchange happens seamlessly, as it should, and when Haddad disappears at the story’s end, we realize that the hearts have been returned to their owners with just a small piece left behind.  We are all richer than when we arrived.

Not for nothing, but I had never heard of Haddad before this show. I am in the minority.  Haddad has an astonishing theatrical resume, and he has enthusiastic followers who make the performance feel like a reunion. And KUDOS to the design team for making the magic appear in three dimensions – specifically  dots and Cha See.

Treat yourself to this show.

Hold Me in the Water, Written and performed by Ryan J. Haddad, Directed by Danny Sharron

The creative team includes dots (Scenic Design), Beth Goldenberg (Costume Designer), Cha See (Lighting Designer), Tosin Olufolabi (Sound Designer), and Alison Kopit(Access Dramaturg).

At Playwrights Horizons through May 4.  TICKETS HERE

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
Review by Brittany Crowell

Something strange has indeed opened on Broadway in the form of the uncanny, magical, terrifying, theatrical show-stopper Stranger Things: The First Shadow. 

Set in the beloved town of Hawkins, Indiana in 1959, the show introduces an eerily familiar cast of characters, including: young thespian Joyce Maldonado (Alison Jayne), A/V nerd Bob Newby (Juan Carlos), and young James Hopper Jr (Burke Swanson) struggling to live up to the expectations of his Chief Hopper Sr.  If these names are familiar to you, then you must be a fan of the global TV sensation, ‘Stranger Things,’ which has had four seasons on Netflix and is expecting the release of its highly anticipated fifth and final season later this year.

Penned by the show’s writer and co-producer Kate Trefry, with the support of show creators The Duffer Brothers and writer Jack Thorne, The First Shadow whets fans’ appetites with delicious tidbits of intel from its source, while distancing itself enough from the Wheelers and Byers that those who may not be familiar with the TV show will find themselves on similar footing to die-hard fans.

Our unruly cast of characters for The First Shadow also feature a few new faces, including a haunting Henry Creel, played with vigorous intensity by Luis McCartney (who also created the role in London), and the girl from nowhere, Patricia “Patty” Newby, played with extra charm and gumption by Gabrielle Nevaeh.  These two make up an unlikely pair that rivals Eleven and Mike Wheeler from the original, and are just as unique and exciting to watch as they grow together, fighting the shadows throughout the play.

Louis McCartney (Henry Creel) in STRANGER THINGS: THE FIRST SHADOW; photo by Manuel Harlan

The true star of the show, however, comes in the form of magic: the amazing tricks and slights-of-hand of Jamie Harrison and Chris Fischer, both of whom collaborated on the similarly stunning Harry Potter adaptation.  The First Shadow performs split-second costume changes with incredible ease, as characters transform from dress to pantsuit and school uniform to showgirl right before our eyes. Chocked full of tricks-up-the-sleeve, there is no lack of jaw-dropping moments of anticipation to delight and impress audiences.  The lighting and sound by Jon Clark and Paul Arditti respectively (with original music and arrangements by D.J. Walde) have viewers sitting at the edge of their seats throughout the theater.

To speak more to the magic would be to spoil it for you, so let’s leave the strange and unreal to the stage and say simply that one must experience the spectacle of a theatrical Stranger Things to fully appreciate it (even if not to understand how it is achieved).

In a nutshell, Stranger Things: The First Shadow is charming, satisfying, and fun.  It’s a great time and will keep you on the edge of your seat throughout the almost 3-hours of performance, which will go by in a flash.  Short, high-energy scenes hop from location to location following more of a film and tv than theatrical energy with no lack of exciting scenic and video design for viewers to soak in and try to catch every detail.  The theatrical Stranger Things lives up to its London reputation and is sure to surprise and delight many New York audiences to come.  It’s not to be missed!

 

STRANGER THINGS – by Kate Trefry; original story by The Duffer Brothers, Jack Torne & Kate Trefry; based on the Netflix series, ‘Stranger Things,’ created by the Duffer Brother.

Directed by Stephen Daldry with co-director Justin Martin

FEATURING: Rosie Benton, Alex Breaux; Janie Brookshire; Kelsey Anne Brown; Malcolm Callender; Ta’rea Campbell; Juan Carlos; Antoinette Comer; Robert T. Cunningham; Ayana Cymone; Tom D’Augustino; Victor De Paula Rocha; Ian Michael Dolley; Dora Dolphin; Nya Garner; Logan Gould; Shea Grant; Andrew Hovelson; Rebecca Hurd; Alison Jaye; T. R. Knight; Ted Koch; Poppy Lovell; Jamie Martin Mann; Louis McCartney; Patrick Scott McDermott; Sean Mikesh; Gabrielle Nevaeh; Burke Swanson; Stephen Wattrus; Maya West; Eric Wiegand; Graham Winton; Azalea Wolfe.

Set design by Miriam Buether; costumes by Brigitte Rieffenstuel; lighting by Jon Clark; sound by Paul Arditti; original music and arrangements by D. J. Walde; illusions and visual effects by Jamie Harrison and Chris Fisher; video and visual effects by 59; movement directions dn choreography by Lynne Page; additional choreography by Coral Messam; wigs, hair and makeup by Campbell Young Associates.  Presented by Netflix and Sonia Friedman Productions.

The Marquis Theatre.   TICKETS
