content.rendered:
By Yuval Jonas

Grief Camp, Eliya Smith’s Off-Broadway debut at Atlantic Theater Company, takes place at a rustic summer camp where bunk beds line the walls, box fans hum, and the chirping of crickets fills the night. There’s even a frisbee stuck on the roof—a lovely little detail that’s easy to miss. The set, designed by Louisa Thompson, convincingly transports us to what might be remembered as a kind of adolescent purgatory. If only the story found as much clarity.

The play opens in the middle of the night, with teenagers whispering across the bunks—some unable to sleep, others kept awake by their neighbors. Morning arrives with the blare of reveille and a loudspeaker announcement about the weather and breakfast. Then, just as we settle in to observe a day at this ‘camp for grieving teens’ (so the title implies), something strange happens—nothing. Then again: night. Reveille. Another day. And again. Nothing. Days pass with no consequence. This repetition of routine may be the point, but instead it feels like Groundhog Day, only lacking the escalation and transformation.

Conversations flicker and vanish. At one point, a camper asks another, “Do you think I’m a terrible person?”—a line that suggests we’re about to arrive at something—but the moment fizzles. A flirtation arises between Olivia (Renée-Nicole Powell) and Cade (Jack DiFalco), the “grief counselor,” which contains the faint outline of a conflict (she’s a camper, he’s older, there are boundaries). Though this relationship could have formed the play’s core, it doesn’t; it appears and disappears in brief stabs of interaction, never deepening.

The dialogue is mostly just teenage chitchat. Some of it is sharply written. But there’s little sense of urgency behind the words. Yes, teens are often aimless, but they’re also full of longing, of friction, of things they’re desperate to express. Here, the stakes stay frustratingly low even though the circumstances—youth, grief, camping—offer such rich potential for action.

The production is most alive when all the campers are on stage together. There’s a believable rhythm in the overlapping conversations and the messy, familiar chaos of teens interacting. One rare moment of genuine emotional connection comes through Alden Harris-McCoy, who appears as the onstage guitarist, in his beautiful rendition of Willie Nelson’s Going Away Party. It’s quietly affecting. But elsewhere, the production leans on theatrical devices to try to create pathos.

Later in the play, Bard (Arjun Athalye), who has barely spoken until this point, delivers a long monologue. Athalye gives a thoughtful, restrained performance, but the moment is unearned. We know nothing about Bard, and so we don’t have a reason to care what he has to say.

When the show reaches for intensity, it often does so through volume or provocation: shouting over a thunderstorm, talk of masturbation, monologues about sex (yes, complete with gongs and dramatic lighting). None of it is earned, and none of it opens a window into the characters’ grief—which, according to the premise and title, they’re meant to be carrying. A few throwaway remarks suggest the kids have lost someone close, but we never really hear what happened, how they’re living with it, or how the camp is supposed to help—or, for that matter, make it worse, as long as it does something.

Grief Camp creates a vivid, fully inhabited world and assembles conditions ripe for drama, but never shapes them into a story. Without conflict or progression, the play drifts, looping through the passing days. And really, instead of these kids, I left thinking of Bill Murray.

GRIEF CAMP by Eliya Smith; Directed by Les Waters.

With: Arjun Athalye, Grace Brennan, Jack DiFalco, Dominic Gross, Alden Harris-McCoy, Maaike Laanstra-Corn, Renée-Nicole Powell, Lark White, and Danny Wolohan.

Sets by Louisa Thompson. Costumes by Oana Botez. Sound by Bray Poor.

Now playing through May 11 at Atlantic Theater Company, Linda Gross Theater, 336 W 20th St. Tickets available here.

Running time: 90 minutes, no intermission.

@graph.name: Tulis McCall
@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

content.rendered:
By Sarah Downs

There’s nothing more fun than watching a musical about creating a musical.   We all love a peek behind the curtain, indulging in some schadenfreude as we experience the agony and the ecstasy, as it were, from the comfort of our theater seat.  SMASH mostly delivers on this promise with broad comedy, flashy, old school musical numbers and delicious backstage drama.

Led by Brooks Ashmanskas as exasperated director/choreographer Nigel, and starring Robyn Hurder as It girl Ivy Lynn portraying Marilyn, Bombshell, the musical within the musical, is definitely a show with big dreams, not least of which is the dream of making a musical about Marilyn Monroe that is unabashedly upbeat.  As Nigel says, the last thing anyone wants is a show where Marilyn ends up naked on her bed wrapped in a satin sheet.  That noble plan of course begins to unravel almost immediately.  Take one highly strung director, two overworked writers, a vulnerable star, an ambitious understudy; add a power-mad, crone of an acting coach, and life begins to imitate art, art imitate art, art become life and life imitate farce.

It’s a whole lot of fun, but it’s also a lot to juggle, making the show more a mash-up than smash.  For the writers of Bombshell, what stories do you tell and what do you gloss over?  The director has one idea, his star another.  Wife and husband writing team of Tracy and Jerry (Krysta Rodriguez and John Behlmann) wrestle with ever-conflicting demands, to both comic and touching effect.  In a rare ballad, Rodriguez sings affectingly of Marilyn’s early life as Norma Jean.  She is joined by Hurder in a duet that brings past and present together.  This song offers welcome relief from a belt-voice heavy score.  Yes, this is pizzazz musical theater, but with so many belt-filled dance numbers, it is such a relief to listen to voices sing in their natural range.  It gives all of us a chance to breathe.

Writers Rick Elice and Bob Martin take on modern concerns, including how social media has altered the theatrical landscape, and adding to the bubbling brew of backstage brouhaha a unique narrative twist that opens another playing space, and unexpected opportunity for more than one leading character.  In examining the one life of two Marilyns – Norma Jean the actress and Marilyn the icon – SMASH reflects on the idea of how differently a single role can be interpreted.  Theater is ever a kaleidoscope, in that no one performance is like another.  Given that inherently limitless nature of this ephemeral art form, why do we place certain limits on who does the interpreting?

It’s a lot to cover in 2 ½ hours, and the elements collide awkwardly, particularly into Act II.  Carrying a  lot on their shoulders, the hearty band of triple threats with enviable six-packs (including the men), manages to pull off its Hydra of a narrative albeit with a degree of overacting and over singing. Every comic moment is played to the hilt, every musical number out loud and proud, with smashing arrangements and energetic choreography.  The big dance numbers, however, do begin to blend together.  It’s a case of more threatens to be too much.  Some judicious editing would not go amiss.

Nevertheless, the cast is excellent.  Robyn Hurder is loaded with “It,” and when she turns on the star quality, you don’t see anyone else.  She is Marilyn.  With his excellent comic timing and flair, Brooks Ashmanskas steals every scene he is in.  As Ivy’s understudy Karen, Caroline Bowman shows that Karen is indeed performance ready, delivering a terrific show stopper in Act II.  She is forced to chew the scenery a bit in order to raise the stakes from the level 10 reached early in Act I.  Adding a parallel meaning concept “triple threat,” there is also Chloe (Bella Coppola), the assistant director and former performer who’s still got it.  Small but mighty, the supporting cast does what must be exhausting triple duty as well, appearing in various guises throughout, including an adorable cameo of a back-stage dresser being driven to distraction.

Alejo Vietti’s costumes, particularly Ivy’s increasingly retro Marilyn wear, and the glamorous multiplicity of evening wear paraded in Act II, delight the eyes.  The parade begins to compete with itself, however, so some of the glamour is wasted.  Beowulf Borritt’s detailed set manages to be all things – smoothly transforming from backstage to chic lounge to ‘it’s showtime’ theatre stage with a minimum of fuss.  Add to that Ken Billington’s ‘look at me’ (in a good way) lighting in plush violets, reds and golds, and the Broadway with a “B” ethos is complete.

I do feel the show peaks way too early.  Having pulled out all the stops in Act I, the team leaves itself little room to up the ante, yet still burdened with difficult, conflicting ends to tie up.  The unique plot twist forces the show to retrace its steps several times musically and narratively.  It’s for a laudable purpose to be sure, but it dissipates the momentum, leading to an anti-climactic end.  The story feels a little ‘queen for a day’ – a fractured fairy tale that opens new vistas, only for them to disappear before one can explore them.   Then again, what a perfect encapsulation of the life of Marilyn Monroe, who had to abandon her true self in order to survive.

However, the talent of this cast and their committed performances carry SMASH show over these bumps through to a happy, human ending that satisfies.  Everyone is beautiful.  Everyone is loved.  Isn’t that how it should be?

SMASH, book by Rick Elice and Bob Martin, music by Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman; directed by Susan Stroman, choreography by Joshua Bergasse.  Scenic design by Beowulf Boritt, costume design by Alejo Vietti, lighting design by Ken Billington, sound design Brian Ronan, music supervision by Stephen Oremus.

With:  Robyn Hurder, Brooks Ashmanskas, Krysta Rodriguez, John Behlmann, Kristine Nielsen,  Caroline Bowman, Jacqueline B. Arnold, Bella Coppola, Casey Garvin,  Nicholas Matos and Megan Kane.

Ensemble:  Wendi Bergamini, Sarah Bowden, Jacob Burns, Deanna Cudjoe, Chelle Denton, Daniel Gaymon, Merritt David Janes, Ndaya Dream Hoskins, David Paul Kidder, Ian Liberto, Libby Lloyd, McGee Maddox, Connor McRory, J Savage, Jake Trammel and Katie Webber.

At the Imperial Theatre (249 West 45th Street).  Tickets: Here or go to www.telecharge.com. Running time 2 and 1/2 hours with one intermission.

yoast_head_json.description: SMASH - There’s nothing more fun than watching a musical about creating a musical.   We all love a peek behind the curtain, indulging in a certain schadenfreude as we experience the agony and the ecstasy, as it were, from the comfort of our theater seat.  Smash mostly delivers on this promise with broad comedy, flashy, old school musical numbers and delicious backstage drama. The elements collide awkwardly at times, leading to awkward peaks and valleys of energy, but the talented cast manages to carry the show with charm and energy.

@graph.description: Sarah Downs is a writer and performer who escaped the suburbs of Boston to pursue a career in the arts. In her theatrical incarnation she has worked both in New York and regional theater, and performed with local opera companies. She has sung arias to the stars, musical theater in barns and torch songs in cabaret. Sarah also toured the U.S. as Marian in The Music Man, and toured the U.S. and Canada as Marie Osmond’s understudy in the national tour of The Sound of Music. In recent years Sarah has focused more on writing, including articles on feminism and politics. She is President of the Professional Women Singers Association and on the board of the Women In the Arts and Media Coalition. Sarah holds an B.A. from Harvard University.

content.rendered:
By Tulis McCall

Talk about circuitous journeys.  Here is a question for you – where were you in 1994?  Or 1996?  Do you remember ANYTHING from those years.  Well, if you are Tina Landau and Adam Guettel you would know that the premier of Floyd Collins was presented in 1994 in Philadelphia, and 1996 was the year it premiered Off-Broadway at Playwrights Horizons.  Its Broadway premier was a mere 29 years later and has now taken a bow at Lincoln Center.  It’s a good thing they waited so long, because Jeremy Jordan (Floyd Colins) clearly needed to grow into a man and be ready to take on the title role.  This part ain’t for sissy’s.

Actually none of these parts are made for sissies.  This is one of the most challenging and complicated collection of characters, music, lyrics and choreography I have ever encountered.  And this is one of the most exquisite ensembles I have ever seen.

It is 1925 of a farm in Kentucky. The story centers around Floyd Collins who was a spelunker, which is a fancy name for a person who likes to go exploring below ground.   I have only gone caving once, and let me tell you it is crazy down there.  People wedge themselves into spaces that look uninviting and impossible.  But our boy Floyd was enchanted by the whole deal, until he got himself stuck a few hundred feet below ground.

Did he make it out?  I cannot tell you.  And if you go on and cheat, you will lose out on discovering the community that surrounded Floyd in his time of need.  They are glorious and worth the wait.

Floyd’s sister Nellie (Lizzy McAlpine) and brother Homer (Jason Gotay) are a tag team of hope.  Floyd has been in these situations before and he will get out.  Nellie in particular has a haunting melodic connection to her brother who is known to serenade himself in the caves he visits.  Gotay shines as the kid brother with gumption and adventure running through his veins.  On a personal note it is wonderful to hear Jessica Molaskey (Miss Jane) singing again.  Her voice is reminiscent of Joni Mitchell and she has the experience to know when and how to use it. Taylor Trensch as Skeets Miller is the character new on the scene.  It is his journey that most guides us through the layers of family, friends and memories, and he never lets us go.

Taylor Trensch and members of the cast of FLOYD COLLINS; Credit Joan Marcus

As I said the ensemble is tremendous.  A special note must be made for the “Reporters” (Dwayne Cooper, Jeremy Davis and Charlie Franklin) a trio of newsmenwho flock to the site of the cave and lead off the second act with “Is That Remarkable.” This is a three part harmony report on the Colins situation combined with chorography by Jon Rua that is nothing short of dazzling.

The difficulty of this piece is that Guettel’s writing leads more toward an operetta style than what we think of as an American musical.  Each piece moves the action in an oblique way.  The music has its own life and often serves to pause and focus the action rather than move the pilot forward.  It is more recitative – somewhere between music and dialogue – and his style never waivers.   Songs appear to pop out of the air and singers must grab them without hesitation and release them with little more than a flick of the wrist.  Tina Landau’s direction gives the piece structure and depth.

Thank goodness for us all that this cast handles everything that is handed to them with grace and skill.  They wear you down with their perfection.  They take no prisoners.  In the end, the story of Floyd Collins lifts you up.  Out of the darkness into the light.

FLOYD COLLINS – book by Tina Landau, music and lyrics by Adam Guettel, additional lyrics by Tina Landau and direction by Tina Landau.

WITH Jeremy Jordan as Floyd Collins, Jason Gotay as Homer Collins, Sean Allan Krill as H.T. Carmichael, Marc Kudisch as Lee Collins, Lizzy McAlpine as Nellie Collins, Wade McCollum as Bee Doyle, Jessica Molaskey as Miss Jane, Taylor Trensch as Skeets Miller, Cole Vaughan as Jewell Estes, Clyde Voce as Ed Bishop as well as Kevin Bernard, Dwayne Cooper, Jeremy Davis, Charlie Franklin, Kristen Hahn, Happy McPartlin, Kevyn Morrow, Zak Resnick, Justin Showell and Colin Trudell.

 

Sets by dots, costumes by Anita Yavich, lighting by Scott Zielinski, sound by Dan Moses Schreier, and projections by Ruey Horng Sun, with dance sequences by Jon Rua, orchestrations by Bruce Coughlin,  music direction by Ted Sperling. Bonnie Panson is the stage manager. Lincoln Center Theater is producing FLOYD COLLINS  in association with Creative Partners Productions and Mark Cortale & Charles D. Urstadt.

Through June 22, atLincoln Center.  Tickets Here

@graph.description: For my money, the theatre is up there in the ten top reasons to be human. I leave my home and go sit in a dark room with complete strangers and watch actors do their stuff because I want to be inspired. I’m asking to be involved. I’m volunteering to be led down any old path they choose as long as they don’t let go of my hand. And if I see a show, and it is NOT so very good – I will try to divert you, because I don’t want you to come to the temple when the preaching isn’t up to snuff. I will bar the door, I will swing from rafters, I will yell FIRE just to set your feet on a path that does not lead to disappointment. Do something different with your evening I will say. Save your money for dinner with a friend you haven’t seen in months because you are too frigging busy. Go take a walk with your dog or your child or your significant other. Go to bed early, I will say. Don’t come to the theatre when it is less than it can be. I’m an usher snob, and that’s all there is to it.

title.rendered: From Basement to Brooklyn: Verdi’s Lost Ballet Finds New Life

content.rendered:
Bt Ed Kliszus

The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra delivered a remarkable premiere in an evening of musical storytelling in the sumptuous acoustic embrace of St. Ann and the Holy Trinity Church. Under the assured direction of Philip Nuzzo, the Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra delivered a concert of extraordinary historical significance and artistic merit. The evening’s centerpiece—Verdi’s Lost Ballet—brought to American ears ballet music by Giuseppe Verdi that had lain dormant in a basement for 175 years. Moreover, the imaginative programming wedded this rarity with compelling Shakespearean-inspired works, creating a tapestry of intellectually stimulating and emotionally satisfying sound.

Rediscovered Treasure: Verdi’s Ballet Music Emerges from the Shadows

The undisputed highlight of this remarkable Verdi’s Lost Ballet and the Sounds of Shakespeare evening was the U.S. premiere of Verdi’s “Divertissements from ‘Nabucco'”—music composed in 1848 for a French production at Brussels’ Théâtre de la Monnaie. These ballet sections, unearthed from the basement of the composer’s Villa Verdi in Sant’Agata, emerged from obscurity with their Verdian identity gloriously intact. The composer’s unmistakable dramatic flair announced itself from the first notes, leaving no doubt of the music’s provenance.

Here’s an NBC news report on the discovery and upcoming premiere of Verdi’s work by the Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra (@bkchamberorch)

In the “Passe a 3,” concertmaster Anna Majcherczyk delivered exquisite solo passages with a honeyed tone that soared above the ensemble. The melody’s sinuous contours, underpinned by Verdi’s characteristically pulsing accompaniment, evoked the operatic world of “Nabucco” while offering something distinctly evoking movement through dance. Furthermore, the “Pas d’Ensemble” revealed the composer’s gift for orchestral color, with excellent contributions from principal flutist Eva Ding and oboist Zachary Pulse.

Giuseppe Verdi by Giovanni Boldini. Public Domain

Nuzzo’s interpretation emphasized the music’s inherent theatricality without sacrificing its structural coherence. His tempo choices honored the score’s dance origins and operatic character. Additionally, one could hear echoes of Verdi’s contemporaneous works—hints of “Macbeth” and premonitions of “Luisa Miller”—suggesting this “lost” music provides a fascinating window into the composer’s evolving style during the late 1840s.

Orchestral Magic: Balance, Placement, and Sonic Splendor

Maestro Nuzzo demonstrated his keen understanding of orchestral balance and spatial acoustics throughout Verdi’s Lost Ballet and the Sounds of Shakespeare program. The scope of the string sections was perfectly balanced with the full winds, brass, and percussion sections. His decision to place second violins to his right—a 19th-century seating arrangement—created a stereophonic dialogue between violin sections that clarified contrapuntal passages. This historically informed approach yielded especially rich rewards in the Shostakovich and Walton works, where conversational exchanges between violin sections created engaging antiphonal effects.

The orchestra responded with remarkable sensitivity to Nuzzo’s nuanced gestures. Dynamic contrasts were meticulously observed, from the most delicate pianissimos in Ophelia’s song from Shostakovich’s “Hamlet” suite to the thunderous battle sequences in Walton’s “Henry V.” Principal cellist Connor Kim delivered impassioned solo lines in the Shostakovich. In contrast, the brass section, led by trumpet principal Samantha Atlas, exhibited grandiose precision and power in Walton’s “Agincourt.”

Shakespeare in Sound: From Soviet Drama to British Cinema

Shostakovich’s incidental music for “Hamlet,” composed in 1932 for Nikolai Akimov’s controversial Soviet production, provided a fascinating opening to Verdi’s Lost Ballet and the Sounds of Shakespeare concert. The selection of the five movements revealed the composer’s sardonic wit and lyrical gifts. In “Flourish and Dancing Music,” Nuzzo emphasized the music’s angular rhythms and piquant harmonies. At the same time, “Ophelia’s Song” received a reading of unexpected tenderness, with harpist Yeonhwa Chung providing exquisite accompaniment to the string melody.

Rising star JOSÉ ESPINOSA narrates William Walton’s “Henry V: A Shakespeare Scenario” THIS Saturday, April 5th, with the BROOKLYN CHAMBER ORCHESTRA AND CHOIR. Courtesy @bkchamberorch on Instagram

The evening’s most substantial offering was William Walton’s “Henry V: A Shakespeare Scenario.” Christopher Palmer arranged this work from Walton’s score for Laurence Olivier’s 1944 film. Actor Jose Espinosa delivered the play’s iconic monologues with a commanding presence and nuanced understanding. His “Once more unto the breach” rang through the cathedral with stirring conviction, while the St. Crispin’s Day speech achieved a perfect balance of intimacy and grandeur.

Shakespeare’s Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark (1890). Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons

Members of the New York Choral Society and the Grace Choral of Brooklyn, prepared by music directors David Hayes and Jason Asbury respectively, brought vocal luster to the battle hymn “Non Nobis Domine” and ethereal beauty to the French court scene. Their impeccable articulation and blend enhanced Walton’s already colorful orchestration. Additionally, the brass instruments soared during the battle sequences, creating a thrilling spatial dimension in the music. Powerful brass and percussion amplified the dramatic intensity.

Sacred Space: Gothic Beauty Meets Musical Glory

St. Ann and the Holy Trinity Church, a Gothic Revival masterpiece dating from 1847, provided the perfect setting for the Verdi’s Lost Ballet and the Sounds of Shakespeare program. The soaring arches and stained-glass windows created a visual counterpoint to the music’s spiritual and dramatic elements. Furthermore, the church’s warm yet clear acoustics allowed orchestral colors to project with ideal clarity.

The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra performing in the St. Ann & the Holy Trinity Church. Courtesy @bkchamberorch on Instagram

The sacred space seemed particularly appropriate for Walton’s “Touch Her Soft Lips and Part,” a movement of transcendent beauty rendered with exquisite delicacy by the strings. In this moment, as in many throughout the evening, one could sense the audience collectively holding its breath, transported by the marriage of music and environment into a realm of pure emotional communion.

Philip Nuzzo: Brooklyn’s Musical Treasure

Maestro Nuzzo’s programming vision for Verdi’s Lost Ballet and the Sounds of Shakespeare concert deserves special praise. By juxtaposing three distinct interpretations of Shakespeare—Soviet, British, and implicitly Italian (through Verdi)—alongside an actual musical discovery, he created an evening of intellectual fascination and sensuous pleasure. Moreover, his skilled leadership drew performances of remarkable cohesion, balance, and expressivity from his musicians.

Phil Nuzzo, Conductor of the Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra. Courtesy brooklynchamberorchestra.org

The audience, notably diverse in age and background, responded with enthusiastic appreciation throughout the evening. This powerful connection between performers and listeners exemplifies Nuzzo’s gift for selecting repertoire that bridges historical significance while garnering immediate appeal. Indeed, his vision for the Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra has transformed it into an essential cultural institution for the borough and beyond.

Legacy and Future: The Continuing Relevance of Rediscovered Works

The significance of Verdi’s Lost Ballet and the Sounds of Shakespeare performance extends beyond a single evening’s pleasure. By bringing Verdi’s long-lost ballet music to American audiences, the Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra has genuinely contributed to our understanding of the composer’s development. While not revolutionary works, these divertissements offer valuable insights into how Verdi adapted his dramatic instincts to meet the requirements of French theatrical tradition.

Similarly, the juxtaposition of Shostakovich’s and Walton’s Shakespearean interpretations illuminated how different cultural contexts shape artistic responses to universal texts. The Soviet composer’s sardonic take on “Hamlet” contrasted fascinatingly with the British composer’s patriotic reading of “Henry V.” Yet, both demonstrated profound musical engagement with the Bard’s timeless characters and themes.

As the Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra continues its 2025-26 season, audiences can anticipate more innovative programming, from silent film accompaniment (“Nosferatu” in October) to holiday celebrations and explorations of Beethoven and Haydn. If the Verdi’s Lost Ballet and the Sounds of Shakespeare concert is any indication, each promises to combine historical insight with immediate emotional impact.

For those fortunate enough to have attended this landmark event, the experience will undoubtedly linger in memory—a reminder of music’s power to transcend time and connect us across centuries. For Verdi’s ballet music, liberated at last from its basement confinement, the journey from 1848 Brussels to 2025 Brooklyn proved worth the wait.

Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra

157 Montague St, Brooklyn, NY 11201
Phone: (718) 801-3811

For tickets and information, go to https://brooklynchamberorchestra.org/.

Click HERE for videos of past BCO performances.

Readers may also enjoy SurRound II: Divine Sonic Tapestry at St. John the Divine, and the Leonkoro String Quartet: Sublime Brilliance at the 92nd Street Y.

content.rendered:
By David Walters

It’s another winner at Irish Repertory Theatre.

Irishtown is a funny send-up of what it means to be Irish, the what and how of live theater, and the expectations an audience brings to what they’re going to see.

Currently, every country worldwide is redefining itself, throwing expectations out the window, and playwright Ciara Elizabeth Smyth, on a deeper level below the comedy, is asking that of Ireland. Who and what do they want to be now? Comedy and a good laugh is a more than valid answer.

The Dublin-based theater company The Irishtown Players is on a roll. After their last hit with playwright Aisling (Brenda Meaney), The Happy Leper of Larne, they have been given the opportunity to open up on Broadway with her next play, Who Are We If We Are Not Ourselves At All. This play is a little different, though, as it lacks Irish themes and takes place in England. “It seems to be about a woman who is sexually harassed and assaulted at work. And, eh, she takes a legal case against the boss. And wins.” This is not what the company feels they represent. Being an Irish company, they don’t do, “sexual assault dramas from England.” And, to start with, there’s a happy ending, “Do you know one happy Irish person?” Aisling, incensed, takes her play and storms out, leaving the company to open on Broadway in two weeks with no play. They decide to improvise one of their own, after all, the great Irish play has already been written hundreds of times; all they have to do is regurgitate. “Where all the peasants are fighting and drinking and making love with their cousins.” “Where they’re all in debilitating pain but possess neither the tools nor the constitution to express themselves.” You can imagine how that goes.

Where it does go is making Irishtown a fun romp, played to the hilt, crackling and crisp, that will have you smiling, laughing, and joyful, as everyone is Irish at an evening like this. In this day and age, the chance to laugh along with a crowd of your fellow earthlings is invaluable. You will come out of the theater a little lighter for having been there.

—–

Irishtown was written by Ciara Elizabeth Smyth and sharply directed by Nicola Murphy Dubey.

The dynamite cast includes: Kate Burton, Saoirse Monica Jackson, Kevin Oliver Lynch, Brenda Meaney, Angela Reed, with voiceover work by Roger Clark

Technical artists: both scenic and lighting design Colm McNally; costume design Orla Long; sound design Caroline Eng; props Nicole Rozanski; movement Prather Rehm; dialects Barbara Rubin.

This world premiere is now running at The Irish Repertory Theatre 132 West 22nd Street, New York, NY, through May 25. Tickets can be purchased HERE.

Premium Seating: $95 – $125; Standard Seating: $80; Rear Seating: $60

Under age 40, Green Seats: $25

title.rendered: GLASS. KILL. WHAT IF IF ONLY. IMP.

content.rendered:
By Kendra Jones

We are suspended in space and time. The selection of four short works by celebrated British playwright Caryl Churchill drops us into mid air, asking us to seek connection between the abstract staging and script of this compilation strung together by James Macdonald. We become grounded by their equally thought-provoking, romantic, and comedic tones, and brutally violent, sudden shifts. All four pieces, making up GLASS. KILL. WHAT IF IF ONLY. IMP. are joined by their asking of the audience to place ourselves in a fantastical, undetermined space and time. We release expectations and embrace dark, gross surprise and comedic classic twists.  

In fact, this whole performance was mythical in one way or another. All of these sets are floating. While we were all immersed into this fantastical set, the distance we had to each narrative was kept far.

A large mantle is illuminated mid-air and the actors are mantelpieces: a clock, figurines, a girl (Ayana Workman) made of glass. These inanimate objects begin our evening of romantic tragedy.

A feathered cloud of where a single woman (Deirdre O’Connell) encompassing all Gods, hovers atop: we’re in a dream-like state—where each happening was as unexpectedly gory and transformative as the next. But in Kill, the name of the piece isn’t abstract. It was over the top, and brought a very straight forward telling of the most vile parts of Greek mythology plots. Incest, violence, incest, and violent incest. At intermission, the group of women emitting bits of laughter and disgust during Kill, next to me, don’t return for the second half of the production.

KILL.; Photo by Joan Marcus

What If If Only sent us into a white sterile room of a man who’s partner has died and he is simply left to grieve and wonder what if. His future is right in front if him, but believably, it is too difficult to imagine just yet as he is still caught in the past. His dead partner appears, a child (Ruby Blaut) that is somewhere in his future, and other ghosts that emotionally pull him apart, as life often does.

WHAT IF IF ONLY.; Photo by Joan Marcus

A gymnast (Junru Wang) and a juggler (Maddox Morfit-Tighe) occupied minutes during intricate set changes just behind the red velvet curtain. The choice to incorporate these fun, highly focused circus acts added a dark tone to even the most innocent parts of this production. The performers, silent with unwavering skill and gazes, added an exciting element that those in the front row had a chance to experience directly.

Between KILL. and WHAT IF IF ONLY., Maddox Morfit-Tighe juggled pins, subtly interacting with the audience–

“That was the most erotic public experience I’ve ever had,” a man said at intermission as he left his front and center seat and reconnected with a friend sitting in a different row. “Did you see what he did?”

“No…”

“I thought the whole theater saw it but I guess it was just me….he was staring right at me.”

Reactions from the audience varied throughout the short plays, the laughter, the reactions to the grotesque, the almost-random, engaging circus acts that stole our minds from the violence of the first two pieces before dropping us back into it again.

Imp, by far the longest of the four shorts, is the most British and the most realistic, with spurts of violence, romantic comedy, and all-too-real moments of unleashed emotions that drive the relationship between a loosely-related but closely-felt family. It’s a romantic comedy as much as it is tragedy: two “kissin'” cousins (Deirdre O’Connell and John Ellison Conlee) decide to fill in as some sort of parental figures to a young woman, Niamh (Adelind Horan). Niamh enters into a tumultuous relationship, as the relationship between jimmy and Dot–and their own personal flaws–are put on full display. Deirdre O’Connell’s wild, darkly vibrant zest, and energy of lead woman–whether floating on a cloud in Kill or choking on breath in an armchair–sparks this piece. A magical imp is the only source of hope. 

IMP.; Photo by Joan Marcus

GLASS. KILL. WHAT IF IF ONLY. IMP. opens April 16 at The Public Theater, in The Public’s Martinson Hallon, 425 Lafayette Street (at Astor Place) New York, NY 10003, and has been extended through Sunday, May 11. Tickets can be purchased here.

Quartet of Short Plays Written by Caryl Churchill; Directed by James Macdonald

CAST:

GLASS: Ayana Workman (Girl); Sathya Sridharan (Brother); Japhet Balaban (Friend); Adelind Horan (Girl’s Friend and Mother).

KILL: Deirdre O’Connell (Gods).

WHAT IF IF ONLY: Sathya Sridharan (Someone); John Ellison Conlee (Present); Cecilia Ann Popp (Child Future; performs Wednesday, Friday,Sunday); Ruby Blaut (Child Future; performsTuesday, Thursday, Saturday).

IMP: John Ellison Conlee (Jimmy); Adelind Horan (Niamh); Deirdre O’Connell (Dot); Japhet Balaban (Rob).

Gymnast (Junru Wang); Juggler (Maddox Morfit-Tighe).

title.rendered: Under the Rainbow – Final Show April 19 at United Solo

content.rendered:
By Alice Klugherz

Do we need another story of a gay man’s coming of age?

Yes, we do, because it pulls us in with the best elements of theater: a story lived and told; sung and danced. In John Gazzale‘s one man show, “Under the Rainbow” John plays Rodger Asthold, an unemployed actor swept by a tornado from a theatre in NYC to an alternate world: part Oz, part black-box theater; a twilight-zone where the humor and pathos are shaken not stirred.

When a cactus named Toto is your pet and the owner, Rodger goes beyond its prickly exterior to love it and there’s a trunk that might have belonged to Judy Garland and you don’t know what the hell is coming next…it gets on the list of must be seen/experienced shows!  Rodger is a Gen-x-er with the soul of a boomer, not young enough to escape the state-approved homophobia and bullying of his time (not that it ever left) He cuts to the center of the experience of the bully and the bullied; only staying long enough to remember it’s horror, but not to mar the humor or heart in the rest of the work.

Rodger is a frustrated actor. He wants fame, equating it with connection and approval.  He’s infected with 50-something syndrome, the sureness that one has not done enough.  This affects gay and straight people – anyone who buys into western culture. It’s a virus, I’m planning on making a vaccine, but until it’s approved, I’ll do theater. I think Rodger has the answer: love and expression; whipping us into a connection so real the ending is worth the price of a New York therapist. Although just like therapy you must go through the whole session.

Near the top of the show after a phone call with his brother he says “What do I have to be for you to be proud of me?” It’s this line that wins me over, it sticks to my ribs; few of us have risen above wanting our family to approve of us.

Each time the trunk on stage is open a memory is realized from his life and the life of Judy Garland. Each time she appears through Rodger or in a voiceover she gives him further permission to become her. They morph further into each other till by the end he is singing, moving and talking as her; drawing a connection between (for example) the hurtful gossip she experienced and Rodgers own travails.

Peter Collier plays the production assistant, who moves like a shadow, dancing the props in and out, never upstaging the performer and it’s like watching the gears in a clock – fascinating.

Under the Rainbow was directed by Padraic Lillis with a nuanced collaboration between director and actor. Under the Rainbow suggests that a rainbow is not only a flag or the effect of rain and light but a permeable shelter, it needs love (from all of us) to shore it up. The 2nd and last show (TILL THE FALL!) is on Saturday April 19th (also) as part of United Solo.

Written by John Gazzale

CAST: John Gazzale (Roger)

CREATIVE TEAM: Padraic Lillis (Director), Margaret Montagna (Sound Design), Kia Rogers (Lighting Design), Darin Presley (Composer), Peter Collier (Actor/Production Assistant), Natalia Carlson (Sound and Light Board)

Under the Rainbow is playing at United Solo Festival at Theatre Row, 410 W 42nd Street, New York, NY 10036.  One more performance this Saturday, April 19 at 8:30 PM.  Stay tuned for a return performance this October at the United Solo Fall Festival!  Run time is 60 minutes.

@graph.description: UNDER THE RAINBOW Do we need another story of a gay man’s coming of age?Yes, we do, because it pulls us in with the best elements of theater: a story lived and told; sung and danced. In John Gazzale's one man show, "Under the Rainbow" John plays Rodger Asthold, an unemployed actor swept by a tornado from a theatre in NYC to an alternate world: part Oz, part black-box theater; a twilight-zone where the humor and pathos are shaken not stirred.

@graph.description: Alice Klugherz has been part of the Downtown dance and performance scene since the 80’s. Her docu-whimsey (talk/move) work has been part of PS 122's Avant-Garde-Arama, Dance Theatre Workshop's FRESH TRACKS, LaMama Club, Wet and Performance Mix. She also appears in the work of others, most recently in Mark Dendy’s NEWYORKnewyork@Astor Place performed at Joe’s Pub. She is a regular reader at Cornelia St Cafe, Big Irv's and Stacy's Salon.

content.rendered:
The Swamp Dwellers, directed by Awoye Timpo in its off-Broadway debut at Theatre For a New Audience, is ambitious in its simplicity. A one act that features a handful of characters and no scene changes might feel strangely minimalist for a play that tackles climate disaster, corporate greed, generational friction, religious questioning, colonial resource extraction, and the complex dynamics of family. And yet, Wole Soyinka’s 70-minute show does it all with poetic richness and subtly brilliant creative decisions.

The writing is what really shines in The Swamp Dwellers. Soyinka’s portrait of a society’s anti-colonial awakening and environmental consciousness is gorgeously crafted. It is an incendiary work that speaks directly to our troubled world.

In a small village in the Niger Delta, Alu (Jenny Jules) and Makuri (Leon Addison Brown) await the arrival of their son Igwezu (Ato Blankson-Wood), who has left home to find better fortune in the city, but has returned to the swamp to find that his crops have been entirely washed away by floods. As Alu and Makuri fret over their son’s physical and spiritual fate, they go back and forth in hilarious, domestic banter. Jules and Brown have an easy chemistry between them that portrays years of hardship, love, and loyalty. Before long, they are interrupted by a blind beggar (Joshua Echebiri) who longs to work the land, but has been forced to become a beggar by the larger society. The defiant beggar sticks out not only for being blind, but being Muslim; an outsider who does not understand the relationship between the villagers and the Serpent, the spirit of the swamp. When Igwezu finally comes home, it is clear that he, too, is a stranger in his own home. He has seen the powerful corrupting forces in the city and also the unjust hierarchy of his village where the Kadiye (Chiké Okonkwo) exercises unquestionable moral authority. Not only that, but his twin brother, Awuchike, has betrayed him. When the Kadiye comes to call on Alu, Makuri, and Igwezu’s home, Igwezu must decide whether to bend the knee as he always has or chart a new path in 1950s Nigerian society.

Leon Addison Brown as Makuri, Jenny Jules as Alu. Photo by Hollis King.

In this play, every detail tells a story. Make sure you arrive early to take in the immersive, dreamlike experience crafted by the creative team behind The Swamp Dwellers. When you sit down, you are instantly surrounded by the sounds of the Niger Delta: rain falling through leaves, frog croaks, animal rustlings, and most importantly, the insistent rhythms of West African drums. According to an interview in the program (another perk of having time before the show), music supervisor Chief Ayanda Clarke brought together a percussion ensemble to record a piece that the Drummer (Olawale Oyenola) could solo over during the pre-show, resulting in a richly textured sonic experience for early audience members. Talking drums have been used in West Africa for centuries to communicate messages across long distances, mimicking human speech. The drums become the Greek chorus for The Swamp Dwellers, building tension, sending ominous warnings, and signaling the arrival of characters who are headed towards conflict.

The Swamp Dwellers is also visually arresting with a set designed by Jason Ardizzone-West that is taken up entirely by a bare house, made of slats of wood suspended over what appears to be oily water. Shrouded in mist, the house has both the feeling of an oasis and a survivor’s raft, creating the perfect visual metaphor for the lives of Alu and Makuri who have chosen to stay in their village while both of their sons have fled. It is in this precarious place that the characters come up against their limits, both socially constructed and physical.

Echebiri plays his role as the Beggar deftly, weaving stories and asking direct questions with the clarity of a man who was seen how people cloak inhumanity in kindness. As a blind man, he has been condemned to a life of asking for charity, and he questions why he cannot work the land like others. He asks Makuri for a plot of land, but is denied one because Makuri explains that the people of his village all have a special covenant with the Serpent to not let anyone else but them tend the swamp. Plus, they all will offer charity to blind men because they are good, godly people. The Beggar questions the logic of this since he has been made dependent on the gifts of people who may actually be terrible sinners, yet use charity to absolve their guilt. He wonders if accepting such alms transfers the dirt of their sins to him. Though the play was written in 1955 for Nigerian and English audiences, the moral questions feel especially relevant to the current stage of capitalism in America. I couldn’t help but think of corporations taking tax write-offs on charitable donations while compensating executives far above their average worker. The Beggar and Makuri ultimately don’t see eye-to-eye, so he turns to the disillusioned Igwezu. Together, they see beyond the conventional wisdom offered by Alu and Makuri and find ways to mock the institutions that dole out these empty promises. The question is: does playing the all-knowing jester ultimately win you anything?

This is not a show that speaks in loud, rallying cries, but through pensive monologues and Shakespearean dramatic ironies. At the end of the show, there is no way to neatly tie up all the loose ends or definitively say what happens next. Soyinka leaves us on unstable ground, and I admit that I initially felt unsatisfied by this. But that is the truth of change. There is no easy resolution, but a promise that what was started here will not fade away. It is impossible not to root for Igwezu, the young man who leaves the safety of his old home for whatever lies in the dangerous night, not knowing if he will make it, but understanding that there is no turning back. Soyinka is asking us all to take a leap of faith, and audiences will be better for it.

THE SWAMP DWELLERS– Written by Wole Soyinka, Directed by Awoye Timpo

WITH: Ato Blankson-Wood (Igwezu), Jenny Jules (Alu), Leon Addison Brown (Makuri), Joshua Echebiri (A Beggar), Chiké Okonkwo (Kadiye)

Scenic design by Jason Ardizzone-West; costume design by Qween Jean; lighting design by Seth Reiser; sound design by Rena Anakwe, music supervision by Chief Ayanda Clarke

At Theatre For A New Audience, 646-553-3880, https://tfana.org/. Through April 20. Running time: 70 minutes. No intermission.
